audits.title: Contingency plans for foot-and-mouth disease, classical swine fever and blutongue

recommendations.text: To transpose and implement Council Directives 2001/89/EC and 2000/75/EC immediately.
To address urgently the outstanding recommendations of mission DG(SANCO)/1143/99. Other contingency plans foreseen in EU legislation should be reviewed in the light of these recommendations.
To take action so that contingency plans are applied uniformly across the regions, and that disease planning, and the response to disease outbreaks, is co-ordinated effectively at national level.
To update existing contingency plans and manuals to take account of changes to EU-level guidelines and legislation.
To ensure that there are sufficient facilities, equipment and resources available at all levels to respond rapidly to outbreaks of major epizootic (OIE list A) diseases.

To finalise, approve and submit to the European Commission the contingency plan and manual for bluetongue. 10. ADDENDUM Despite a reminder, the Competent Authority has not responded to the draft report. 16
To complete transposition of all the provisions of Council Directive 64/432/EEC, as amended8.
To accelerate the introduction and full operation of the central database for bovine animals in order to have it approved by the European Commission as fully operational.
To establish an effective system to co-ordinate and audit activities at regional level in order to assure that all regional authorities comply with national and Community legislation9.

To improve the quality of epidemiological studies of infected herds; to consider the use of comparative tuberculin testing to exclude M. avium infections; to carry appropriate laboratory examinations to confirm M. bovis infections.

To promote the development of special plans for the eradication of bovine tuberculosis in regions with continuing high disease incidence or specific problems. An action plan, indicating the actions taken or planned to address the conclusions and recommendations (7.1.1. to 7.1.5) of this report, and including a timetable for the completion, should be submitted to the 7 In their response to the draft report the Italian Authorities noted that the difficulties encountered in Calabria concerning the order issued by the Mayor are a completely isolated case and that the regional authorities of Calabria already have taken steps to issue the necessary instructions. 8 See footnote 1, page 6. 9 See footnote 4, page 7. 14 Commission services within two months of receiving the translated final report. 7.2. To the Commission Services 7.2.1. To monitor closely the actions taken by the Italian competent authorities to address the above conclusions and recommendations, and to consider what further action is required if their response is found unsatisfactory. 15 Addendum Response of the Italian Authorities to the draft mission report The Italian Authorities offered comments on the draft report in a letter dated 15 May 2003. Where appropriate, these comments have been incorporated into the final report. They also provided an initial reaction to certain conclusions and recommendations in the report, in particular by providing details of action already taken, or to be taken, to correct deficiencies noted.

audits.title: Import controls on products of plant origin

recommendations.text: Enhance central guidance and policy to harmonise the rates of analyses for at risk products at the point of import.
Carry out analysis at laboratories that meet the operational criteria specified in Article 3 of Council Directive 93/99/EC.
Ensure that sampling of products of plant origin for mycotoxin analysis, and the preparation of samples in laboratories is carried out strictly in accordance with Directive 98/53/EC.
Allow importers the opportunity for second instance analysis as required by Article 7 (1) of Council Directive 89/397/EEC.

Develop analytical capability for irradiated foodstuff analysis and 3-MCPD to enhance controls on these at the point of import. Written assurances should be forwarded to the European Commission with regard to the above recommendations within two months of receipt of the final mission report. The Competent Authority should provide detailed information on the actions that will be taken and propose deadlines by which these actions will be completed. 27 9. ADDENDUM In their response to the draft report the Italian Authorities provided details of actions already taken, particularly at a regional level, to address the recommendations of the draft report. They also undertook to provide a comprehensive and co-ordinated response to all the recommendations on receipt of the final report. 28
Undertake an immediate vaccination campaign in the regions concerned, using the appropriate serotypes, in order to prevent any potential spread of BT.
Improve the CCA's coordination of application of the surveillance plan, taking account of the shortcomings noted during the mission.
Correct the deficiencies in transposing and applying the requirements for identification and registration of bovines and sheep/goats, in accordance with Community legislation.
Consider setting up an adequate sheep and goat identification system for implementation of the surveillance plan.

Continue with implementation of the BT Contingency Plan. The Italian authorities are asked to submit an action plan, including a timetable of measures in response to the report's conclusions and recommendations, to the Commission within two months of receipt of the final report. 9.2. To the Commission 9.2.1. Consider taking long-term measures to restrict the risk of BT spreading in the Mediterranean region. 9.2.2. Monitor action by the competent Italian authorities closely and take action as appropriate. 10. ADDENDUM In their reply of 6 February 2004, ref. DGVA.VIII-2603-P I.8.d/18 to the draft report, the competent Italian authorities commented on certain factual errors. 3

audits.title: Traceability of Beef and Beef products

recommendations.text: Without delay, introduce legal provisions enabling penalties to be imposed for infringements concerning the identification and registration of bovine animals and the labelling of bovine meat and meat products.
Strengthen the system of official controls to ensure compliance with regulations on the identification and registration of bovine animals and checks on their movements.

Ensure that the checks provided for under the system for the identification and registration of bovine animals are carried out in accordance with the minimum requirements set out in Regulation (EC) No 1082/2003. Make sure that only the checks carried out under the system are reported to the Commission.
Take the necessary steps to remedy the deficiencies observed as regards the identification and registration of bovine animals and checks on their movements.
Without delay, update the NDB and rectify the shortcomings noted during the mission.
Take all the necessary steps to ensure proper harmonisation of the procedures for capturing, processing and using information in the NDB.

Within a short period, develop a system of official controls in food establishments (from slaughterhouses to sales outlets) to ensure compliance with the regulations on the traceability and labelling of bovine meat and meat products.

Take the necessary steps to rectify the shortcomings noted at different points in the food chain (from slaughterhouses to sales outlets) as 2 regards the traceability and labelling of bovine meat and meat products (compulsory and voluntary labelling). Within two months of receiving the final report, the Italian authorities should forward to the Commission an action plan setting out a schedule for measures to be taken in response to the conclusion and recommendations in this report. 9. Addendum The Italian authorities submitted their comments on the contents of the draft report in two letters addressed to the Commission (dated 4 February 2004 and 30 January 2004, from the Ministry of Health and MIPAF respectively). In the same letters, they informed the FVO of the measures already taken or planned with a view to addressing certain conclusions and recommendations of the report. 3

To ensure that at least the minimum conditions for carrying out plant health checks in the Community are available at inspection posts, including access to destruction facilities and written up-to-date inspection guidelines, as required by Commission Directive 98/22/EC.

To ensure that inspectors have access to the whole consignment, adequate resources (including staff) and other facilities, in order that meticulous inspections can be carried out on plants, plant material and other objects listed in Annex V Part B of Council Directive 2000/29/EC, either in their entirety or by representative sample, as required by Article 13(1)(a) of the same Directive. In the case of Gioia Tauro seaport, this should include the equipment and facilities necessary to give inspectors adequate access to containerised consignments, in order to enable them to carry out the meticulous inspections referred to above.

To ensure that notifications of interceptions are sent to the Commission and other Member States within the timeframe envisaged in Article 2 of Commission Directive 94/3/EC, i.e. `no later than two working days after the date of interception and preferably more rapidly in the case of an interception having involved a refusal'.

To systematically endorse original phytosanitary certificates and re- forwarding certificates, received when the consignment is landed, with an entry stamp from the competent service showing at least the name of the service and the date of entry, as required by Article 12 (3) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC.

To increase the number of controls on consignments suspected or known to contain wood packing material that does not comply with the provisions of Commission Decision 2001/219/EC. The competent authorities in Italy are advised to consider: (6) harmonising and clarifying the policy and approach towards inspecting consignments of plants, plant material and other objects listed in Annex V Part B of Council Directive 2000/29/EC, that are being transhipped. (7) issuing publicity material on the concessions for travellers and carrying out controls on passengers to monitor compliance. (8) increasing the level of co-operation and communication with the Customs authorities, at national or central level. (9) establishing a national data base or harmonised data recording system to facilitate the exchange of data between the Regional and Central Services. 20 Italy is requested to report to the Commission two months after receipt of the final report, on action taken and/or planned on the recommendations. For planned action, a deadline for completion should be indicated. 21 Addendum At the time of finalising the report, the Italian authorities had not yet submitted any comments that addressed the recommendations contained in the draft report. 22

The competent authority should consider measures to improve the reliability of the information in the central database in order to be able to guarantee the date of birth and the presence and origin of the animals.

The competent authority should develop official control measures with regard to eligibility and traceability at the slaughterhouse, the channelling to and the 11 traceability at the butcher shop, in order to ensure that only eligible meat can effectively avail of the derogation.

The competent authority should develop official control measures at butcher shops approved for the removal of the vertebral column, to ensure that only eligible meat can avail the derogation for the removal of the vertebral column. With regard to the enforcement of the total feed ban

The competent authority should consider implementing the necessary enforcement measures of the official control of the total feed ban in order to prevent and detect cross-contamination of feed with PAP circulating in the Region of Tuscany. In particular, the correct application of the derogation for the use of PAPs as foreseen in Commission Decision 2001/9/EC should be ensured.

The competent authority should undertake to obtain the documentary evidence necessary to support the proposed date of the enforcement of an effective feed ban or, in its absence, to review this date on the basis of available documentary evidence.

The competent authority should consider additional control measures to further ensure the provision of safe feed to the herds covered by the requested derogation. With regard to BSE epidemiosurveillance

The competent authority should consider further improving the level of training and awareness for veterinary practitioners and the farming community as regards the clinical signs of BSE and their responsibilities in relation with the notification of BSE clinical suspects.

The competent authority should clarify the current provisions as regards the categorisation of the bovines sampled for BSE as laid down in Annex III, Chapter A, section I, point 2, to Regulation (EC) 999/2001, to all parties involved in the monitoring programme.
The competent authority should consider additional measures to ensure that all fallen animals over 24 months are notified and sampled without delay.

The competent authority should take measures to ensure that reliable and updated information on the reference bovine sub-populations and the sampling programme are available for the purpose of monitoring and supervision of the BSE epidemio-surveillance programme. ___________________ 12

audits.title: Animal welfare of laying hens, transport/salughter

recommendations.text: Amend legislation to comply with Directive 1999/74/EC, in particular to: · Prohibit bringing into service for the first time unenriched cages, even if they have been commissioned before 31 December 2002. · Bring stocking densities in line with Article 5 of Directive 99/74/EC and clarify contradictory requirements regarding cage area and area bellow the non-waste deflection plate. · Require claw shortening devices in cages and that this requirement should not depend on approval by an EU body. · Require litter and nests for alternative systems and only allow those systems operating before 3 August 1999 to operate at the higher stocking density of 12 birds/m2.
Registration of farms in compliance with 2002/4/EC is completed in all the regions.
Provide adequate guidelines, instructions and training to carry out checks.
Deficiencies such as overstocking are promptly corrected, not just at the end of the production cycle, and dissuasive measures are applied.

Take measures to ensure that each region submits results of inspections in compliance with Decision 2000/50/EC. 8.2. Regarding animal welfare during transport Take further measures to obtain from the regions the information required by Article 8 of Directive 91/628/EEC. In addition, this information should be used by all levels of the CA to monitor the quality of checks and ensure an adequate level of surveillance and enforcement. 8.3. Regarding animal welfare at slaughter (1) Adequate training and instructions are provided regarding welfare at slaughter. (2) All levels of the CA are involved in monitoring the quality of checks and ensuring an adequate level of surveillance and enforcement. 14 9. ADDENDUM In their comments on a draft version of this report, the CCA provided the following initial reaction to the recommendations: 9.1 Regardi 1(1), ¾ An explicit exclusion of such cages is already being examined by the Italian parliament. ¾ Italian legislation concerning non-waste deflection plates is not contradictory. The Italian government is awaiting the European Commission's response to their letter of 9 June 2004. ¾ Claw shortening devices used experimentally up to now in Italy are detrimental to hens' health and do not perform the required function satisfactorily. ¾ The adoption of a decree containing details of the technical characteristics of nests and litter areas is foreseen. (2) Regardi (2), no national list is available, but this will be provided for by an inter-ministerial decree, adopted in cooperation with the MAFP, on the subject of egg marketing (explanatory decree relating to Regulation (EC) No 2295/2003). (3) Regardi 1(3), ¾ On 8 July 2004 they wrote to the health departments of the regions and autonomous provinces to obtain a general picture of the level of compliance with the legislation. ¾ In addition a new ministerial circular is being prepared, which will provide precise information on inspection procedures, including a complete checklist. This new circular will also cover alternative systems. (4) Regardi 1(5), a report on the 2002­2003 period based on the available data is now being compiled and will be sent to the European Commission as soon as possible. 9.2 Regardi 2, a report based on the available data is now being prepared, covering the year 2002, and will be sent to the European Commission as soon as possible. Information covering 2003 is also being collected. 9.3 Regardi 3, the CCA will take action to prepare a circular containing appropriate instructions on this subject in order to ensure compliance with Community legislation. 15
To ensure that the official control programmes are drawn up taking account of all criteria set out in Art. 4 of Directive 95/53/EC. With regard to the application and supervision
To ensure effective application of the protocol of understanding as regards the co-ordination between the official control programmes at national and regional level.
To ensure uniform implementation of the official controls at regional and local levels.
To take measures which provide assurance that EU criteria for the authorisation of feed mills are met uniformly and on a continuous basis. With regard to the laboratories
To ensure that laboratories are designated on account of their capabilities.
To take appropriate actions to ensure that results of MAT are provided without undue delay and the backlog of samples is cleared.

To review the resources attributed with a view to ensure that CReAA fulfils its duties efficiently. __________________ 10 DG (SANCO)/7042/2004 ­ MR ­ Final ADDENDUM Response of the competent authorities to the recommendations Comments from the Italian CCA on the draft report were received on 18 June 2004, and included an outline of the actions planned and/or undertaken to address certai s contained in the report. These may be summarised as follows: · A meeting was held in May 2004 between the MdS and ICRF in order to adopt a common approach for the distribution of samples according to various parameters. More detailed instructions on risk analysis will be produced and distributed by September/October 2004. · The ICRF has produced guidance for the peripheral offices in order to ensure observance of Commissio s in this field, and to focus controls on premises considered at risk. · The implementation of the protocol of understanding at local and regional level will be evaluated by October 2004. · Visits to the feed mills concerned will start in September 2004. · Remedial actions will be undertaken in the IZSs displaying analytical problems. · Various actions will be undertaken in order to provide results in a timely fashion, including new organisational arrangements, training, a ring test, and procedures on the prioritisation of analyses. All samples taken by the ICRF during 2003 have been analysed and it is foreseen that the new structure will be fully operative by October 2004. · The financial needs of the CReAA will be reviewed by the end of this year. ____________________ 11

Given the lack of information at central level with regard to regional official control activities, the competent authorities should ensure that office VII, which now has responsibility for auditing food safety controls in the regions, has sufficient resources to evaluate regional official controls. Legislation

The competent authorities should resolve the apparent conflicts between older existing national legislation on hygiene of foodstuffs and Legislative Decree No. 155, transposing Council Directive 93/43/EEC. Good Hygiene Practice Guides

The competent authorities should encourage the dissemination of Good Hygiene Practice guides to the food sectors which require them, and where they exist give due consideration to such guides when carrying out official controls as foreseen in Art 8.1 of Council Directive 93/43/EEC. Laboratory Services

While it is acknowledged that the situation has improved with regard to the number of official laboratories which have been accredited the competent authorities should ensure that those remaining laboratories carrying out official analysis meet the requirements of Art.3 of Council Directive 93/99/EEC. Organisation of Controls
The competent authorities should ensure that official controls cover all aspects of Council Directive 93/43/EEC during inspections, as foreseen in Art 8(1) of that Directive.

The competent authorities should ensure that inspection staff receive adequate training in order to adequately assess whether the necessary monitoring and verification controls are being operated by food businesses. 20
The competent authorities should ensure that inspection staff have adequate equipment and protective clothing with which to carry out controls. Enforcement

The competent authorities should ensure that food premises are inspected at a frequency which has regard to the risk associated with the premises as foreseen in Art 8(2) of Council Directive 93/43/EEC. RASFF

The competent authorities should ensure that the regional authorities develop appropriate procedures to ensure the efficient operation of the RASFF system between the regional and central level. A programme in response to these recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission Services within a period of two months after the dispatch of the final translated report. 21 ADDENDUM In their response to first recommendation in the draft report, the Italian authorities stated that "In the 2004 audit programme Office VII included three regions for official control of foodstuff hygiene and four regions for the alert system.The aim of this programme is to check the approach, coordination and control of the regions and of the activities programmed and carried out by the local ASLs. 22
To put an effective system in place to co-ordinate and audit activities at regional level in the sector of eradication programmes.
To continue with implementation of the sheep and goat brucellosis eradication programme in Italy.

To implement the special plan for the eradication of sheep and goat brucellosis in Sicily as approved in the framework of the Italian programme for the eradication of ovine and caprine bucellosis in Commission Decision 2003/849/EC.
To address the deficiencies in the implementation of the current eradication programme identified in Sicily.

To urgently review existing national and regional legislation related to eradication of buffalo brucellosis and to ensure that only legislation, conforming to EU standards (in particular with regard to Council Directive 92/46/EEC and Council Directive 78/52/EEC) is in force.

To fully implement and enforce all elements of the EU approved and EU co-financed national and regional eradication programme for buffalo brucellosis as specified in Article 72 (1) of Commission Decision 2003/849/EC without delay.

To urgently implement effective controls over milk from brucella infected dairy buffalo and over milk from healthy buffalo on not Officially Brucellosis Free/Brucellosis Free holdings. To ensure that such milk is treated in conformity with Community requirements as specified in Article 3 of Council Directive 92/46/EEC.

To address the problems with regard to animal identification and movement controls noted during the course of this mission, in particular with regard to the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 and Council Directive 92/102/EEC. The Italian authorities should submit an action plan, detailing the actions taken, and planned, to address the above recommendations within one month of receiving the draft translated report. 10.2. To the Commission Services (1) To review the action plan submitted by the Italian CA. (2) To consider further measures in light of the failure of Campania to implement the approved eradication programme for buffalo brucellosis and their continued failure to comply with relevant EU requirements, in particular as regards the use of milk for human consumption and the retention of brucella reactors. 24 ADDENDUM In their comments on the draft report of 5 August 2004 the Italian competent authorities indicated the following action in response to certain findings: 1. With regard to the document management at the local health authority in Caltanissetta, a new filing system has been introduced. 2. The shortcomings detected in the slaughterhouse visited in Sicily have been rectified. 3. Farms visited during the mission in Sicily have been re-visited by the CA and shortcomings with regard to small ruminants have been rectified. 4. With regard to the formal repeal of Regional Law n. 30 of 31 December 2003 the health and agricultural committees of the Regional Council have approved the draft repeal law, which requires only final approval by the Regional Council at this stage. 25

Regular and systematic surveys are carried out in all regions and that the results of these are submitted to the Commission annually, in order to comply with Article 2(1)h of Council Directive 2000/29/EC.
Eradication measures are always imposed following an outbreak of Citrus tristeza virus. These measures should be imposed without delay.

Nurseries producing planting material and the surrounding areas are known to be free from Citrus tristeza virus, or ensure that the conditions of either point 10(b) or point 10(c) of Annex IV Part A section II to Council Directive 2000/29/EC are complied with, before plant passports are issued for plants of Citrus, Fortunella, Poncirus and their hybrids.
The SCA has the necessary powers and resources to enable it to effectively co-ordinate the work of the RPS, and to fulfil the role envisaged in Article 1(4) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC.

The RPS have adequate human and financial resources to enable them to carry out regular and systematic surveys for CTV and to implement appropriate measures following confirmation of an outbreak. 19 The competent authority in Italy is advised to consider:

Whether those regions that have not carried out a regular and systematic survey for CTV and submitted the results of these surveys, or areas/regions where an outbreak of CTV has been confirmed and no eradication measures have been taken, should be removed from the protected zone.

Increasing the level and effectiveness of the collaboration and exchange of information between the RPS, in particular on the issue of Citrus tristeza virus, and possible changes to the Ministerial Decree.

Whether the Ministerial Decree should be changed, in the light of practical experience and resource limitations, to enable the available resources to be used optimally and eradication measures to be imposed as soon as possible after the confirmation of an outbreak. Italy is requested to report to the Commission two months after receipt of the final translated report, on action planned or taken to address the recommendations. For planned action, a deadline for completion should be indicated. 20 ADDENDUM The Italian authorities did not submit any comments on the draft report or a response to the recommendations. 21

In order to ensure that Commission Decision 2004/92/EC is correctly applied and enforced, the competent authorities should address the issue of lack of co-ordination between the regional Health authorities, the Anti Adulteration and Health body of the Military police, and the Fraud Suppression Inspectorate of the Ministry of Agriculture, concerning the sampling for Sudan I-IV on the market place. In addition, the competent authorities should ensure the collation of data from all 19 regional Health authorities.
The competent authorities should ensure better co-ordination between the regional health authorities in particular with respect to ensuring that all contaminated products are traced and destroyed.

The competent authorities should ensure that Maritime Frontier Offices are provided with adequate guidance to enforce Community legislation, in particular with regard to the provisions of Art 2(3) of Commission Decision 2004/92/EC concerning the responsibilities of importers.

The competent authorities should urgently ensure that there is adequate analytical capability for samples which are taken on the market and at the point of entry, and that methods are developed and validated for Sudan I- IV to ensure that the requirements of Art.3 of Commission Decision 2004/92/EC are complied with.

The competent authorities should ensure that there is adequate procedures in place at regional level to ensure the timely transmission of rapid alerts to central level. An action plan in response to these recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission Services within a period of two months after the dispatch of the final translated report. 19 9. ADDENDUM Regarding the recommendations made in the draft report, the following initial comments were provided in relation to actions that have been or will be take (3): "a letter has been sent to all USMA offices concerning further clarification of the text of Decision 2004/92/EC relating to the responsibility of importers, and the opportunity is also being taken to provide further information on the clearing process." Recommendation(4): "the Region of Tuscany points out that the analysis method adopted by the ARPA Laboratory at Livorno for Sudan II, III and IV dyes has been operational since 2.04.2004." 20

audits.title: Residues and Contaminants in live animals and animal products, including controls on veterinary medicinal products

recommendations.text: Ensure that all mandatory substance groups in all species/commodities are tested for in accordance with Council Directive 96/23/EC.
Extend the scope of testing, taking into account relevant factors, including usage patterns of VMPs. 16

Improve communication channels between all levels to allow the CCA to have an up to date overview of progress made in the execution of the NRCP by the regional and local services. With regard to the laboratories
Ensure that the NRL is accredited to ISO 17025 and fulfils all requirements as laid out in Article 14 of Council Directive 96/23/EC.
Ensure that analytical methods for Group A substances are validated in accordance with Commission Decision 2002/657/EC and provide a timetable for this activity.
Ensure that all analytical methods used for the NRCP are elaborated in SOP format and are fully validated in accordance with Community legislation.
Increase the number of accredited and fully validated analytical methods in the NRL and in control laboratories.
Minimise the turnaround time for confirmed non-compliant results and follow-up analyses. With regard to VMPs
Ensure that an updated register of all authorised VMPs is available to the CA.
Ensure that batch numbers are recorded at wholesale and retail levels in accordance with national legislation;

Implement the requirements for own-control in accordance with Council Directive 90/167/EC also for on-farm mixing of medicated feed. 9. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT 7263/2004 Competent Autority response to the draft report. The Italian authorities stated in their written comments (dated 9.12.2004) on the draft report that several actions had been taken in response to findings made during the mission. These actions are detailed in footnotes inserted at the relevant points of this report. Evaluation of the actions taken and the planned will be made after receipt of the comprehensive action plan, which the competent authorities are invited to provide within 25 working days of receipt of the translated final mission report.
To ensure adequate training for staff at CCA level on animal nutrition issues.

To ensure that the CCA can avail of all relevant information in the Regions as regards implementation of the relevant measures in the field of animal nutrition, and to guarantee their compliance with EU requirements. With regard to the official inspections in the feed sector
To ensure that, where consideration is given to the criteria referred to in Art. 4 of Directive 95/53/EC, this is documented.
To ensure that controls on imports are adequately and uniformly implemented.
To ensure official controls to representatives of establishments located in third countries, as defined in Art. 6 of Directive 98/51/EC.
To continue progress in the monitoring of the laboratory network and that its supervisory authority is designated. 11 With regard to the approval and registration of E/I
To ensure that controls on the conditions for the legal use of forbidden additives are complied with. 12

The competent authorities of Italy should ensure that a. results on inspections of plant protection products and b. results on residue monitoring are reported from every region to the central authorities within the time outlined by the specific legislation. This should be 22 enforced, so that the information forwarded to the European Commission is complete and representative for the country.

Consideration should be given to improving co-ordination between parallel activities concerning inspections and residue monitoring by the Services of the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Agriculture and the NAS with a view to enhancing the effectiveness of the control systems.

The competent authorities should lay down clear specifications regarding sampling under the co-ordinated Community monitoring programme, in terms of exact crop-commodity sample numbers to be taken by each region. This should ensure representative sampling all over the country.

The accreditation of the laboratories carrying out pesticide residue analysis should be ensured as quickly as possible. The competent authorities should ensure that participation in the co-ordinated Community monitoring programme is restricted to laboratories which are accredited and which have participated in a previous round, or which will participate in the next round, of the European Proficiency testing. The implementation of the EU guidelines on Quality Control procedures should be encouraged.

The work towards accreditation of laboratories analysing formulations should be continued. Emphasis should be put on validation of formulation analysis methods. Taking part in Proficiency testing and working according to CIPAC methods would be desirable for the formulation laboratories.
The competent authorities should improve the communication between the different competent authorities, speeding up the transmission of information and informing all relevant services.

The competent authorities should ensure that the label and the authorisation status of plant protection products are adequately checked at market and user levels to prevent unauthorised uses of pesticides.

The range of pesticide substances, and their metabolites, being sought in the laboratories should be increased to allow adequate enforcement of pesticide MRLs as specified in Council Directives 76/895/EEC, 86/362/EEC and 90/642/EEC as amended.
The time-lapse between sampling and analysis for pesticide residues should be such as to allow adequate enforcement and follow-up actions, as well as any necessary emergency measures.
A decision that a lot is non-compliant should take into account the accuracy and precision of analysis, in accordance with Commission Directive 2002/63/EC, Annex I, point 5.
In cases of MRL infringements, the competent authorities should ensure that systematic consumer risk assessments for adults and children are conducted.

The competent authorities should ensure that any information relating to a risk to human health from pesticide residues is notified to the national contact point for the Rapid Alert System, and to the European Commission in accordance with Article 50 of Regulation (EC) No. 178/2002 of the European Parliament and the Council. 23 An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. ADDENDUM Regarding the recommendations made in the draft report, initial comments were provided in relation to actions that have been or will be taken. With regard to recommendation (1), the Italian authorities stated that the regional authorities have asked all ARPA laboratories to respect the deadlines for electronic submission of data on the analyses and controls to the Ministry of Health. The Region of Sicily has launched all procedures and formalities necessary to ensure implementation of the control plans both for pesticide residues and for the formulations. With regard to recommendation (4), the Region of Puglia intends to reinforce the staff of the Bari provincial department. In addition, for the Bari and Foggia laboratories the procedure for accreditation by the National Health Institute is now in progress and the Brindisi laboratory has already obtained accreditation. 24
Take urgent measures to ensure that disinfection principles and procedures (as described in Annex II of Council Directive 2002/60/EC) are known, correctly applied and documented;

Ensure close cooperation among the various administrative and professional bodies (at national, regional and local level) which may play a role in prompt and efficient implementation of the control measures related to the control of ASF, and ensure that those responsible all share the same view about the priority which has to be given to this aim;

Ensure that local human resources and equipment are adequate for a complete and strict implementation, supervision and control of the measures to be taken in case of suspicion or confirmation of outbreaks of ASF; apply and control corrective actions in case of identification of deficiencies; 33 In their comments to the draft report the CA of Sardinia stated that the problem of identifying meat that is eligible for movements outside the territory of Sardinia is resolved by internal procedures, validated by the competent veterinary service and adopted by the various slaughterhouse facilities. These provide for various measures : separate slaughter of pigs eligible for movements outside Sardinia (in some cases also separate slaughtering days), storage of meat in separate store rooms, locking these rooms under the supervision of the OV, shipment of eligible meat only after the health certificate to be drawn up on loading has been issued. 26

Ensure a rapid and complete transmission of information to all the concerned bodies, including the European Commission and other countries, in line with the provisions of Council Directive 82/894/EEC and article 3 of Council Directive 2002/60/EC;

Set up and implement an action plan to regularise the situation regarding holding registration and movement control at least in conformity with Council Directive 92/102/EEC; update the register database in accordance with provisions of Commission Decision 2000/678/EC so that it can be used for the determination of restriction zones and its control;

Implement a comprehensive eradication plan for the feral pig population in accordance with article 16 of Council Directive 2002/60/EC, integrating the possible links with free-ranging pigs, the results of the serosurveillance campaigns in wild boars, and investigation about possible vectors;

Ensure that carcasses and fresh meat obtained from pigs which do not fulfil the requirements of Commission Decision 2003/514/EC are not given the health mark provided for in Chapter XI of Annex I of the Directive 64/433/EEC, as stated in Council Directive 72/461/EEC;
Apply control measures over catering waste, as required by article 24 of Council Directive 2001/89/EC;
Revise the system of compensation for owners of pigs slaughtered in accordance with Council Directive 2002/60/EC so as to ensure a swift but adequate compensation;

Consider the development of a comprehensive and detailed action plan for eradication of ASF in Sardinia, addressing all the identified critical points and evaluating the resources needed. ADDENDUM The competent authorities by means of a fax received from the Ministry of Health, on 07.04.2005, provided their comments and included also assurances from the competent authorities of Sardinia that the recommendations in the report have been addressed in the ASF eradication plan for 2005. 27

audits.title: Import Controls and Border Inspection Posts

recommendations.text: To consider amending the approval for the below mentioned BIPs, as follows: (1) - BIP Roma-Fiumicino IC Cargo City ADR (HC)(2), NHC(2) (2) - BIP Gioia Tauro HC, NHC-T(FR), NHC-NT 14 (3) - BIP Ancona airport HC(2), NHC(2) (4) - BIP Ancona port: HC(2) (5) - BIP Milano-Malpensa IC Cargo City HC(2), NHC(2), O IC Magazzini aeroportuali as three ICs: (IC1 NHC; IC2 HC-T(2), O; IC3 U, E) provided that all deficiencies found are corrected for all BIPs and ICs.
To consider amending the approvals, as follows: (1) - BIP Ancona port IC1 HC(2), IC2 NHC provided that all deficiencies found in IC2 are corrected.

To consider the withdrawal of the approval of the IC Cargo City ADR in Roma Fiumicino, IC Cargo City in Milano-Malpensa, IC Porto di Voltri in Genova, BIP Gioia Tauro and BIP Ancona airport, if satisfactory guarantees in relation to the correction of the deficiencies found are not received from the CCA within 6 months of the receipt of the translated final report.
For BIPs not visited, to consider delisting Venezia port and the category other animals (O) from Reggio Calabria as no satisfactory guarantees were given for these facilities.

To consider further development of TRACES in relation to difficulties noted by the Italian authorities for completion of sampling checks in the second part of the CVED. 15 ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7529/2005 In response to the recommendations in the report the CCA indicated that it is already taking action to follow up the FVO's recommendations within the stated time limits and will provide the relevant information; they also indicated the followi s with regard to the competent authorities: 5.1.1 Organisation of veterinary administration: The Ministerial Decree of 30 December 2004 instituted territorial conferences of the field office Directors and the Decree of 20 April 2005 set up the central coordinating committee for these conferences. Among the goals pursued is better cooperation between the authorities operating within the same territorial unit (primarily the BIPs and the port and airport health offices, but also the other authorities involved, such as the customs, port and airport authorities, CITES, etc.). Periodic meetings have been held at territorial level and problems are then discussed in the central coordinating committee, which meets monthly at central level. Proposals and operational protocols in the various sectors are discussed and scrutinised in this forum. One of the first points on the agenda was the production of an operational protocol, in cooperation with the port and airport health offices, for treatment of galley waste. 5.1.2.1 Legislation: The Decree transposing Council Directive 2002/99/EC is in course of publication in the Official Gazette; after the mission the CCA provided the information that the Decree no 117 of 27 May 2005 was published on 02.07.2005. The Interministerial Decree of 20 April 2005 applying Regulation (EC) 998/2003 was published in General Series No 221 of the Official Gazette of the Italian Republic of 22 September 2005. For the Decision 2002/349/EC, the BIPs have implemented this Decision properly from the veterinary point of view, either taking account of it for the controls or by informing the competent customs offices. 5.1.3 Official publication 1999/C 356/02: As regards specimens included in the lists of the CITES and of Regulation (EC) No 338/97 animals can be imported at the customs offices, solely and exclusively if there is a BIP authorised for live animal controls at the same location. At the CITES entry points where there is no BIP it is permissible to introduce other articles not subject to veterinary inspection and non-commercial pet animals accompanying passengers covered by the Regulation (EC) No 998/2003. 5.1.4 Supervision of the BIPs: A supervision programme has been drawn up and is already under way. The first phase of the programme was carried out with the production of a questionnaire, which is used to acquire information preparatory to subsequent inspections and will also be used for an initial assessment of the BIP. Its design takes account of the FVO's observations during the recent mission in 2005. The following BIPs will be inspected in the second half of the year: BIP Bari port, BIP Milano Linate airport, BIP Venezia port, BIP Venezia airport, BIP Trieste port, BIP Palermo port, BIP Palermo airport, BIP Trapani port. 5.1.5 Co-operation between different authorities: The Customs agency provided the information that effective and synergic cooperation has been established with the Ministry of Health and for that aim a Presidential and Cabinet Decree has been prepared with provisions implementing decree-Law 35 of 14 March 2005, including the creation of a "one-stop shop", highlighting the function of the Customs agency in relation to the various authorities involved in the clearance procedure. Recommendations with regard to the infrastructure: 16 5.2.2 Facilities, equipment, hygiene: The BIP Venezia port has reported that it now satisfies the requirements for HC-T and NHC-T products and a CCA inspection is planned in the coming months. The BIP Reggio Calabria, in the current circumstances, approval for the category "O animals" should be suspended. For the BIP Milano Malpensa the CCA will shortly provide further explanations. For the BIP Roma Fiumicino the points raised for its approval have been carefully checked and suitable changes were made by the head of the BIP. The CCA is carrying out an assessment, the results of which will be forwarded within the prescribed time. For the BIP Genova the CCA agrees that the IC Vado Ligure should be recognised as a BIP in its own. For the BIP Gioia Tauro the CCA stated that the movement of consignments from the terminal to the BIP is without leaving the customs area and it is only after the CVED has been duly issued, on completion of the whole customs procedure, that they can leave the customs area. For the BIP Ancona, where consignments seized by the customs were found to be stored, steps have already been taken to ensure that such goods are stored in other premises not belonging to the BIP. The hygiene deficiencies noted have already been wholly or partly rectified. The CCA stated overall that concerning the changes in the categories of approval indicated for some BIPs, the necessary checks are being made, in conjunction with the authorities concerned, taking account of the FVO's comments and suggestio s with regard to the procedures: 5.2.6 procedures: The problem of transhipments in the BIP Gioia Tauro will be dealt with at local and central level, involving the other competent authorities (customs) in producing a control system in line with Community legislation. The CCA will approach the Customs Agency to seek territorial-level coordination between the customs and the BIP Gioia Tauro to devise health control procedures for transit/transhipment goods. Special manuals of procedures for all Italian BIPs will result from the work already started by the coordinating bodies. The BIP Malpensa keeps the live animal registers in the offices of the facilities authorised for live animals. The BIP Genova was not informed with regard to illegal imports of protected live animals and subsequently has taken action to ensure better coordination with CITES and the customs so that illegal imports can be checked more effectively. The ship supplier supplying ships in Gioia Tauro was inspected by the official veterinary services ASL and the veterinary office for intra-community trade, which found that the contained goods were in conformity with the Community legislation. 3.3 procedures-Veterinary checks: All the points raised in connection with procedures have been assessed by the CCA and the BIPs. Some observations will have to be looked into in greater depth in order to produce programmes for improving all import control activities.

audits.title: Illegal Imports of products of animal origin and live animals

recommendations.text: Competent authorities The "DGSVA" from the "Ministry of Health" (MH) is responsible for the import controls at the BIPs. The Customs authorities from the Customs Agency of the "Ministry of Economic Affairs and Finance" (MEF) execute import controls for freight and supervise BIP and non-BIP crossing points for personal baggage checks, non-commercial pet animals, and check for illegal imports of veterinary products and live animals. In particular for illegal imports the antifraud service "SVAD" is responsible with its Central Antifraud office which assists the Director of the Customs Agency. For CITES live animals and products of animal origin the Customs, the "Forestry Department of the Ministry of Agriculture" (FDMA), and a scientific committee of the "Ministry of Environment" and the "Ministry of Foreign Trade" are responsible. The "ASL" (Local Health Unit) belonging to the provinces of the regions are veterinary services responsible to investigate inland the illegally imported consignments. "UVAC" (Veterinary Offices for Community Affairs) are veterinary services in the provinces belonging to the "Ministry of Health" and are responsible for supervising ASLs.

Legislative and administrative measures ¾ Implementation of Commission Decision 2002/995/EC(e) for personal baggage imports of products of animal origin was delayed (implemented by decree of 10 March 2004 signed by both MH and MEF). ¾ Regulation (EC) No 745/2004, which replaced the above Decision has not been fully implemented: it is not planned to issue an implementing decree. However, some elements of the regulation have been implemented by means of amendments to the above mentioned decree (administrative circular on 13 May 2004 from the MH and circular 59/D from MEF on 14.10.2004). ¾ Circular 59/D is not sufficiently detailed and, as a consequence, implementation of legislation is not harmonised in all the Regions visited. 2 ¾ There are no detailed instructions to customs and the list of BIPs points of entry in the circular dated 14.10.2004 is not in accordance with Commission Decision 2001/881/EC(f) (e.g. Cagliari, Catania, Gorizia, Prosecco are included as BIPs in the customs' circular). ¾ For the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 no penalties are foreseen for travellers(2). ¾ Regulation (EC) No 998/2003(g) for non-commercial movement of pet animals has not yet been implemented as it is still under review(3). ¾ Commission Decision 2002/349/EC(h) for the positive list of products subject to veterinary checks has not yet been implemented and there is no positive list at customs (see also point 5.2.1).

Co-operation between different authorities ¾ There is no formal agreement between Customs and DGSVA on co-operation and allocation of responsibilities. Customs controls of veterinary products in personal baggage and live animals are not co-ordinated with the veterinary services. The veterinary services do not have access to Customs databases. ¾ While data relating to controls carried out and seizures of illegal imports (freight, personal baggage, non commercial pet animals, including CITES live animals and products) is collected by Customs at local level, the system is not uniform and is not made available on a national basis to the CCA. ¾ Levels of co-operation are insufficient with airport authorities (e.g. out-of-date posters displayed) and with air transport operators (e.g. information leaflets out-of-date and/or not provided to passengers; lack of in-flight announcements). 5.2. CHECKS ON ILLEGAL IMPORTS "Illegal imports" in the context of this report, is the introduction onto the territory of the Community of products of animal origin or live animals which, either accidentally or intentionally, have not been subject to, and cleared following, the veterinary checks foreseen in Community legislation. 5.2.1. Organisation and operation of Customs Customs authorities are part of the MEF, operating under a central General Directorate and for BIP matters the administrative section "Checks and Control" of the Customs Agency is responsible. At peripheral level they are organised in the relevant 20 Regions, Provinces (4 - 5 Directorates per Region) and Operational Units (several per Directorate), all belonging to the MEF. SVAD has independent central and peripheral offices. ¾ Responsibilities are not clearly defined for products of animal origin in personal baggage, non-commercial pets and CITES live animals and products (2) In their comments to the draft report the CCA stated that the requirement for the confiscated products to be destroyed and the costs borne by the holder or any other person responsible for the goods is an indirect penalty. (3) In their comments to the draft report the CCA stated that on 18 February 2005 the Customs Agency was sent a draft circular setting out operational instructions on how to carry out checks on the animals covered by Regulation (EC) No 998/2003 at all entry points. 3 of animal origin and some overlapping was noted between the competent authorities involved. ¾ Customs controls on personal luggage and parcel-post sent to private persons are based on a circular issued by MEF. ¾ No specific measures have been introduced to detect illegal imports of animals and animal products and staff have been specifically allocated to these tasks which are integrated into general Customs tasks. ¾ The Customs authorities do not accept full responsibility for the checks and they stated that if products of animal origin are found they would call the veterinarians of the BIPs. Such contacts were very rare or did not occur, in particular at the non-BIP points of entry. ¾ No system is in place to ensure that customs have current information to use in their risk assessment in relation to the disease risk posed by third countries. No lists of authorised third countries are available to customs. ¾ There is no customs database for seized personal baggage consignments nor are there records at central level. SVAD at central level is responsible for collecting data for seized illegal imports of products of animal origin in personal baggage. There was no detailed information on the controls carried out, in particular in accordance to Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004, and no central Customs authority was responsible for collection of this information(4). ¾ For non-commercial pet animals customs guidelines are outdated, as Regulation (EC) No 998/2003 is not yet implemented and responsibility for these controls is unclear. A list of 381 points of entry for non-commercial pet animals was provided although these were not adequately equipped for documentary and identity checks to be carried out (no model certificate, no microchip reader). ¾ For freight consignments, customs receive a summary declaration containing general information in form of an unloading list. After unloading, they receive the cargo-manifest, mostly electronically. ¾ In the customs database used for free release of consignments "AIDA" the relevant CN-codes were not linked with the requirements for veterinary checks, as the positive list of the Decision 2002/349/EC has not yet been implemented by customs and no guidelines had been received for its implementation. The customs database used for transit to third countries and clearance in other Member States "CNTS" does not contain a link to veterinary checks. ¾ CITES products and live animals are under customs control. Customs stated that in case of doubts for live animals and products of animal origin they inform the FDMA who is responsible. The BIP would not be informed as no CVED is required. (4) In their comments to the draft report the Customs authorities stated that the abandonment of products of animal origin contained in travellers' personal baggage can take place before passengers arrive at the customs area. In such cases, nothing can be done, given that the Customs Authority cannot be held responsible for the behaviour of travellers outside their areas. If goods are abandoned after the baggage check or following the passenger's declaration, a record is taken of the abandonment and the goods are destroyed in accordance with the national legislation in force. Reports constitute data entered into a system for subsequent processing. 4 5.2.2. Imports of products for personal consumption 5.2.2.1.Background Customs stated that they are responsible for personal baggage checks of travellers for products of animal origin but if these are found the follow up action is up to the BIP veterinarian. However, this is not applied at the non-BIP points of entry. ¾ No specific training was provided for customs for checks for illegal imports of products of animal origin for personal consumption and for non-commercial pet animals. 5.2.2.2.Information to passengers/travellers ¾ Posters are displayed in the airports and in one sea-port visited. Some posters were out-of-date. The CCA could not confirm that posters are displayed in all points of entry from third countries (e.g. in ports etc). ¾ The airport/port operators do not provide information to passengers by other means (e.g. in-flight announcements or leaflets). ¾ The leaflet distributed to passengers by the cruise company, was not updated and not in accordance with Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 (all meat, milk and their products were prohibited). ¾ The leaflets distributed by customs were not updated, only in Italian language and in some cases the information was not in accordance with Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. 5.2.2.3.Organisation of controls/sanctions ¾ Customs stated that they are permanently present and control all points of entry, either BIPs or non-BIPs for all arriving means of transport. However, this did not apply for points of entry for sailing boats, where no controls are carried out for products of animal origin. ¾ Information was not available about the number of points of entry for products in personal baggage, nor for mail posts. ¾ The CCA and Customs did not have information about the controls carried out and the consignments seized/abandoned in the individual points of entry for the whole country. There was limited information available at local level about the checks carried out for personal luggage at the ports, either BIPs or non-BIP points of entry. ¾ Instructions for Customs (Circular 59/D) are not sufficiently detailed as they do not specify which products from which countries are permitted. Customs at local level were unclear as to the actions to be taken when products of animal origin were detected or surrendered: in some cases they required veterinary certificates for all products of animal origin consignments in personal baggage; for fishery products under 1 kg Customs, in some places, permit the import from any third country and in others, they either require a veterinary certificate or do not permit the import, or in non-BIP points of entry they insist on destruction. Some BIPs had issued guidelines to the local Customs authorities but these were not up-to-date. ¾ Customs stated that they have to ask the passenger if they have illegal product in personal baggage and if it is voluntary abandoned, the product is not seized and customs have to store the product for 3 months giving the possibility to the passenger to take the product back to the relevant third country of origin. Many 5 of these consignments were stored at the BIP-storages. Records for these cases were kept in one point of entry visited but in other points of entry no such records were kept. ¾ If the passenger declares falsely or customs discover by chance an illegal import then the consignment is seized. No penalties are imposed (as required by Article 4 paragraph 3 of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 and by Article 17(5) of Directive 97/78/EC). ¾ In the entry points where there were no stores, no waste bins as foreseen in Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 are provided. Travellers are not liable for the cost of destruction of seized or surrendered product. ¾ No large volumes of personal baggage are screened by customs to detect illegal consignments of meat and meat products and milk and milk products. ¾ For CITES live animals and products of animal origin there was an overview for the number of consignments seized (in 2004: 108 consignments of live animals, 389 consignments of dead animals and 4412 consignments of products of animal origin) but not for the controls carried out by customs in all points of entry. ¾ There is no or incomplete supervision by customs for the destruction of seized consignments in the different points of entry visited and for CITES animals and products, BIP staff did not know the fate of these seized consignments. ¾ Where seized consignments had been incinerated, no written confirmation was kept by Customs. It was not known if such records are kept by the airport- operators. It was not clarified if the incinerator used for the destruction of the consignments is approved in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002(i). At the three BIP-airport-entry-points visited Customs use locally developed risk based approaches to target illegal consignments (e.g. drugs, weapons, counterfeited products) and specific third countries. ¾ However, there was no overview of the checks carried out for each third country and no records or no results of the checks were available per third country, which then could be used for further risk analysis. ¾ There are no animal health risk criteria provided for products of animal origin. When passengers come from a risk country chosen at local level e.g. China, Senegal, then 15% of baggages might be opened. Two or three times per week they find some illegal personal luggage imports of products of animal origin. ¾ No equipment (e.g. scanning, sniffer dogs) is used for the screening of large volumes of personal baggage of travellers for products of animal origin. The proportion of baggage open varies depending on the perceived risk: routine ­ 2%; risk countries ­ 25 %; interline EU airports baggages ­ 30 %. For unaccompanied baggage 1 % is scanned. ¾ Specific findings for Roma-Fiumicino: - For seized consignments the Customs complete a report and notify the sanitary service of the airport in order to destroy the consignments. Weights/quantities/descriptions of product are not recorded by the airport authorities in the delivery documents which accompany product sent for destruction. No written confirmation of destruction is received by Customs 6 - In 2004, 750 illegal consignments of products of animal origin (about 4 - 5 tonnes) were seized by customs or abandoned by travellers from their personal baggage. - A general overview of CITES consignments of live animals, dead animals and products of animal origin controlled and seized by customs during 2004 (about 200 consignments were seized in 2004) was available. - No CVEDs were issued as described in report 7529/2005. ¾ Specific findings for Ancona airport: - 169 consignments, about 600 kg, were found as illegal imports in personal baggage of travellers in 2004. Two consignments of CITES skins were seized in 2004. The consignments were sterilised in a garbage centre near the BIP and then sent to landfill. It was not known if the sterilising facilities and landfill were approved under EU provisions. In January 2005 33 consignments were found. - For each seized consignment a receipt was given to the passenger and there were records kept by customs which are sent every month to the region; however, it was not known if these are sent to central level of customs. No records of checks are kept per third country of origin. There were no detailed rules given from central level of customs concerning the procedure for records and seizures and customs had developed their own system based on their own initiative. ¾ In two BIP-port-entry-points visited similar findings as above were noted. Additionally, - X-rays are used in 5 % of baggage arriving by ferries. Some baggage is opened depending on the season (from 30 % to 100 %). No illegal imports of products of animal origin in passenger baggage was found by Customs in 2004 in Ancona. - 2 ­ 3 % of baggages from ferries and cruise ships from third countries were physically checked, based on risk analyses, for drugs and CITES- consignments. No scanners and sniffer dogs were used for products of animal origin. ¾ At a non-BIP-port-entry-point (Savona) in 2004, approximately 200 cruise ships (500000 passengers) arrived from third country and EU ports in the Mediterranean. Customs are permanently present for the controls. No consignments of products of animal origin were found in personal luggage in 2004. - About 25-30 % of baggage is scanned and 3-4 % of baggage is opened. However, the scanner used is a of metal detector and the dogs used are trained for narcotic drugs. Products of animal origin in personal baggage is not a target and there is no risk profile of third countries. The positive list of Commission Decision 2002/349/EC was not available on-the-spot, nor was there a list of authorised countries. - There are no waste bins for the collection of seized/abandoned products of animal origin. No procedure is foreseen for the destruction of such consignments (USMAF is the responsible authority). - The point of entry was also approved for CITES live animals and products of animal origin, the responsible authority is Customs and if there is any 7 problem they ask the FDMA (the last seized consignment was turtle shells in 2001 but there were no records kept), no veterinary staff is contacted for CITES checks for products subject to veterinary checks. 5.2.3. Import and transit of freight ¾ The selection of consignments subject to veterinary checks is not reliable as relevant Customs databases are not linked with the requirements for veterinary checks, as described in report 7529/2005. ¾ Customs are not involved in the identification and selection of veterinary consignments and it is not ensured that relevant consignments have a CVED, when they are released for importation or transit by Customs. ¾ Consignments may be released without the required veterinary checks having been performed. This has been demonstrated by the SVAD who carry out periodic checks at destination and, from time to time, find some consignments inland having escaped veterinary checks at the border. No detailed information was given to local customs and BIP authorities from central level as to what happened with the consignments found. ¾ Consignments can be stored up to 45 days in temporary Customs warehouses without veterinary checks performed. ¾ Veterinary checks for transhipments are not carried at the BIP in accordance with the provisions of Commission Decision 2000/25/EC(j), as described in report 7529/2005. ¾ Customs carry out from about 1% to 5% physical checks and from about 0.0002% to 3% scanning. Documentary checks range from about 15% to 50% in the different entry points visited. No checks are carried out on about 40% to 80% of the consignments received. ¾ Customs find a number of cases per year (no figures were given) where there are differences between customs declarations and bills of lading, however, no details were provided to the mission team. ¾ In some points of entry the SVAD local office carries out specific controls for illegal imports. ¾ Specific findings for Genova port: - SVAD stated that, in 2003, two consignments of illegal imports of poultry meat from China in containers of vegetables were found inland, the information was sent only to central level but local customs were not informed. In 2004 SVAD seized a number of consignments of illegal imports of poultry meat from China in containers of vegetables, which are still present at the port. No detailed information was provided by customs to the mission team although requested. SVAD stated that 8 containers (6 of them with frozen chicken breast meat and 2 with dried fishery products mixed with other products) have been seized in 2005. All were illegal imports from China which were declared ro Customs as soya beans or spinach or frozen bread. No CVEDs were issued by the BIP, although the BIP carried out sampling for laboratory checks and salmonella was found in 4 containers. No information had been sent to other Member States and the Commission. Local customs stated that they 8 informed the central antifraud service of Customs. The mission team was informed by the BIP that there were 5 containers with about 95 tonnes of smuggled chicken breast meat from China (two of them in December 2004 and three of them in January 2005). No detailed information was received by customs although the mission team requested it. - Since the beginning of 2005 the results of scanning are entered in the customs database. Some illegal imports have been found in scanning but no details were given although requested. ¾ Information was not available in all entry points about the number of illegal imports of consignments of products of animal origin and live animals in freight seized/abandoned in 2004. No information was kept for the most frequent third countries checked and the results of the checks. ¾ Specific findings for Ancona port: - For freight there were 20 consignments of smuggled products of animal origin (about 500 kg of meat) and 200 birds seized by Customs as illegal imports in 2004. For CITES there were 4 consignments of live turtles and 30 consignments of game trophies seized in 2004. Some consignments of game trophies went to a zoo about 6 km from Ancona instead of being destroyed. - Freight consignments arriving by ferries or containers are moved on public roads to other Customs areas with a local customs procedure (A-77) without having a CVED issued. For the movement of the consignments to the ICs, Customs stated that these consignments are escorted by "Finance Guards". It is not possible for large container ships to arrive in Ancona and the containers are transhipped through other approved and non-approved BIPs in EU and non-EU ports.

Import and transit of live animals ¾ Guidelines for non-commercial pets were issued locally from some BIPs to customs, airport authorities and operators. In other entry points listed for the entry of pet animals there were no guidelines and no microchip readers identity checks were available. ¾ In BIP-entry points for pet animals the responsibility for the checks was not clarified between customs and BIP-staff. ¾ No information was received for the checks carried out for non-commercial pet animals in 2004 for which the relevant BIP staff stated that they were responsible. ¾ Information was not available fo

Ensure that all methods used under the NRCP for monitoring residues of veterinary medicinal products are fit for purpose i.e. are capable of detecting residues at EU MRLs in line with the requirements of point 3 in Annex III to Council Directive 96/23/ EC and point 2.2.(b) in the Annex to Commission Decision 98/179/EC, and that confirmatory methods are in line with the definition laid down in point 10.1. of chapter 1 in the Annex I to Commission Decision 2002/657/EC.
Ensure that appropriate quality control measures are put in place in laboratories in line with Article 5 of Commission Decision 2002/657/EC.

Ensure that when equidae arriving at slaughterhouses are not properly identified in accordance with Commission Regulation (EC) No 504/2008, appropriate measures are taken as required by Section II, point 3 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 and animals are not accepted for the food chain.

Ensure that foreign equidae are tested under the NRCP and, where testing reveals illegal treatment, the matter is referred to the Member State of origin or to the Commission if animals were imported from a third country, as required by Article 15(3) of Council Directive 96/23/EC.

Ensure that on the slaughter or death of a foreign equine animal, an attestation is communicated to the issuing body in the Member State where animal was identified as required by Article 19(c) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 504/2008 and that deficiencies in identification of foreign equidae are notified to the competent authority of the Member State of dispatch as required by Article 38 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Ensure that scope of testing carried out under the NRCP includes all relevant substances in line with the range of veterinary medicinal products on the market taking into account the requirements of Article 7 of Council Directive 96/23/EC.

Ensure that food business operators are not informed in advance of the scope of testing under the NRCP (i.e. by not publishing the scope of testing and geographical distribution in advance) in order to ensure that the element of surprise in the checks is constantly maintained, in accordance with the requirements of Annex III to Council Directive 96/23/EC.

Ensure that sampling and testing (including turnaround times) for residues is implemented in accordance with planned arrangements, if necessary taking appropriate corrective action to ensure this outcome as required by Article 8(3)b of Regulation (EC) 882/2004.
Ensure that follow-up investigations are carried out without prior warning as required by Article 12 of Council Directive 96/23/EC and Article 3(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Ensure that all official controls on the use of veterinary medicinal products are carried out on a risk-basis, consistently and in accordance with documented procedures in line with the requirements of Articles 3(1), 4(4) and 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Ensure that all medicinal treatments (including with left-over veterinary medicines) given to food producing animals are recorded in line with Article 10 of Council Directive 96/23/EC and Part A III, point 8(b) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.

Ensure that officials in charge of controls in slaughterhouses carry out inspection tasks related to the food chain information and take appropriate measures when necessary as required by Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

Ensure that verification of official controls in relation to the use of veterinary medicinal products in food producing animals, food chain information accompanying animals to slaughterhouses and identification of equidae at slaughter ensures the effectiveness and appropriateness of these controls as required by Article 4(2)a of Regulation (EC) 882/2004.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the regional plant health services are effectively supervised by the Single Authority, within the limits established by the national legislation, in line with 2nd indent of Article 2(1)(g)(ii) of Directive 2000/29/EC. In particular tools considered essential by the Single Authority to perform the coordination and guidance related activities (e.g. Audit programme) should be developed and implemented. Furthermore, the system in place should be adapted to timely deliver decisions, tools and guidance to Regions.
Ensure that there is close cooperation between the regional plant health services and the Single Authority as required in Article 2(1)(g) 6th paragraph of Directive 2000/29/EC.
Ensure that staff performing plant health checks have technical competence especially in the detection of harmful organisms as required in paragraph 2 of the Annex to Directive 98/22/EC.

Ensure that up-to-date national manual of procedures for inspectors is available in all points of entry as required in indent 6(a) of paragraph 1 of Annex to Directive 98/22/EC. In particular the manual should contain detailed instructions on how documentary, identity and plant health checks should be performed including the check of additional declaration and the minimum sample size for visual inspection.
Ensure that instructions on plant health checks are adapted as quickly as possible in the light of new plant health risks as required in indent 7 of paragraph 1 of the Annex to Directive 98/22/EC.
Ensure that any change to the list of places designated as points of entry is notified to the Commission and the other Member States in writing and without delay.

Ensure that plant health checks are only carried out at places that have the appropriate minimum conditions specified in the Annex to Directive 98/22/EC as required in Article 1 of the same Directive. In particular, at seaports, plant health checks should be carried out in areas covered where consignments can be unloaded, equipped with inspection tables and appropriate lighting.

Ensure that documentary checks are always meticulous as required in Article 13a (1) of Directive 2000/29/EC, in particular so as to ensure that the additional declaration is appropriate and the phytosanitary certificate is not fraudulent.

Ensure that identity checks are always meticulous as required in Article 13a(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC in particular by ensuring that inspectors have access to the whole consignment and perform the identity check against the phytosanitary certificate.

Ensure that plant health checks are always meticulous as required in Article 13a(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. In particular for those commodities where the frequency of interceptions of harmful organisms is significantly lower in Italy than in the EU, the method for inspection should be appropriate.

Ensure that plant health checks are always based on a representative sample as required in Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC. In particular the minimum sample size should take into account the phytosanitary risk presented by the commodities and should result in a satisfactory probability for finding pests in accordance with ISPM 31.

Ensure that non-declared regulated lots or consignments are inspected as required in Article 13b(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC, in particular by ensuring that inspectors have access to the whole consignments for performing the identity and plant health checks.

Ensure that plant health checks carried out on WPM specified in Annex 1 to Decision 2013/92/EU are meticulous. In particular these checks should be carried out on unloaded consignments and should be performed in order to detect any signs of presence of harmful organisms as well as the presence of mark. When performed, sampling should target marked WPM so as to detect fraudulent marking and inadequate treatment.

Ensure that notification of an interception is only made in the event of an action taken as required by Article 2 of Directive 94/3/EC. In particular, attention should be paid to the Commission guidelines for submitting notifications in EUROPHYT.
