recommendations.text: Ensure that, an effective communication campaign at national level aimed at informing and engaging with the stakeholders and the general public about the risks of Xf is implemented, in line with point 8 of Art. 6 of CID 2015/789/EU.

citations.text: The RPS Apulia informed the FVO audit team that there is continuous regional media coverage of Xf. The media in other regions and at national level deal with the outbreak periodically. Articles, reports and documentaries broadly reflect the opinion and arguments of those circles, who oppose the cutting of olive trees for eradication or who doubt the existence of Xf in Apulia and its role in the quick decline of the olive trees. The opinion of the RPS and scientific institutions gains limited or very limited coverage and it is usually presented in an unconvincing manner in response to the arguments of opponents to eradication measures. This in not in line with Art. 7 of CID 2015/789/EU.
The audit team found very limited direct engagement with stakeholders in particular following a finding of Xf, see sections 5.8.3 and 5.9.1. Conclusions on communication and information

There is considerable communication to the stakeholders and the public regarding Xf. However, there is limited direct engagement with stakeholders and the message that, in the absence of concerted control measures, the disease has, and will, continue to spread rapidly with the resultant significant loss of olive trees and other host plants, is often not conveyed effectively. This undermines the ability for an effective implementation of the necessary control measures for Xf.

citations.text: There is currently no reference laboratory for Xf in Italy, however, the SA informed the FVO team that MIPAAF intends to nominate the Agricultural Research Council-Rome 7 to act as the national reference laboratory for this purpose. No timeline for the nomination was available.

MIPAAF informed the FVO team that it has commissioned the Institute of Plant Virology of the University of Bari (IPV) to carry out ring tests to assess the proficiency of the RPS laboratories, who analyse samples, using ELISA and/or PCR tests. The SA stated that the ring test would be completed by end of August 2015. 5.4.2 Laboratories testing official samples for Xylella fastidiosa in Apulia

The FVO team was informed that the RPS laboratory of Tuscany uses PCR for testing plant and insect samples and for confirmation, while the RPS laboratory of Liguria uses ELISA for plant sample testing and PCR for insect samples and for confirmatory purposes. There are no MIPAAF recommendations for RPS laboratories concerning the methodology of mass and confirmatory Xf tests.

The FVO team visited the RPS laboratory of Liguria and noted that The laboratory is involved in testing of a wide-range of pathogens of import control and plant health monitoring samples. The number of samples depends on the import volume and timing of the surveys. They apply different, pathogen specific methods. There are peaks in test needs, which regularly create a workload which is difficult to manage for the laboratory staff; The laboratory has facilities for ELISA and PCR, however due to limited possibilities for physical separation of the test steps, the laboratory staff confirmed that extra care is needed for avoiding sample contamination during the tests; 9 The laboratory staff has work experience in serological and molecular tests, however less experience in Xf testing. They did not have any training related to PCR and to Xf analysis; The laboratory does not apply a comprehensive sample and test result administration system, only certain individual records are taken; The Xf tests for samples processed in the laboratory in Liguria are not fully reliable as required by point 3 of Art 2, Art. 3, Art. 4 and Art 6 of CID 2015/789/EU.

The FVO team noted that: The RPS laboratory in Liguria performed the ELISA and PCR tests broadly following the IPV protocols, however with some adaptation, including the application of certain elements of the relevant EPPO protocols which, according to the experts is quite outdated; During the ELISA test for the repetition of the same sample, two plates were used rather than two wells of the same plate. As the laboratory has no photometric facilities the results were evaluated visually. The plant sample gave colour reaction on both of the plates, however the colour was slightly different from that of the positive controls (brownish, instead of yellow). The laboratory considered that the sample was positive and the colour difference was the result of additional reactions, caused by the plant extract. The ELISA test of the same sample was not repeated; For the confirmatory test, different leaves of the same sample were used. The test was performed according to the IPV protocol. The FVO team found that the electrophoretic pattern of the sample was misinterpreted, as an unidentified DNA fragment was considered as Xf DNA; After the confirmatory test both the original leaf sample and the plant, which was assessed as Xf positive were destroyed. 10 Conclusions on laboratories and testing

In contrast, the facilities and expertise available to other RPS has not been established. The ring test being carried out by the IPV should provide at least an indication of the proficiency of these laboratories at detecting Xf in samples, however, until that becomes available, the reliability of the confirmation analysis referred in point 3 of Art 2, Art. 3, Art. 4 and Art 6 of CID 2015/789/EU is not ensured. Therefore, there are no full guarantees that the surveys carried out clearly identify Xf in the pest free areas.

recommendations.text: To ensure that, when confirmation of receipt/exit of consignments is not received within the 30 day limit, appropriate follow-up is implemented by the entry BIP/ approved warehouse as required by Article 11(2) of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 2 of Commission Decision 2000/571/EC.

citations.text: Article 11(2) of Directive 97/78/EC requires BIP staff to ensure that they receive confirmation of arrival (from an approved warehouse) or confirmation of exit from the EU (from the exit BIP) within 30 days after a transit consignment leaves their BIP. If no confirmation is received within 30 days then official staff should seek confirmation either by contacting the officials in charge of controls at the warehouse or the BIP), or by asking Customs. The audit team noted that: At one of the BIPs, confirmation from destination was received for the vast majority of consignments. However, the system to promptly identify when confirmation of receipt was not received within the 30 day legal time limit was not effective. The system to identify such consignments was paper-based and the BIP was considering the introduction of an electronic register to identify consignments requiring follow-up. At the other BIP, an electronic register was maintained to follow-up the consignments and the follow-up worked well. For consignments destined for approved warehouses, BIP staff stated that all consignments were followed up if required and confirmed as being received at destination via telephone contact with official staff responsible for the warehouse. There was no evidence of this follow- up kept on file. Documentary evidence on file of confirmation of receipt was the completion of box 41 of the CVED by the destination, and in some cases was six months after the consignment had left the entry BIP. (see finding 20)

All consignments in transit entering Italy are checked at BIPs although not all requirements related to pre-notification are enforced. Veterinary checks are carried out in line with the requirements of EU legislation ensuring that only eligible consignments are accepted for transit. 7 The system to promptly identify and follow-up consignments for which no confirmation of receipt at destination has been received by the entry BIP is not effective, reducing the ability of the system to identify non-conforming consignments that have not left the Union as planned. 5.2.2 Controls at approved warehouses 5.2.2.1 Approval and listing

Before non-conforming consignments can leave the approved warehouses, the operator must submit a request to the competent authority who subsequently checks the consignment, seals the means of transport after loading and issues the CVED (linked with the original CVED via box 24) or the document for the Captain's Declaration. The audit team noted the following at the two approved warehouses visited: Approved warehouse A ­ for ship supplies, a register is in place to verify that confirmation of receipt by the ship is received back, and that follow-up action is implemented if required. The warehouse had only issued two CVEDs during 2014 for which box 41 was completed for one within 30 days and for the other after 55 days. For consignments accompanied by a CVED, there is no system in place to ensure that appropriate follow-up is triggered if confirmation of receipt from the destination was not received within 30 days, contrary to the requirements of Article 2 of Commission Decision 2000/571/EC. Approved warehouse B ­ an effective system was in place to ensure that confirmation of receipt was obtained or appropriate follow-up action was implemented if necessary for all consignments. Conclusion on the official controls at approved warehouses

Official controls on transiting consignments stored in warehouses are implemented but their compliance with EU legislation is compromised by the decision of the competent authority to issue single CVEDs for consolidated consignments, which does not permit effective traceability of the goods and cannot ensure the effectiveness of the controls up to the point of delivery. 10 5.2.3 Controls at the exit Border Inspection Posts 5.2.3.1 Documentary, identity and physical checks

recommendations.text: To modify the existing verification system so that it covers the relevant official controls including those which do not involve the issuing of a certificate as required by Article 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: Approved warehouses are currently not included within the scope of internal audits by the central competent authority. One of the warehouses visited had an internal audit by the regional level in 2013, but there is no formalised plan for internal audits at approved warehouses at any level.

The main elements of the performance reporting system with relevance for transits is the requirement to check the compliance of a percentage of the certificates that are issued. The overall target was 5% at both BIPs visited due to a high throughput of consignments. The audit team noted that: Genoa Port BIP: checked no transit related documents based on a risk assessment (these were regarded as low risk consignments because they were not destined for EU market). Livorno Port BIP: checked 100% of transit related documents based on a risk assessment (these were regarded as high-risk consignments which should be prevented from reaching the EU market). These checks had identified similar issues to those described in finding 10. At one warehouse visited, the review of 15% of documents issued identified the issue of hand-written CVEDs (see finding 21) but no corrective action was requested. At the other warehouse visited, there was no verification on the compliance of the certificates issued.

The audit team noted that the following issues identified during the FVO audit were not identified by the national verification system: issues with pre-notification (as described in finding 8); issues at entry BIPs with confirmation of receipt at destination (finding 15); issues with exit controls (finding 26). The current performance reporting system checks a percentage of the documents issued by the location being assessed. Recording the controls referred to in findings 15 and 26 usually involves completing box 41 in TRACES on a CVED issued by a location other than the one carrying out the follow-up control. Therefore these controls are not checked as part of the current performance reporting system. 12 Conclusion on the verification and review

The verification system of official controls related to non-conforming transit consignments is based on a combination of internal audits and a performance reporting system. The detection and correction of shortcomings is not ensured because official controls at approved warehouses are not covered by internal audit and not all types of transit controls are checked within the performance reporting system.

Verification of the official import controls is implemented in recent years by the Ministry of Health via a system which evaluates its activities and objectives in accordance with Public Administration rules, i.e. "System for measuring and evaluating the performance". This system is implemented at BIPs and according to the competent authority, verifies official import controls by amongst other things, setting the following objectives for each BIP: to plan and carry out inspections of the structures of the BIP/Inspection centre; to respect the sampling activities for laboratory checks according to the percentages established by monitoring plan (3%); to verify the compliance of the certificates issued by the BIP on a percentage basis based on throughput of the BIP; to respect the percentage physical checks of consignments as set out in Commission Decision 1994/360/EC. The audit team verified that for the BIPs visited, all of the above objectives were reported on and the targets were achieved or exceeded, e.g. the quantitative target of checking 5% of the documents issued by each BIP was confirmed in the database. 13 The table below summarises the follow-up to recommendation number 1 from FVO report DG(SANCO)/2012-6501: Number Recommendation Assessment 1 "To ensure that appropriate actions are taken when Partially addressed needed to correct the deficiencies detected at BIPs in order to ensure that all operating BIPs maintain compliance with approval requirements of See findings No 35 and 36 Commission Decision 2001/812/EC and Directive 91/496/EEC."

audits.title: Microbial safety of primary production of food of non-animal origin

recommendations.text: Review the planning of official controls taking into account specific higher risks concerning certain type and use of produce to ensure that official controls on microbial safety in primary production of FNAO are effective and appropriate, as required by Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The risk ranking set out in the EFSA scientific opinion was not taken into account in the framework of the above-mentioned exercise. This negatively affects the effectiveness of official controls as the major risks identified in EFSA scientific opinion do not contribute to the risk basis for those controls, contrary to Article 3.1(a) and 4.2(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, the CCA, regional CAs and local CAs informed the audit team that microbiological hazards will be considered in the risk based planning for 2016. The CAs are planning to evaluate the risk assessments by the end of this year in order to take into account the microbiological risks identified in scientific opinions of EFSA and probably increase the frequency of inspections regarding microbiological risks in relation to certain produce.

In addition, in September 2015 the regional authorities in Calabria started to develop a new procedure for the official control on primary production of FNAO with relevant checklists containing certain microbiological risks. In 2015, the authorities were responsible for controls on approximately 2400 farms producing FNAO and they carried out approximately 200 inspections at those FBOs. However, at the time of the audit, inspections did not consider any microbiological risks except for contamination of water used at primary producers. Moreover, at the time of the audit, microbiological risks (other than relating to water) identified by EFSA concerning FNAO were not included in the risk-based planning of official controls nor were the inspections targeting high risk crops prone to the microbiological contamination identified by EFSA.

While official controls on primary producers of FNAO cover the risk of microbiological contamination of irrigation water, the remaining major microbiological risks identified by EFSA are not considered (with the exception of one region visited) in the planning of official controls. This circumstance, coupled with the fact that the design of official controls does not make specific provision for targeting the high priority crops identified by EFSA as particularly prone to microbiological contamination, weakens the effectiveness of official controls in this area. 5.2.4 Implementation of Official Controls over Food Business Operators Obligations Legal requirements Article 10(2)(b)(i), Article 10(2)(c), Article 10(2)(d) and Article 15(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Article 4(1), Article 7, Article 8 and Part B of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 3 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 208/2013, Regulation (EU) No 211/2013 and Annex I of Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 Findings

responses.response: With reference to the recommendation laid down in November 2015 report audit on "Reference number: DG(SANTE)/2015-7455 -MR Audit in Italy from 03 November 2015 to 13 November 2015 in order to evaluate the system of official controls relating to microbial safety of primary production of food of non-animal origin", we inform you that we developed a specific guideline on the frequency of official controls, according to Reg. (CE) 882/2004; the guideline was discussed and approved at a meeting of inter-Regional technical group on the 2nd of March 2016. We are now waiting for the approval by State-Regions conference. In order to harmonize all official controls in Italy, guideline establishes frequency of official controls on primary production of non-animal origin products as well, paying particular attention on controls on sprouts and sprouts seeds. After the final approval, guideline will be sent to all Regions; anyway in the meantime we are sending to all Regions a specific planning document for primary production, in which we invite all Competent Autorities to respect recommendation before guideline approval.

recommendations.text: Make commodity specific instructions available to ensure that inspectors performing import checks of consignments representing high plant health risk obtain technical competence especially in the detection of harmful organisms as required in paragraph 2 of the Annex to Directive 98/22/EC.

citations.text: The audit team noted that: 6 At Marghera, Salerno and Gioia Tauro ports, no commodity specific instructions were available for inspectors to carry out import checks of consignments representing high plant health risk. The newly recruited staff at Malpensa Airport received a comprehensive induction training of three months, involving external institutes. The ERSAF had developed a training programme and a programme to ensure that the professional competence of staff performing checks is maintained, as part of its preparation for its application for International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO) 17020 accreditation. The staff present during the visit by the audit team was competent to perform plant health checks, which is an improvement compared to the previous audit in 2013. In Veneto, a newly recruited inspector received on-the-job training from the regional chief inspector. In Campania, RPS staff is provided with 150 hours/year training on plant health issues, most of which, however, does not relate directly to import controls. In the case of new trade (e.g. potatoes in Veneto) training is received from colleagues from other import points with experience of that trade.

There are no commodity specific instructions available at the sea ports reviewed for performing import checks of high-risk consignments. The roll-out of the national manual of procedures has a significant potential to address this shortcoming.

recommendations.text: Ensure that plant health checks are always meticulous as required in Article 13a(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. In particular for those commodities where the frequency of interceptions of harmful organisms is significantly lower in Italy than in the EU, the method for inspection should be appropriate.

citations.text: During the audit visits the audit team noted that: An inspection facility for plant health checks, including binocular microscope, a kit to detect nematodes and a desk-top computer, was available at the Venice- Marghera sea port but not used for other than documentary work and checks of cereals. Inspections are carried out outdoor and in the warehouse on the floor. The warehouse had a recently allocated room dedicated for plant health inspections which had an inspection table. This was intended to be used to inspect potatoes, however, none had yet been imported. At Malpensa airport a dedicated plant health inspection post was available with suitable equipment including magnifying glasses, binocular microscope for performing visual examination of samples and an inspection table with adequate lighting. At Salerno port, inspections of citrus fruits were carried out in a container which was covered but open on the sides. An inspection table was available but the inspector did not use it to spread out the produce to carry out the visual inspection. The inspectors were exposed to sun and high temperature while inspecting refrigerated commodities such as citrus fruits. A different inspection facility was used for another inspection, which the audit team considered as adequate. The port has a container office for RPS which has an inspection table, binocular microscope and tools necessary for phytosanitary inspection. The office facilities are generally not used. Conclusions on points of entry, inspection posts and approved places of inspection

Recommendation 10 of report 2013-6790 was to "Ensure that plant health checks are always meticulous as required in Article 13a(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. In particular for those commodities where the frequency of interceptions of harmful organisms is significantly lower in Italy than in the EU, the method for inspection should be appropriate." In response to this recommendation, the Single Authority stated that: 15 The NPHC is planned to identify non-regulated commodities which will be subject to random checks on the basis of EUROPHYT interceptions and the EPPO alert list. Specific control procedures are planned to be provided for goods with a low ratio of interceptions to the volume of import compared to the EU average. The above actions are in line with the Action Plan of the Single Authority submitted to address this recommendation. These measures are to be linked with the SIAN system and the deadline for implementation is by end of 2016. The plant health inspection facilities were described in section 5.4.2.

The audit team witnessed plant health checks and examined PCs that had already been considered compliant by the RPS/ERSAF at Venice-Marghera and Salerno ports, and Malpensa airport and noted that: There were significant differences in the sampling procedures followed by the RPSs visted. At Venice-Marghera port, the inspector explained that they use 80% confidence level and 5% detection level to determine the size of the sample to be taken. Although these are minimum values in ISPM31, the RPS stated that the sample size was too large to implement in practice. However, the RPS could not explain what was meant by this, or what the actual sample size applied was. At Malpensa Airport the audit team observed an inspection of orchids from Thailand. The inspector explained that it was considered to be a medium risk commodity as such commodity had not been subject to interceptions for a long time. He picked a confidence level of 90% and used the smallest unit declared on the phytosanitary certificate, in this case stems, to calculate the size of the sample, in stems. In practice the inspector applied the suggested sample size to bunches to increase the number of sampled units. In this case the sample was taken from 20% of 16 the boxes of the consignments. The inspection observed was carried out thoroughly using a standard inspection technic for such products. At Salerno port the audit team witnessed inspections of citrus fruits. A fixed sample size of 200 fruit was taken regardless of the origin. The RPS stated that the fixed sample size is based on the minimum sample size specified in Decision 2014/422/EU for citrus fruits from South Africa considered to be a high risk of citrus black spot. The conditions and the way the visual checks observed by the audit team were carried out were not ideal to detect quarantine harmful organisms (see section 5.4.2). 5.5.4 Reduced frequency of checks Legal requirements Article 13a(2), last sub-paragraph of Directive 2000/29/EC and Commission Regulation (EC) No 1756/2004 apply regarding reduced frequency checks. Findings

Plant health checks carried out at the sea ports visited are not in line with Directive 2000/29/EC as adequate facilities are not used and the conditions do not ensure that the plant health inspection is meticulous enough to detect pests.

recommendations.text: Ensure that interceptions of harmful organisms are notified not later than two working days as required by Article 2(1) of Directive 94/3/EC.

citations.text: Recommendation 14 of report 2013-6790 was to "Ensure that notification of an interception is only made in the event of an action taken as required by Article 2 of Directive 94/3/EC. In particular, attention should be paid to the Commission guidelines for submitting notifications in EUROPHYT." In response to this recommendation, the Single Authority stated that: The Single Authority stated that the system for the submission of notifications has been revised since the previous audit. The RPS are responsible for submitting a draft notification in EUROPHYT, this is then verified and validated at central level, at which point it is submitted in the EUROPHYT system. The Single Authority confirmed that notifications are only approved in the event that action is taken by the RPS. The EUROPHYT Annual Report for 2014 includes an analysis of the time taken by Member States and Switzerland to submit notifications of interception. For 2014, Italy notified interceptions of harmful organisms on average within 8 working days; interceptions for other reasons were notified on average within 10 working days. Although the time taken to notify interceptions is in line with the EU average (of 10 and 9 working days respectively) for 2014, it is considerably longer than the two working days or preferably sooner, specified in Directive 94/3/EC for interceptions of harmful organisms. In the event that a consignment is found to be infested with a harmful organism, or is accompanied by incorrect documents, the RPS either refuses entry or destroys the consignment. The audit team noted that in such cases, the RPS endorses the phytosanitary certificate with a triangular stamp in red, marked `certificate cancelled', in line with Article 13(c)7 of Directive 2000/29/EC. 22 The Single Authority and the RPSs visited informed the audit team that they do not adapt their established programme of checks in light of new plant health risks associated with non-regulated material. However new risks associated with regulated materials are taken into account during the import checks. Conclusions on notifications of interception, and action taken
However, the average time taken to notify interceptions of harmful organisms is considerably more than the two working days, required by Article 2(1) of Directive 94/3/EC.

audits.title: evaluate the production and use of certain proteins of animal origin in feed for aquaculture animals

recommendations.text: To update the procedures for official controls to provide all necessary information and instructions, as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in order to ensure that checks on the production and use of PAP and aquaculture feed containing such PAP, and the authorisation process of those business operators which handle products of ruminant origin, are carried out in a regular and consistent manner.

citations.text: The audit team visited two establishments, located in two different Regions, which required an authorisation because they were handling ruminant and non-ruminant materials, and noted the following: In one case the establishment is a processing plant producing blood products of porcine origin to be used for the manufacture of feed for aquaculture. It was noted that, although the establishment largely fulfilled the necessary conditions to obtain 4 an authorisation, there was no evidence available to demonstrate that these conditions had been actually checked during official controls (see paragraph 16). In the second case the establishment is a feed manufacturer (see paragraph 19). It was noted that a report with a favourable opinion was issued by the local inspector and most of the relevant conditions were mentioned. This was followed by a clearance issued by the local competent authority. In both cases the authorisation required by the relevant Section of Chapter IV of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 had not been issued.

Slaughterhouses/cutting plants, processing plants handling ABP destined to be used in the aquaculture feed and transporters of ABP and derived products are subject to inspections according to risk-based frequencies which are determined taking into account the recommended frequencies decided at central level and the specific risks identified at local level. In the feed sector, the PNAA valid from 2015 to 2017, highlights the need to inspect all feed business operators according to risk criteria and provides comprehensive explanations on, among other things, the risk factors to take into account. In both sectors (i.e. the ABP and the feed sector) guidelines and checklists to carry out official controls have been issued by the central competent authority. However, although a draft document with explanations and clarifications was about to be issued by Office VII (hence, for the feed part of the chain), the audit team noted that, in general, no checklists/guidelines for official controls currently contain the new provisions on the feed ban. This is not in line with Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 because it results in inspectors paying limited attention to the new provisions (e.g. authorisation of establishments handling ruminant products and cross-contamination during transport) and in a lack of records of relevant checks (see paragraphs 15, 16, 17 and 18). Sampling plans:

Business operators, establishments and plants along the chain are subject to risk-based official controls; however, the competent authorities have not yet put in place the necessary arrangements (notably, updated checklists/guidelines) to ensure that: a) the checks along the chain of the production and use of PAP for aquaculture purposes are carried out and recorded on a regular basis, and b) that the process for the authorisation of operators handling products of ruminant origin is followed in a consistent manner. Although no sampling plans to detect the presence of ruminant proteins in PAP and aquaculture feed containing such PAP were organised in 2013 and 2014, a plan has been developed for 2015 onwards and relevant analyses will be carried out by an accredited network of laboratories.

The audit team visited a processing plant supplying PAP of poultry origin in big-bags or bulk for aquaculture feed. The operator had devised a largely comprehensive own-control system based on Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) principles and regular samples from the final products are analysed to detect the presence of ruminant DNA (always resulted negative). However, the audit team noted that the risk of cross- contamination during the transport of incoming ABP was not considered in the hazard analysis and had not been included in the agreements with outsourced transporters even 6 though it is one of the conditions laid down in Section D of Chapter IV of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2011. This weakness had not been identified by the inspector in charge.

In the second processing plant visited the products placed on the market for aquaculture consist of whole dried blood and dried haemoglobin both of porcine origin, dispatched in big-bags or in bulk. The whole blood is processed in a dedicated production line physically separated from another line which processes blood of other species (including ruminants), whereas the haemoglobin is purchased, as such, stored in dedicated silos and dispatched. Although satisfactory arrangements were in place to avoid the risk of cross- contamination and these were verified by sampling final products, there was no evidence these had been checked during official controls, as the checklist used does not yet include the relevant new feed ban requirements. This is not in line with the requirements on official controls laid down in Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

The audit team visited two transporters, located in two different Regions, one handling ABP and the other PAP, both of poultry origin, for aquaculture. Both of them had been authorised as transporters of ABP or derived products, according to a national rule and were subject to planned official controls (although in one of the three Regions visited the competent authorities declared that no checks of transporters were planned due to the lack of resources). According to the aforementioned national rule, the authorisation is granted by the local competent authority for each individual truck owned by the transporter and the transport of ABP/DP and feed in the same truck is prohibited. The audit team noted that although none of the transporters were active in the transport of products of ruminant origin, the authorisation given by the competent authority did not indicate any restrictions or conditions (e.g. use of authorised cleaning procedures) which would apply to the transport of such products and the own-control measures put in place by both the transporters did not refer to the risk of cross-contamination with products of ruminant origin. This shortcoming had not been identified during official controls, although a recent inspection of one of the transporters identified a number of deficiencies (related to the cleaning and commercial documents). This is not fully in line with the requirements on official controls laid down in Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001. 5.2.2 Use of processed animal protein to produce compound feed Findings

The audit team visited a trader of, among other things, PAP, and two feed manufacturers producing feed for aquaculture using PAP as raw material, one of which produced for both aquaculture and other farmed animals (including ruminants). All of them had largely comprehensive own-control systems and were subject to official controls (once or twice per year) according to the risk-based criteria set up by the central competent authority. However, the audit team noted that no evidence of the official checks on the relevant feed ban requirements, as required by Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001, could be provided by the local competent authorities.

Operators along the chain are mostly checked according to the planned frequencies and non-compliances are followed in a structured and systematic manner. However, the absence of evidence of checks on the relevant feed ban requirements (notably, when an authorisation is required) and a low attention paid to the risk of cross-contamination during transport, undermines the overall reliability of the official controls. This weakness is mitigated by largely comprehensive own-control systems put in in place by the operators. 8

citations.text: The CCA does not have an up-to-date list of all the holdings and keepers which keep pigs in Sardinia, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(a) of Directive 2008/71/EC. The authorities provided data on pig farms and number of pigs (see Annex II). Those data do not describe the full pig population because a number of pigs are still kept uncontrolled in some parts of Sardinia, which is illegal according to national law. The regional authority estimates that there are still "3000 to 4000 uncontrolled pigs in nine to ten municipalities, and may be on a few more locations". The majority of such pigs are in the ASF infected area. There is no estimation of the number of keepers of such pigs. 5

A significant number of pig movements are not notified and registered in the national pig database (Banca Dati Nazionale dell'Anagrafe Zootecnica), contrary to the requirement of Article 18(c) of Directive 1964/432/EEC. Pig movements are not registered into the database within seven days. The audit team visited two provinces and selected movement documents randomly in the ASL. In one, all movements were registered in the database; in the other, none of the movements selected for verification were registered in the database (the movements took place in June and August 2016 - two to four months before the audit). Slaughterhouses do not always notify the slaughter of pigs within 7 days. In one province, consignments of pigs which arrived at the slaughterhouse in June and August 2016 had not been registered in the database at the time of the audit. The regional authority identified non-compliances during the annual desk-top verification of registration of movements in the database in 2016, including: number of pigs slaughtered not in line with the number of pigs sent to the slaughterhouse, notification of slaughtered animals for which no movement to a slaughterhouse was registered and notification of consignments sent to a slaughterhouse for which the slaughter was not registered in the database. The regional authority has no insight into movements of uncontrolled pigs.
The existence of uncontrolled pigs in some parts of Sardinia compromises the reliability of pig population data and undermines the traceability of pig movements on the island.

Under-registration/under-notification of the number of piglets and movements of pigs, hampers the confidence in the data stored in the database. As a consequence, the pig identification and movement registration system does not fully support planning and implementation of ASF eradication measures. It also does not fully allow for reliable/targeted planning of official controls, taking into account risks associated with, for example, movements of pigs from infected to non-infected parts of the island.

citations.text: Although EU and Italian legislation established the current BZ in May 2016 (see chapter 5.1.2) the full scale 2016 surveys started there only in August after the Prosecutor's ban was revoked (see chapter 4.2) and the necessary financial and human resources were put into place including the training of the surveillance staff.. The work was being carried out by ARIF, based on a 100m x 100m grid approach, as required by the EU legislation. It was decided to start the work at the northern border of the BZ and to move progressively southward in order to first detect any infection situated farthest from the IZ (see figure II).

After recruiting and training the necessary personnel, the survey started on 29 August 2016 and full capacity was reached in September, involving 172 ARIF agents working in 86 teams. ARIF agents have the status of public agents and Ministerial Decree 2014/2005 gives them the right to enter private property. Each team has an average capacity of 20 squares per day enabling ARIF to check around 1,500 squares and collect 2,000-2,500 samples daily. A complex and sophisticated IT system supports the activity.

The visual inspection and the sampling are carried out following a very detailed guideline. ARIF regularly controls the quality of the work of its agents. The guideline lists the main elements of the methodology as follows: The survey team shall identify the physical borders of each grid square with the help of orthophotos, high resolution satellite images and by using GPS coordinates. The system ensures that there is no overlap of the inspected squares and that no gaps are left uninspected in the territory; The entire area of the square shall be scouted and checked visually. The host and specified plants shall be identified with particular attention to visible symptoms. As the first symptoms of Xf, in particular on olive trees are very similar to the damages caused by other common mechanical and environmental impacts, each possibly symptomatic plant shall be meticulously checked; Each specified plant with symptoms shall be sampled. If no visible symptoms are observed, at least one sample shall be taken from a host plant with a high share in the flora of the square. In the BZ, this shall be generally olive, however some samples shall be taken from other asymptomatic hosts also; At least eight sub-samples must be taken from an olive or other host tree from each cardinal and from the middle and upper parts of the canopy. Small twigs may be cut with the help of high reach pruning poles. Fresh leaves and twig tops shall be taken for samples. The agent carefully checks the leaves and ensures that no vectors are on them before packing into plastic sample bags; The precise position of the sampled plant shall be identified by GPS and the coordinates together with a picture of the plant are automatically recorded by a mobile device used by the agents; Before leaving the inspection site, an electronic report shall be prepared, which is filed together with the unique identification code and GPS data of the square. The 10 report shall include information about the specified plants, their share in the vegetation, any symptoms observed and details of the sampling; The mobile device issues a unique alphanumeric sample identification code and indicates the testing laboratory. A sample label shall be prepared with the identification number and relevant information for identification and trace-back. It shall be attached to the sealed sample bag. The logistics system shall ensure that the samples arrive at the laboratory on the same day and they are cooled during transport; All data is uploaded to a central database after the inspection as soon as the agents have internet access. The laboratories receive a daily extract of the sample data stored in the system and they cross-check this with information on the label. Figure II. Xf monitoring in 2016 in Apulia, in the BZ and in the "20km zone", until 11 November Source: RPS Apulia

The audit team observed a survey carried out by an ARIF team and noted that: The agents were experienced and had good knowledge about the legislation and about the host and specified plants; ARIF organises the sampling properly; the activity of the teams and the logistics of the samples are fully coordinated; The IT system used ensures the proper identification of the squares and the host and specified plants present. The electronic report, which is prepared according to a template, contains all information necessary for the authorities and for other statistical and analytical purposes; The agents carried out the visual checks and the sampling fully in line with the provisions of the guideline. In particular, the possible origin of the symptoms (e.g. mechanical damage) was meticulously checked in order to select those, which could be caused by Xf infection; In the square surveyed, no symptomatic plant was identified. Nevertheless in line with the protocol, a sample was taken from an olive tree as this was the most representative host plant of the site; At the time of the audit (late autumn), visual symptoms could be observed on olive trees, on oleander, on other evergreen plants and on certain herbaceous specified plants. However, olive trees have already dropped a part of their leaves, which were dried up during the vegetation season. Therefore this period was not considered as the most appropriate for surveying olives; At the time of the audit, the majority of the deciduous plants were dropping their leaves, the remaining leaves changed in colour and some herbaceous species also changed their appearance preventing the detection of symptoms, caused by Xf. Therefore the time of the surveys for these plants was inappropriate for visual inspections and requirements of Article 6(7) of the Decision were not met in this respect; The intensity and coverage of the surveys goes beyond the requirements of the Decision. Practically the entire area of each square is subject to meticulous visual check. Sampling and testing is not limited symptomatic plants or to cases of any suspicion of infection. Instead at least one sample is taken in in each square even in the absence of symptoms or suspicion. This could, to an extent, mitigate the negative impact of doing the survey at a time, which is inappropriate for inspection and sampling of certain specified plants. 5.2.3 Surveys in the "20km zone"

From September 2016 onwards, ARIF started its activity also in the "20km zone". First they checked some high risk spots while the systematic survey with the method described in chapter 5.2.2 started in October after the work in the BZ was largely completed. At the time of the audit, in the "20km zone" 11.6% of the area had been checked and sampled. The work started at the border of the BZ and was to continue at the rate of 1,500 squares a day until completed. RPS expects the completion of the work in January 2017 (see table III). For the same reasons as set out in relation to the BZ (see paragraph 36), the audit team considers that the timing of the survey was inappropriate or not the most appropriate in the "20 km zone". Table III. Surveys in the "20km zone" in 2016, as of 11 November Total area (ha*) Grid squares Total number of Laboratory samples from Positive inspected** laboratory samples symptomatic plants samples 106,764 12,333 12,816 447 18 Source: RPS Apulia * Equal to the number of 100m x 100m grid squares ** The Decision requires annual surveys, based on a grid split into 100m x 100m squares in the "20km zone"

The surveys were carried out at times not being the most appropriate for certain specified plants or even inappropriate for some other specified plants. Therefore the effectiveness of the visual inspections as a means of identifying symptomatic plants and suspected cases of infection were compromised. The impact of this could be mitigated to some extent by the 2016 sampling and testing regime, which goes beyond EU requirements.

recommendations.text: Ensure that all necessary measures to eradicate, or if that is impossible, inhibit the spread of the pest are taken, in line with 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC, in particular to increase the intensity of survey in the buffer zone.

citations.text: Visual inspections were concentrated in the areas not infested by Japanese beetle, i.e. the buffer zone, and were carried out between mid June and mid August 2016. The three km buffer zone is subdivided in three concentric bands of one km in width within which a 1000 m square matrix grid is used and the sites for inspection were as equally distributed as possible. This density of survey points is significantly lower than that required in EU legislation in other outbreaks, e.g. for buffer zone surveillance for Xylella fastidiosa (100 x 100 m), however, the RPSs performs more dense visual inspections in the area closer to the infested zone. The sites contained preferred host plants on which the adults 9 were found in 2014 and 2015. These included: Rubus, Urtica, Ulmaria, Oenothera, Humulus lupulus, Vitis spp., Rumex, Salix, Ulmus, Corylus, Prunus avium, Robinia, Centaurea phrygia, Tilia, Hibiscus and Rosa. Both RPSs informed the audit team that private persons are contacting them regularly about potential findings of the pest which have been systematically followed up.

In 2016 the RPS in Lombardy carried out 1 825 visual inspections and the RPS in Piedmont 430. With the recent update of the demarcated area in the summer 2016, the area of the buffer zone was extended and is very large. As mentioned above, a 1 000 m x 1 000 m survey grid is not very dense for a secure delimitation of the infestation and the number of inspections indicates that Piedmont in 2016 was far from achieving even that coverage. Thus the authorities might not obtain sufficient information on the current distribution of the pest and may not delimit the outbreak adequately. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC that all necessary measures must be taken to eradicate, or if that is impossible, inhibit the spread of the pest.

The surveys for Japanese beetle in Italy are organised appropriately, however, they are unevenly distributed between both affected regions and the implemented intensity does not provide sufficient information about the actual distribution of the pest.

Ensure that buffer zones are wide enough to ensure that infected material are not inadvertently moved to free areas, including other Member States, as required by Article 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC. A contingency plan for the possible infection of commercial fruit plantations of J. regia, in particular with respect to preventing such plantation contributing to further spread, should be elaborated between relevant RPSs and industry associations in line with Article 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC. Measures to address the possible dissemination of the disease via infected bark strippings from sawmills from within DAs to other areas outside, should be taken, in line with Article 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC, to eliminate this potential source of regional and wider spread.

citations.text: Despite a high degree of homogeneity with respect to the monitoring approach and overall surveillance strategy, the level of monitoring intensity varies between regions but, in each case, is considered insufficient to reliably delimit the presence of Thousand canker disease and provide for the protective measures required by Article 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC (see paragraphs 40 to 52). Veneto

Veneto manages a total of 50 strategically positioned monitoring sites across its region. Identified from the public nursery database (of Veneto Agricultura) and the regional register (see also paragraph 33), the sites are also selected, as much as is practically possible, to a defined geometrical grid.
Trees at all 50 sites are subject to visual inspection. Thirty of the sites are complemented with a pheromone trap. Sites are inspected on a monthly basis.

In addition, the RPS stated that one trap is positioned in one plantation which is also subjected to monitoring. No Thousand canker disease has been observed there to date. Furthermore, both producers and an industry association met during the audit stated they have never witnessed Thousand canker disease, nor the vector, in their plantations. Piedmont

Piedmont has a total of 15 strategic monitoring sites across its region. Of the four pheromone trap deployments, two are located at each of the notified outbreak sites. Eleven other sites are subject to visual monitoring only. Sites, as well as traps, are inspected on a monthly basis.

From their observations, Piedmont stated that no Thousand canker disease has been observed on varieties of J. regia for walnut fruit production. Therefore, the commercial walnut fruit plantations to the South east and south west of the region have not been included in their monitoring regime.

Lombardy monitors 10 strategically selected sites with pheromone traps within its region each year. Each site typically comprises up to 20 trees. Each site is visited on a monthly basis during which the traps and trees are checked for the vector and 12 Thousand canker disease, respectively. This regime, in place since 2014, was preceded by a less stringent preliminary monitoring approach in 2013 following notification of the first outbreak case in Veneto. The location of some of the monitoring sites are changed each year.

In addition to selected sites for visual inspections, Friuli Venezia Giulia originally deployed 21 pheromone traps in 2016 (on loan from the University of Padua), 16 of which are currently operational as five were removed for operational reasons. Deployment is partially random, but some are strategically positioned close to road and railway lines, the others in small young commercial timber plantations of typically 0.5 to 1 Ha. Sites are visited once per month.

As commercial walnut fruit plantations of J. regia are limited in Friuli Venezia Giulia they are not included in the RPS monitoring regime. 5.2.5 Commercial availability of Thousand canker disease pheromone

However, given the relative low level presence of the host, particularly in Piedmont and Lombardy, where outbreaks have occurred, the variation in susceptibility, as well as the issue of latency with respect to delayed symptom expression, the current level of monitoring intensity of timber producing trees is inadequate to reliably delimit for the presence of Thousand canker disease.

Similarly, in Veneto, despite a higher presence of host trees, predominantly plantations of J. nigra, and based on the same issues with respect to susceptibility and latency, the current level of monitoring intensity there is also inadequate to reliably delimit the disease.

Insufficient monitoring is carried out for mono-cultures of J. regia in commercial walnut fruit production in all of the regions, and for which no contingency plan exists. Such absences pose particular potential challenges with respect to disease management and further control should Thousand canker disease enter the fruit production industry.

responses.response: In line with the application of protective measures under Article 16(2) of Directive 2000/29/EC, a more reliable and accurate delimitation of the presence of Thousand canker disease, should be conducted via increased monitoring intensity in all regions. citations.text: The person responsible for the load submits to the BIP staff part 1 of the CVED for food and feed of animal origin using TRACES as well as in hard copy to notify the consignments prior to their physical arrival. However, the audit team identified that a significant number of consignments subject to enhanced controls are not notified prior to the physical arrival in the BIPs visited. However, the audit team identified that a significant number of consignments subject to enhanced controls are not notified at all prior to the physical arrival in the DPEs/DPIs visited. In BIP Genova, the competent authorities stated that they took some measures to discourage the late prenotifications of the consignments but with partial success. Conclusion on the mechanisms to ensure that consignments are presented for import controls

There is an adequate mechanism (including good cooperation with Customs) to ensure that consignments requiring enhanced controls are presented for official controls. However, the competent authorities do not systematically implement measures to ensure that food and feed business operators or their representatives provide prior notification before physical arrival of the consignments in the BIPs and DPEs, which potentially can have an impact on the planning and organisation of the official controls.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the supervision procedures in place at different competent authority levels guarantee that the design and implementation of the monitoring provide for sample representativeness, as set out by Article 2(1) and points 2.3 and 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. 15

citations.text: The audit team noted that in 2016 over 90% of sampling was completed for all categories. The achievement of the targets set in the sampling plan improved from 2014 when only 83% and 66% of the planned caecal samples were achieved for broilers and turkeys respectively. Regarding 2015, the competent authorities achieved over 95% for all categories except for bovines under 1 year of age where only 74% was achieved.

The central competent authority has introduced in the 2017 AMR monitoring plan a new supervisory element that consists of the obligation for the regional authorities to submit the regional sampling plans for review to central level. Nevertheless, the audit team noted that the instruction does not specify the different elements to be included in the information provided in order to verify effectively compliance with certain elements of 2 In their response to the draft report the competent authority provided information on actions taken after the audit to address this issue. For more information please see the action plan presented by the competent authority to address the recommendations made in this report. 3 the requirements such as percentage of the population covered and even monthly distribution of samples throughout the year which have undermined sample representativeness in the past (see points 23 and 24) 3.

The competent authorities responsible for the monitoring of AMR are clearly designated and have the necessary powers for the implementation of the harmonised monitoring of AMR. Recent improvements in the coordination between the competent authorities have had a positive impact on the achievement of the objectives of Decision 2013/652/EU, although there are still gaps in in this respect which limit the number of Salmonella isolates available for AST (when the minimum numbers are not achieved), and in the supervision of the implementation of the sampling plan, which negatively affect sample representativeness 2,3.

The audit team noted that the central competent authority did not verify if the slaughterhouses included by the regions in their sampling plans covered at least 60% of the domestic population which is the minimum percentage required by point 2.3 Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. During the audit and at the request of the audit team, the competent authority performed an evaluation of the 2015 sampling plan concluding that for bovines under 1 year of age 69.2% of the population was covered by the regional sampling plans while for pigs the figure amounted only to 47.1%. The data available did not enable the competent authority to perform the same exercise for poultry for 2014 and 2016 5.

The requirement set out in point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU that caecal samples collected at slaughterhouses shall be distributed evenly over each month of the year was not adhered to in 2014 and 2015 when sampling took place from May to December. The situation improved for 2016 and 2017 with sampling commencing in February and January respectively. The audit team noted the following: The time of approval of the AMR monitoring plans, which for 2014 and 2015 was March and for 2016 and 2017 late December of the previous year, did not allow the regions to design and issue the plans at regional level early enough to ensure that all months of the year were covered evenly. As an example, in the two regions visited the 2016 plan was issued to the local health units in February/March. Also in 2016, in the Veneto region two major poultry slaughterhouses only received the plan in May. The assignment of samples by the regions visited to the local health units did not include a monthly distribution. As a consequence the audit team noted that, in the local health units visited, sampling was not evenly distributed. 5 In their response to the draft report the competent authority noted the introduction of the updated procedure referred to in footnote 3 and confirmed that for 2017 the sampling plan has covered 71.8% and 72.5% for fattening pigs and bovines under 1 year of age. 6 The regions visited did not supervise the design and implementation of the sampling plan by the local health units to ensure both an even distribution of sampling and the successful completion of the plan 6. The competent authority have committed to approving the next sampling plans by November in order to allow the regions and the local level to implement sampling early in the subsequent year.

In the two regions visited, samples were generally taken on a Monday and Tuesday and on a few occasions on a Wednesday. This approach reduced the randomisation of the sampling days. The audit team noted that the NRL for AMR accepted samples until Friday which implies, with the sample delivery service available, that sampling could be routinely randomised from Monday to Thursday to fulfil the requirements of point 2.3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU and the EFSA guidance document 2014 9.

In the bovine slaughterhouse visited, samples were taken randomly selecting the day, with the constraints described above, and the animals to be sampled using an IT programme. In the poultry slaughterhouse visited, on the selected sampling dates most of the available lots were sampled in order to fulfil the required number of samples. In the pig slaughterhouse the sampling days and the carcasses to be sampled were selected by the sampling officer for reasons of convenience, which is not fully random 9.

The documented procedures and instructions in place could ensure adequate implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. The competent authorities have over time improved the design and implementation of the sampling plan addressing some issues that weakened this plan in the past. However, the gathering of AMR monitoring data in Italy is still not fully comparable with those obtained by other Member States. This is because further strengthening of the procedures is necessary, notably to verify that the minimum required slaughtered population is covered by the sampling and that an even distribution of sampling takes place during all months of the year.

responses.response: The central competent authority sent additional recommendations and specifications (Annex III-Letter 0003440-09/02/2017- DGSAF-MDS-P) to the regions in order to improve the sampling design and the implementation of the AMR Plan. The letter considers: - sampling strategy; - proportional allocation; - monthly distribution; - random sampling; - Salmonella isolates forward. It has already allowed to better verify the right implementation of the percentage of the population covered, the monthly distribution of samples at local level, the random sampling of day, batch(es) of carcasses. See comments in points No 8, 10, 13, 23, 24, 38 and 39.

citations.text: The activities of the sectoral offices in relation to planning and development of programmes of official controls are not covered.

The internal procedure requires an annual programme be drawn up based on available documentation and new alerts. All Territorial Offices must be audited at least once every five years. On-site audits include all relevant official control activities and specific sectors are not targeted. The activities of the central office responsible for planning and development of programmes of official controls are not covered. No annual audit programme was provided to the DG SANTE audit team.

In relation to the MH cascade audit system The programming ensures that all RPHSs and ASLs receive multiple audits within each audit cycle. The degree to which sectors are covered varies according to the planning of the sectoral offices and the RPHSs and efforts are made to prioritise according to risk; While the coverage of audits is intense, in common with the situation seen by DG Health and Food Safety in a number of other Member States, there is a gap 3 In their comments on the draft report the Veterinary and Prevention Service of the Region of Lombardy stated that they will formalize, in the next planning documents, the criteria on which to define the priorities for sector audit activities. They will take into account the relevant risk factors emerging from results of previous verification activities, as well as any other documented evidence that leads to identify possible critical areas and/or areas for improvement. 4 In their comments on the draft report the ICQRF informed the Commission services that actions had been taken, following this audit, to ensure they had access to NAS Network reference documents. 19 in coverage of the planning and programming activities carried out at the central level; The RPHSs vary in their approaches. Examples seen demonstrated that relevant risk factors were considered but final selection of topics is very much based on professional judgement of auditors and other experts. Risk-based prioritisation processes/methodologies were not transparently defined and/or documented; There is effective coordination between the Ministry and the RPHSs, and this is attributable in large measure to the co-ordination efforts of Office III and the various structures put into place.

In relation to the ICQRF, audit programming is based on covering the full range of official control activities of each Territorial Office within a five-year cycle rather than on a risk-basis. In common with the situation for MH (and in a number of other Member States), there is a gap in coverage of the planning and programming activities carried out at the central level.

recommendations.text: To ensure that cattle, sheep, goats and horses sent from other EU Member States to Italy for direct slaughter for human consumption, are eligible for sampling and testing under the national residue monitoring plan, as required by Annex IV of Directive 96/23/EC and point 2.2. of Decision 98/179/EC and that the criteria for the selection of targeted residue monitoring samples from farmed game also take into account the species as required by point 2.3.3.1 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC.

citations.text: FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS Legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex I and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version. Relevant articles or sections of the legislation cited in Annex I are referred to in the individual findings in this section of the report.

Residue monitoring plan samples from farmed game were planned to be taken from farmed game birds and not from farmed cervidae like red or fellow deer, for which farms and primary processing establishments exist in Italy. This is not in line with point 2.3.3.1 of Commission Decision 98/179/EC which requires considering the species when selecting targeted samples from animal carcasses at primary processing establishments. 80% of samples from wild boar to be tested for heavy metals were planned to be taken in one region, while wild boar is also plentiful in other regions. Representatives of the Directorate-General for Food Hygiene, Food Safety and Nutrition (DGFHFSN) met by the audit team, stated their intention to amend the residue monitoring plan for wild and farmed game to rectify above mentioned shortcomings.

Notwithstanding certain shortcomings noted for not including all animals sent for direct slaughter to Italy from other Member States in the calculation of samples to be taken, not subjecting equidae sent from other Member States for direct slaughter to residue monitoring and sampling of farmed and wild game, the timely and largely comprehensive planning contributes to the effectiveness of controls on residues. 5.1.3. recommendations.text: To ensure that sample analysis turnaround times established by the residue monitoring plan are met to ensure analyte stability and sample integrity in accordance with part 2.9 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC and to ensure the adequate implementation of measures required by Articles 15-19 of Directive 96/23/EC.

citations.text: The national residue monitoring plan stipulates that the sample analysis turnaround time is 10 working days for Group A substances and 30 working days for Group B substances . The audit team noted that these turnaround times count from the moment the sample arrives at the laboratory which analyses the sample. In many cases IZS laboratories (IZSs) sent samples to another IZS laboratory for analysis (see also findings 32 and 45), which leads to the fact that the turnaround times from sampling to finalising the laboratory report are longer than 10 or 30 days.

The audit team was provided with sample analysis turnaround time statistics. These showed that 80% of all samples analysed by the IZS laboratory were processed within the required turnaround time. However, 49% of the samples to be analysed for beta-lactam antimicrobials exceeded the 30 day turnaround time and were analysed within 70 days, and one sample within 165 days. Samples sent by the visited IZS to other IZS laboratories exceeded the 30 day deadline for 81.4% of all samples and 4.2% of samples had a turnaround time of 91 to 218 days. The long processing times may affect the analytes' stability and sample integrity (in particular for beta-lactam antimicrobials), which is not in line with the requirements laid down by part 2.9 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC. In addition, the delay with the samples' analysis may hinder the timely implementation of the follow-up measures required by Articles 15-19 of Directive 96/23/EC.

The competent authority can largely have confidence in the laboratory performance and the reliability of analytical results as all laboratories are accredited, methods are generally appropriately validated and staff well-trained. However, a few factors weaken the system, such as the long sample analysis turnaround times, the non- adequate validation for a few rare matrices/species combinations and the fact that the NRL for residues of veterinary medicinal products does not completely meet its NRL obligations and has deficiencies in its quality assurance procedures.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 are implemented.

citations.text: Staff from the Ministry of Health informed the audit team that the provisions of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/262 have not yet been implemented, and that those of Commission Regulation (EC) No 504/2008 are still applied. This is not in line with the entry into force date of Regulation (EU) 2015/262, which was 1 January 2016.

The audit team was further informed that the overall responsibility for the system of equine identification and registration had been transferred as of 20 November 2017 from the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Forestry Policy (MIPAAF) to the Ministry of Health by national law No 167. Staff from the Ministry of Health stated that the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 will be implemented as of May 2018, thus 180 days after the Law number 167 entered into force. They stated further that the `Guidelines for the managing of equidae register' (ministerial decree, 29 December 2009), the related 'Operating manual' (ministerial decree No 20318, 26 September 2011) and newly issued equine passports, which are still based on requirements of Regulation (EC) No 504/2008, will be updated by May 2018 to those of Regulation (EU) 2015/262.

A representative of the Ministry of Health informed the audit team that Italy, to comply with the single equine identification database requirement of Article 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262, intends in future to require that all equine registration data are directly inserted into the existing national animal database (BDN). Staff from the DGFHFSN met by the audit team stated that their aim is to complete this task by the end of 2019.

The MIPAAF has delegated the responsibility of supervision of the equine identification for all ANA passport issuing bodies and AIA registered equines to the representatives of the AIA. One representative of AIA met by the audit team stated 14 that he had access to all databases of ANA as well as to the AIA database in which he could see whether an equine was registered or not, alive or not and whether the equine was allowed for human consumption or not. A representative from the Ministry of Health informed the audit team that ASL staff responsible for controls at slaughterhouses and farms with regards to equidae have full access to the databases of all equine passport issuing bodies, the BDE and the BDN database. The audit team checked the validity of several living and slaughtered equines in the BDE database and found that these had been correctly reflected. In one case the information in the BDE stated the horse was stolen when accessed by the AIA official, while the publicly available data of the BDE stated that the equine was dead.

Five percent of all holdings with equidae shall be annually controlled to verify the correct application of the equidae identification and registration system, as outlined in point 31 of the operating manual for the management of the equidae register. The selection of these holdings is risk-based using clearly defined criteria. The above is in line with Article 3(4) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262. However, the audit team found, based on information provided by the MIPAAF, that out of the 19 regions and 2 autonomous provinces, 5 had met this target, 5 achieved between 4% and 5%, 1 between 3% and 4%, 3 between 2% and 3%, 3 between 1% and 2% and 4 less than 1% of the required controls. This is not in line with nationally established inspection frequencies targets.

A checklist has been developed, to check the relevant equine identification and registration requirements of Regulation (EC) No 504/2008 at holdings. This had been used during official controls on the horse farm visited by the audit team confirming compliance with equine passport and registration requirements. The audit team found at this farm, that the national requirements for the register of equidae and the equine passports requirements of Regulation (EC) No 504/2008 were fulfilled, but not yet of the equine passport content structure as foreseen by Annex 1 to Regulation (EU) 2015/262. The audit team randomly selected several 15 horses and confirmed that they had been provided with a microchip as indicated in the passport.

Current EU rules governing the equine passport system have not yet been implemented and the control system based on previous EU rules demonstrates several weaknesses with regards to controls on equine identification requirements. Notwithstanding this, documented guidance on how to assess equine passport and food chain information in slaughterhouses decreases the risk that equines, ineligible for human consumption, enter the food chain.

citations.text: The audit team noted that The method of grid based visual inspection and the associated sampling is in line with requirements of Article 3(1) of the Decision; In both annual surveys, a considerable percentage of the grid squares in the BZ and '20km zone' were inspected during winter months. recommendations.text: Ensure that any exemptions from the application of Article 13(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC, established for plants and plant products, apply only to small quantities provided that there is no risk of harmful organisms spreading in the Community, in line with Article 13b(3) of the same Directive.

citations.text: The Single Authority stated that the concession applies to all 'non-commercial' imports, which includes imports by passengers, by post and courier. Due to the relatively large quantity of plants to which the concession applies, most non-commercial imports fall within its scope, and do not therefore need to be accompanied by a phytosanitary certificate or be subjected to systematic inspection.

In addition, the Single Authority, and the RPS visited by the audit team, stated that the small quantity concession prevented the effective control of passenger, postal and courier imports. They elaborated that this was because the scope of the concession, in terms of both maximum weight and modes of entry it applies to, means that it effectively captures all such non-commercial consignments. Consequently, the controls of these modes of entry were focused almost exclusively on detecting prohibited articles, rather than controlling regulated commodities.

Furthermore, the Single Authority stated that the scope of the concession was historic and that they were not aware of any risk-assessment used to arrive at the maximum quantities or the modes of entry it applies to. It has therefore not been established that there is no risk of harmful organisms spreading in the Community as a result of this concession, which is not in line with Article 13b(3) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The extent of the small quantity concession, in terms of the maximum quantities covered and the modes of entry it applies to, means that most non-commercial imports of regulated articles are effectively excluded from the scope of systematic plant health checks. As such, the imports which take place under the concession present a potential risk of introducing harmful organisms into the Community. 14
