recommendations.text: Ensure that comprehensive documented procedures are put in place containing information and instructions for staff performing the official controls required under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2017/675, in line with Article 12 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (previously Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004). 8

citations.text: FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS Legal acts quoted in this report are provided in Annex I and refer, where applicable, to the last amended version in force at the time of the audit. Relevant provisions of those legal acts that are audited against in the chapters of this report are specified in the appendix.

Neither of the two ports visited have the necessary infrastructure for implementing biosecurity measures, i.e. facilities for the inspection, cleansing and disinfection of livestock vehicles. Whilst the competent authorities at the port of Palermo could provide a short list of companies able to carry out such disinfection either on-the-spot or in the vicinity of the port, these companies are not listed in the Memorandum of Understanding and the audit team did not see evidence of any formal agreement or contract in place to procure these services. The Memorandum of Understanding between the Ministry of Health and Customs at Civitavecchia Port names the cleansing and disinfection company, located within the port area, to be used if required, although the only equipment they have are sprays and nebulisers. Poor cooperation on the Civitavecchia port authority's side, despite repeated requests by Customs (seen by the audit team) to set up an appropriate area on the quay where cleansing and disinfection of vehicles could take place, means that such facilities have not yet been established. The Memorandum of Understanding at Livorno port mentions that the cleansing and disinfection should be carried out by authorised companies and in specifically identified areas of the terminals but does not go so far as to identify either the companies concerned or the areas of the terminals where cleansing and disinfection should take place. This means that the competent authorities cannot confidently avail of the option provided for in Article 3(4)(a) or Article 3(4)(b)(ii) of Decision (EU) 2017/675. 5.1.4. Designation of crossing points

Ports where livestock vehicles or vessels could enter Italy are limited by the current shipping routes. In theory, all Italian ports are a potential point of entry for livestock vehicles or vessels. Although not legally required to do so, the fact that the competent authorities have not designated specific ports for the entry of livestock vehicles means that they are obliged to ensure that the requirements of Articles 2 and 3 of Decision (EU) 2017/675 are respected at all entry points, including those without a BIP. The audit team 4 only saw evidence of local procedures (Memoranda of Understanding) in place at 3 out of 110 sea border entry points notified to the European Commission under Article 39(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/399 (Schengen Borders Code) and published in the Official Journal of the European Union, (4) and 17 of these sea borders are ports with BIPs. Whilst the Ministry of Health has requested Customs to carry out checks on returning livestock vehicles and on the drivers' declarations (see findings 1 and 3) as part of their routine duties in all ports of entry, it has not provided any detailed instructions to Customs on how these checks should be done to ensure that only compliant vehicles may be allowed to enter. 5.1.5. Administrative provisions implementing EU rules

The instructions for checks on livestock vehicles provided in these memoranda are not sufficiently detailed with regard to the provisions laid down in Articles 2 and 3 of Decision (EU) 2017/675 regarding documentary checks, visual checks, disinfection, action to be taken in case of non-conformity and requirements for record-keeping, to be fully in line with the requirements of Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 (5) (see also findings 5 and 8). 5.1.6. Use of databases

Whilst local Memoranda of Understanding between the Ministry of Health and Customs have been formalised recently for three ports, these are insufficiently clear or detailed as regards responsibilities (who does what, when and how). Lack of harmonisation of these memoranda, lack of specific training of staff and information on how to identify livestock vehicles and on those disinfectants/active ingredients which are effective against Foot and Mouth Disease, collectively undermine confidence in the effectiveness and consistency of official controls, were such controls carried out. These weaknesses are mitigated by the fact that the competent authorities stated that there has been no traffic in livestock or feed vehicles for several years.

The placing of responsibility on the shipping companies for ensuring that livestock vehicles entering Italy are notified to the authorities in advance and making the companies liable for the costs of disinfection should such vehicles arrive without having been appropriately cleaned, mitigates the risk of unclean and non-disinfected 6 vehicles entering the EU. However, should the competent authority decide to carry out disinfection on-the-spot or in the vicinity of the port, the memoranda do not provide sufficient practical guidance to officials on how to arrange this, especially given that no formal agreements or contracts have been concluded with companies capable of carrying out the cleaning and disinfection in appropriate premises.

recommendations.text: The CCA should provide the necessary guidance and tools to regional and local authorities to ensure that controls over compliance with the applicable EU legislation on FIA at the level of the FBOs, and with particular attention to the FIA users, are carried out in a consistent manner at all levels, in accordance with article 4, point 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: There is no common checklist or guidance at national level to control FBOs regarding FIA use, hence the local authorities using different approaches for these controls (documents to be requested, aspects to be covered, controlling FIA either during inspection or audit). In one of the Regions visited, the local authorities prepared a detailed checklist which acts as guidance for those controls. In the other Region, officials are advised to use a checklist prepared for the controls of FIA in approved establishments handling food of animal origin, also in controls at registered establishments. The depth of the controls also depends on the expertise and knowledge of the individual inspectors. Different levels of knowledge on FIA requirements were noted amongst the inspectors.

Regarding the FIA users, local authorities in the first Region visited explained that they have recently prepared a pilot checklist which will allow them to cover the aspects not covered to date. The audit team noted that, since this is a relatively new development, inspectors do not follow a structured approach, and sometimes rely solely on the information provided by the FBOs. Some of the elements that the inspectors omitted to examine were: the specifications of raw materials for possible presence of FIA, the recipe of the product examined (which should be the starting point of such controls), the identification of the correct food category; in addition, no requests were made for additional clarification as to why certain additives were not added on the label of the final product although found present in one of the ingredients (carry-over principle).

With regard to FIA users, as indicated at regional level, there is no specific checklist for registered establishments. The approach followed by the inspectors during controls of FIA users was, in the majority of the cases, not consistent (as to what, when and how to 10 check) and not well structured. Some of the inspections were detailed and complete (checking specific requirement for labelling, knowledge of Aluminium-lakes requirements for colours) whereas in others certain elements were not addressed.

Some of the omissions observed by the audit team were: absence of checks of the specifications of the different ingredients to see if some additives could be present, and which of these additives could have a technological function in the final product; failure to note that the specifications regarding purity criteria were incomplete; and conduct of calculations using the weight of the intermediate product (dough) and not of the final product, as appropriate. Nevertheless, when asked by the audit team, in all cases the inspectors were able to re-evaluate or seek for more information for those aspects.

In the second Region visited the audit team was informed that inspectors cover the topic of FIA at FIA users' level during audits. Only in one case the inspectors confirmed that they would start using the dedicated checklist for approved establishments, also for registered establishments as recommended by the regional authority.

Official controls at FIA users' level are lacking in completeness and depth resulting in an insufficient verification of the compliance with FIA legislation. The absence of specific guidance or instructions creates inconsistencies in the approach followed by the inspectors (i.e. omission to ask for the recipe of the product being examined in relation to FIA used, define the product category and examine the specifications of all the raw materials used in the production of a that product). Adding to that, the limited hands-on experience of the inspectors leads to the oversight of certain issues regarding FIA during such controls. 16

citations.text: Substantial resources have been allocated for research purposes particularly for understanding the parameters of A. bungii biology such as behaviour and host acceptance of young trees with trunks of less than 6-7 cm diameter or tree species other than Prunus through artificial diet and oviposition trials. The studies have been carried out on Olea europaea, Punica granatum, Diospyros kaki, Populus alba, as well as on the ornamental Prunus cerasifera cv. pissardii. Despite historical data indicating the opposite, Prunus cerasifera cv. pissardii cannot be excluded from being a potential host as A. bungii females are capable of laying eggs on this species in the absence of other more suitable hosts of Prunus.

The RPS stated that at the time of the audit, coinciding with the beginning of the A. bungii adult flight period in Lombardy, all infested plants had already been felled. The audit team visited a public green site with Prunus cerasifera cv. pissardii, a private backyard garden and a disposal site of felled and chipped plants located in one of the municipalities of the demarcated area and noted that: Ornamental plants of Prunus cerasifera cv. pissardii in both public and private green sites although not excluded from surveillance are not subject to systematic 12 inspections. The RPS stated that of the 1,156 cherry plum trees checked during 2018, they never came across infested trees of Prunus cerasifera cv. pissardii and that from the statistical point of view the intensive surveillance required by the legislation does not necessarily require the compulsory inspection of all trees located within the demarcated area (see also section 5.3.1); In early 2019, the RPS inspectors found exit holes of A. bungii in one out of two trees of Prunus domestica located in a private garden. Both trees under suspicion were felled. The second non-symptomatic tree was felled due to its proximity to the symptomatic one; it was proved not to be infested. However, not all Prunus plants were felled within a 100m radius of the infested sites, which under the Decision was not compliant with the eradication approach in place at the time of the audit; Felled Prunus plants had been chipped by using a tree trunk grinder and were ready for dispatch in an energy producing plant outside the demarcated area. In general, the size of many chips was more than 2.5cm thickness and width, which is not compliant with Article 8.3(b) of the Decision. The RPS stated that the risk of A. bungii larvae surviving to adulthood is minimal as there are no records or scientific evidence that the pest is capable of completing its development under adverse environmental conditions outside tree trunks.

Both RPSs carry out intensive surveillance for the detection of new outbreaks of A. bungii on Prunus plants. However, the exclusion of Prunus cerasifera cv. pissardii from the systematic inspections is based mainly on observations and not on justified scientific evidence.

recommendations.text: To effectively verify that feed business operators meet the requirements for hazard identification in their respective hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) plans.

citations.text: For the establishments listed in section 2 of this report, the audit team scrutinised the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on the assessment of operators' HACCP plans. The audit team noted that the assessment of the hazard identification part of the HACCP-plan by the inspectors was deficient in five establishments out of the nine visited: 1) In general, the hazard identification part of the HACCP plans seen was either absent or was very generic without the level of detail necessary for proper hazard identification and subsequent risk assessment. Notwithstanding that one inspector met could notice this deficiency during the interview, the failure of the operators to identify relevant hazards, as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, was not reflected in any of the most recent inspection reports seen. 4 2) During the interviews, the inspectors experienced difficulties to identify relevant hazards for calcium carbonate, amino acids produced by fermentation, and the feed additives butylated hydroxyanisole and propyl gallate. In relation to pesticides, only those referred to in section IV of Annex I to Directive 2002/32/EC (banned substances) had been taken into consideration while authorised pesticides referred to in Annexes II, III and V to Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 were largely not considered for the purposes of the hazard identification.

Planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that official controls are carried out on all operators, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. However, the effectiveness of the inspections is weakened by shortcomings in the competent authority's assessment of (i) operators' HACCP plans, (ii) appropriateness of operators' tests on homogeneity of mixing and cross-contamination, and (iii) operators' traceability systems. The fact that these issues were often not identified in the inspection reports meant that operators were unaware that they were not operating in compliance with legislation. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To effectively verify that feed business operators meet the requirements for appropriate checks of the effectiveness of mixing (homogeneity) and minimisation of cross-contamination.
recommendations.legal_basis: part 2(b) and 3(b) of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: Verification of establishments' tests on homogeneity of mixing and minimisation of cross- contamination, required by part 2(b) and 3(b) of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, forms part of the inspections, when applicable. In three compound feed manufacturers visited, the audit team scrutinised operators' documentation on the related testing and interviewed the inspectors normally controlling those establishments. The following observations were made: 1) For the controls on homogeneity of mixing, all three operators used naturally occurring markers (e.g., nutritional constituents or salt) which does not provide sufficient information on the homogeneity since the markers are already homogeneously distributed in the matrix. In addition, the number of samples taken (1-3 at two establishments) was statistically inadequate. The operators' written procedures did not contain a comprehensive description of all the steps necessary for the assessment of homogeneity of mixing. 2) For the controls on cross-contamination, the operators' documentation seen did not contain clear procedures for sampling which is critical due to heterogeneous distribution of analytes in non-target feed. In one case, the sensitivity of the analytical method used was not sufficient to detect the presence of the analyte at the levels deemed acceptable for unavoidable transfer of the substance to non-target feed. The deficiencies identified by the audit team were not reflected in any of the most recent inspection reports seen. Thus, combined, the official controls examined by the audit team only partly verified that the operators met the requirements laid down in part 2(b) and 3(b) of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

Planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that official controls are carried out on all operators, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. However, the effectiveness of the inspections is weakened by shortcomings in the competent authority's assessment of (i) operators' HACCP plans, (ii) appropriateness of operators' tests on homogeneity of mixing and cross-contamination, and (iii) operators' traceability systems. The fact that these issues were often not identified in the inspection reports meant that operators were unaware that they were not operating in compliance with legislation. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To effectively verify that feed business operators meet the requirement for taking and keeping samples of ingredients and from each batch of products manufactured and placed on the market.
recommendations.legal_basis: part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: Routine inspections include the verification of operators' traceability systems, including the operators' obligation to take samples of ingredients and from each batch of products manufactured and placed on the market, or from each specific portion of production (in the case of continuous production) in sufficient quantities, using a procedure pre-established by the manufacturer (hereinafter retained samples), as required in part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The audit team scrutinised this verification and noted that neither of the two food business operators visited had taken and kept the retained samples of the feed materials produced. All three compound feed manufactures did not take retained samples from packaged feed additives/premixtures (the representative of one operator stated that those were kept at the headquarters, which could not be verified by the audit team). In two compound feed producers, the retained samples were not sealed. These observations are not in line with the legal requirements established in part 4 of the section "Quality control" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and were not recorded in any of the most recent inspection reports seen.

Planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that official controls are carried out on all operators, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. However, the effectiveness of the inspections is weakened by shortcomings in the competent authority's assessment of (i) operators' HACCP plans, (ii) appropriateness of operators' tests on homogeneity of mixing and cross-contamination, and (iii) operators' traceability systems. The fact that these issues were often not identified in the inspection reports meant that operators were unaware that they were not operating in compliance with legislation. 5.2.2 Sampling and analysis 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authorities' samplers have appropriate equipment (i.e. a mechanical or automatic divider necessary for preparation of final samples in case of the control of constituents or substances likely to be distributed non-uniformly in feed), and that they consistently apply sampling techniques ensuring the legal and technical validity of the samples.
recommendations.legal_basis: parts 3, 5.2, 9.4 and 10 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, Articles 2(1), 5(1)(f) and 34(1)(5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team observed official sampling at the three compound feed manufacturers visited (the matrix and parameters to be controlled were suggested by the audit team). In addition, a number of sampling records from 2018 and onwards were scrutinised. Based on these, the following observations were made by the audit team: 1) Due to the absence of mechanical or automatic dividers, the samplers prepared all of the final samples by quartering, which for the purpose of measuring constituents or substances likely to be distributed in a non-uniform way in feed, cannot ensure a representative sample (e.g., in case of control for cross-contamination in compound feed ­ as clearly outlined in the PNAA). This is not in line with the requirements laid down in part 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. However, this deficiency is mitigated in case of controls for mycotoxins and GMOs in unprocessed feed materials (grains) where the whole aggregate sample is sent to the respective official laboratory (see findings 26 and 35). 2) In one sampling observed, the collection of the material was performed by the operator's staff, using the operator's equipment. A similar approach was suggested in another sampling exercise (which did not eventually happen after discussion with the audit team which did not endorse the sampler's suggestion). This methodology is not in line with the requirement that official samples shall be taken by persons authorised for that purpose by the competent authority, see part 3 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. 3) In another sampling observed, the size of the sampled portion recorded in the sampling protocol was not consistent with the sampled portion actually sampled. Moreover, in a number of sampling reports seen, no sampling portion was recorded ­ this is not in line with the requirements laid down in part 10 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. 4) In several sampling reports seen for the control of cross-contamination, the distribution pattern of the analyte was erroneously determined as uniform thus leading to taking considerably fewer incremental samples than required in part 5.2 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. Collectively, the above deficiencies seen by the audit team undermine the utility and legal validity of the official feed samples taken. 7 5.2.2.3 Testing of official feed samples

recommendations.text: To ensure that the procedures adopted by official laboratories for the preparation of aggregate samples of unprocessed feed materials (grains) for testing mycotoxins and GMOs, are appropriate to achieve complete homogenisation of the material. 10
recommendations.legal_basis: part 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

citations.text: In the two official laboratories visited, the audit team scrutinised the system of preparation of the aggregate samples of unprocessed feed materials (grains) provided by the ASLs' samplers for testing on mycotoxins and GMOs (see finding 26), and following division into final and laboratory samples. The audit team noted that in neither laboratory was there documentary evidence that the procedure applied achieved complete homogenisation of the aggregate samples required in part 9.4 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009 (control of constituents, including GMOs, or substances likely to be distributed non-uniformly in feed materials). In one laboratory, there was no standard operating procedure on the preparation of pertinent aggregate samples. recommendations.text: Ensure that all existing risk factors are appropriately taken into consideration during the statistically based surveys in the demarcated areas of Apulia and Tuscany, as required by Articles 10 and 15 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201.

citations.text: The audit team noted that: · As the 2020 surveys were carried out with a non-statistical, square based approach, the direct comparison of the results with the 2021 survey results is not possible; · The statistical surveys were designed in line with the relevant provisions of the EU legislation. The higher risk category was correctly applied for the first 400m parts of the BZs and for the epidemiological units with olive groves and Prunus sp. orchards; · The repeated detection of Xf in certain parts of the containment area indicates the presence of the inoculum in that area. Consequently, the categorisation as high risk of the first 400m part of the area from the border of the BZ instead of the rest of the IZ could have enhanced the chance of the detection of any positive there and so reassure the protective function of the BZ; · Only the first 50m part of the 400m circles around the positive plants, removed earlier in the containment area, were considered as high risk, which is not in line with the EFSA guidelines; · With the number of inspections and samples the level of confidence and targeted prevalence of the pathogen, required by the relevant provisions of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 were met or exceeded in each part of the DAs; · The number of samples taken from each square was in line with the requirements of the statistical method. However, the presence of symptomatic specified and other plants in the square was not taken into consideration as a risk factor for selecting the plants for sampling; · The surveys were carried out in a period which is appropriate for the detection of the infection of the specified plants; · In the central database, information is available about the individual plants which were sampled during the previous surveys. This information was not made available for the ARIF agents, although it could have been a useful asset for the selection of plants to be sampled; · ARIF agents implemented the surveys fully in line with the RPS guidance documents. The relevant data are thoroughly registered in the IT system, which ensures full traceability; · The applied pooling system enables the analysis of higher numbers of samples with the existing laboratory capacities, however, it increases the time needed for the confirmation of positive results by 5-10 days on average; · The figures for the 2021 surveys clearly indicate the considerable efforts made by the authorities. Although the number of positives is relatively small compared to the total 16 number of samples, their territorial distribution indicates certain patterns of the distribution of the disease in the DAs, which necessitates the fine-tuning of the 2022 surveys according to the identified risk. · Except for the Alberobello outbreak, Xf was not detected in the Salento BZ during the 2021 surveys. In the Salento containment area there are outbreak hot spots, which require particular attention and quick actions. · The high number of positives in the Monopoli DA indicates the strong presence of bacterial inoculum and the associated risk of spread.

The 2021 statistical surveys were planned and implemented generally in line with requirements of the EU legislation and the achieved level of compliance and targeted prevalence exceeded the minimum required by the EU legislation. Although a generally risk-based approach was used for targeting the specified plant population with the surveys, not all existing risk factors were taken into consideration. Therefore, the achieved results may not reflect entirely the actual spread of the disease in the DAs.

The audit team noted that: · The planning of the statistical surveys was in line with provisions of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. The fine-tuned design of the 2021 took into consideration sufficiently the risk factors, including those which were identified during the 2020 surveys; · The implementation of the statistically sound inspections and sampling was compromised, as access to some parts of the squares was impossible or limited (hilly landscape, impenetrable forests, holiday properties); · Due to high number of plant species tested positive in the IZs, which are all present in each of the established epidemiological units, the pragmatic approach used for the distribution of the samples among host species may not provide comprehensive feedback about the actual spread of the disease; · The number of positive tested plants and vectors indicate that the bacterial inoculum is present in the BZ, mainly in its promontory part. 26 5.7.3 Surveillance in the infected zone

Significant efforts were made to implement the surveys in the DA and in its vicinity in line with the EU rules. The existing risk factors were correctly considered for the planning, however access issues to certain parts of the Monte Argentario promontory and to private properties and the very high number of host species present compromised the possibility to obtain a full picture about the spread of the disease.

citations.text: The inability of the surveillance to detect promptly the virus in wild birds (detection in wild birds happened after outbreaks in poultry establishments) contrasts with the fact that all competent authorities considered circulation of the virus in wild birds as the main cause for most of the initial outbreaks of the disease in both regions. The NRL confirmed this a posteriori by virus phylogenetic studies. That sub-optimal effectiveness cannot be considered in line with provisions laid down in Articles 26(2) and (4) and 27 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, on the need to design and apply surveillance in a way that is appropriate and proportionate to the objectives pursued and to the risk factors involved in order to ensure the timely detection of the presence of the targeted disease.

Although the competent authorities have made considerable efforts to increase the sensitivity of surveillance for HPAI in wild birds, the tool however was not effective as an early warning system. That raises questions about the suitability of the design, the proper application, and the cost-effectiveness of that surveillance, as there is consensus among all relevant parties that the HPAI virus was circulating in wild birds in the affected areas before it was detected in poultry.

citations.text: In the cases checked by the audit team, turkey producers notified suspect cases of HPAI quickly, in most cases timely. In contrast, the audit team saw examples of affected layer hen establishments where the operator had not notified the authorities despite experiencing mortality rates of four or five times the usual daily average for a few days, or of other significant deviations in other production parameters. That is not in line with 10 requirements laid down in Article 18(1)(a) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The effective systems to raise and maintain public awareness and the good laboratory support helped the authorities to identify and confirm most cases of HPAI in poultry quickly. The delayed notification of suspect cases by certain operators is still a cause for concern as it may facilitate the spread of the disease in areas with a high density of 13 poultry.

recommendations.text: To make appropriate arrangements to accelerate the analysis of the results of epidemiological enquiries in case of suspicion and confirmation of HPAI so that the competent authorities can take well informed decisions on the application of temporary restrictions before the disease is confirmed, and on the establishment, boundaries, and prioritisation of disease control measures in restricted zones. Articles 55(1)(e) and (f), 56(a)(ii), 57(2)(e), 62(1) and 64(1)(f) and (2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and Articles 8(3), 9, 21(1)(c) and 23(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687 ­ on the contribution of epidemiological enquiries to inform which disease control measures to apply and where. Articles 5(1)(a) and 12(2) and (3) (read with point 5 in Chapter II of Annex II thereto) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 ­ on procedures and/or arrangements to ensure the effectiveness of official controls and other official activities, to verify them, and to take corrective action and update them as appropriate when shortcomings with their application are identified. Article 43(2)(d)(iii) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 ­ on the availability of operational expert groups as part of the contingency plan for HPAI. , and

citations.text: According to representatives of the field epidemiology teams and to SVL staff who performed those enquiries, the current model of epidemiological enquiry is too burdensome, and it requires gathering too much information, especially in the face of multiple outbreaks, and thus, it was not a suitable tool to inform quickly on the best possible measures mentioned above. That is not in line with general requirements laid down in Articles 5(1)(a) and 12(2) and (3) (read with point 5 in Chapter II of Annex II thereto) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, for the competent authorities to have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness of official controls and other 11 official activities, to verify them, and to take corrective action and update them as appropriate when they identify shortcomings with their application.

The shortcomings mentioned above did not allow the competent authorities to analyse quickly a sufficient number of records and information to ascertain quickly the likely spread of the disease and determine which preliminary disease control measures they had to take to prevent it. Thus, they could not fulfil the fundamental objectives of the epidemiological enquiries to inform decisions on application of control measures as provided for in Articles 55(1)(e) and (f), 56(a)(ii), 57(2)(e), 62(1) and 64(1)(f) and (2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and Articles 8(3), 9, 21(1)(c) and 23(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The competent authorities did not obtain timely the necessary information from the analysis of the epidemiological enquiries carried out in affected establishments to understand the likely spread of the disease, notably in areas with a high density of susceptible establishments exposed to a high level of environmental infection and frequency of contacts between them. Hence, they could not take the right decisions and adopt preliminary restrictions and additional control measures rapidly to contain the spread of the disease, as they had undertaken in response to a previous recommendation of the Commission services.

The competent authorities were aware of the dense and frequent network of contacts occurring between many of those establishments, especially because most of them belong to the same few companies. The fast evolution of the disease confirmed that those circumstances were not properly considered in accordance with Article 64(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 21(1)(c) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687, when the authorities delimitated the boundaries and size of the restricted zones to contain the spread of the disease and did not establish a further restricted zone immediately, precisely to prevent that.

The competent authorities did not evaluate swiftly all relevant epidemiological criteria and establish immediately a further restricted zone in the area of Veneto where the epizootic began and which they considered of very high risk for the spread of HPAI. That delay undermined the effectiveness of the additional control measures they applied, which therefore were not sufficient to stop the spread of the disease before it reached epizootic proportions and expanded far beyond the initially affected area.

However, certain shortcomings, such as a) the lack of adequate epidemiological expertise to analyse the dynamics of the disease quickly, anticipate its evolution, and advice appropriately on actions to curtail its spread, b) the delays during the initial stages of the epizootic to decide on establishing a further restricted zone, and c) the incapability to find quickly adequate solutions to the problems experienced with application of animal depopulation, indicate that the operation of the national and regional disease control centres was not fully operational, which is not in line with Article 43(2)(a) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The disease control centres established at national, regional, and local level during the epizootic coordinated application of the main control measures in the affected areas effectively. However, they all failed to take certain important decisions at critical times, and thus, they did not prevent the spread of the disease effectively.

recommendations.text: To take appropriate action to improve the effectiveness of the biosecurity measures applied by operators of poultry establishments, by: a) evaluating their suitability to mitigate the prevailing risk factors involved in the areas where they are situated according to the local circumstances and practices, b) organising awareness and training initiatives tailored to the results of that evaluation, and c) applying official controls to verify their proper application. Thus, they will be able to prevent the introduction and minimise the spread of HPAI, in particular in areas with a high risk of incursion of the disease via migratory wild birds. Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (b) and (c), (4) and (5), and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 ­ on responsibilities on disease prevention and biosecurity. Articles 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 ­ on general obligations of the competent authorities to have procedures and/or arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness of official controls. and 35

citations.text: According to the analysis of the competent authorities, local airborne spread played a significant role in transmitting the infection in areas with a very high density of establishments (e.g., facilitated by the proximity between establishments and by the use of force ventilation), together with the risk of environmental infection associated with wild birds. However, the industry had not adapted disease preventive measures properly to mitigate the impact of those critical risk factors, and the competent authorities had not adapted their verification activities to ensure that the measures applied by the industry were suitable for that purpose. Therefore, all that evidence had not been properly considered to guarantee that operators in the poultry industry can fulfil their responsibilities to minimise the risks of spread of HPAI applying appropriate biosecurity rules in line with the requirements laid down in Articles 10(1)(a)(iii), (b) and (c), (4) and (5), and 11(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The official controls, despite their extensive application and largely positive outcome, did not contribute sufficiently to correct the shortcomings related to biosecurity that likely facilitated the spread of the disease during the 2021-2022 epizootic. The shortcomings mentioned above did not allow the competent authorities to analyse quickly a sufficient number of records and information to ascertain quickly the likely spread of the disease and determine which preliminary disease control measures they had to take to prevent it. Thus, they could not fulfil the fundamental objectives of the epidemiological enquiries to inform decisions on application of control measures as provided for in Articles 55(1)(e) and (f), 56(a)(ii), 57(2)(e), 62(1) and 64(1)(f) and (2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, and Articles 8(3), 9, 21(1)(c) and 23(a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The competent authorities did not obtain timely the necessary information from the analysis of the epidemiological enquiries carried out in affected establishments to understand the likely spread of the disease, notably in areas with a high density of susceptible establishments exposed to a high level of environmental infection and frequency of contacts between them. Hence, they could not take the right decisions and adopt preliminary restrictions and additional control measures rapidly to contain the spread of the disease, as they had undertaken in response to a previous recommendation of the Commission services.

The competent authorities were aware of the dense and frequent network of contacts occurring between many of those establishments, especially because most of them belong to the same few companies. The fast evolution of the disease confirmed that those circumstances were not properly considered in accordance with Article 64(2)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 21(1)(c) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687, when the authorities delimitated the boundaries and size of the restricted zones to contain the spread of the disease and did not establish a further restricted zone immediately, precisely to prevent that.

The competent authorities did not evaluate swiftly all relevant epidemiological criteria and establish immediately a further restricted zone in the area of Veneto where the epizootic began and which they considered of very high risk for the spread of HPAI. That delay undermined the effectiveness of the additional control measures they applied, which therefore were not sufficient to stop the spread of the disease before it reached epizootic proportions and expanded far beyond the initially affected area.

In both regions, however, given the size and evolution of the epizootic, there were important delays (several days and even weeks) in the process of killing of poultry in infected establishments and, in removing the carcasses of killed or dead poultry and of other contaminated products (e.g., feed and litter) from affected establishments. The preliminary studies carried out by the national reference centre for the epidemiology of avian influenza seem to demonstrate that those delays contributed to the local spread of the disease. Those studies indicated as well that the risk of transmission was exacerbated by force ventilation, in particular between establishments keeping turkeys, that used it, and other situated nearby keeping mainly broilers and layer hens. These shortcomings are not in compliance with EU requirements laid down in Article 61(1)(b) and (c) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 12(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. 5.1.1.4 Contact (epidemiologically linked) establishments ­ Specific measures

The competent authorities did not obtain timely the necessary information from the analysis of the epidemiological enquiries carried out in affected establishments to understand the likely spread of the disease, notably in areas with a high density of susceptible establishments exposed to a high level of environmental infection and frequency of contacts between them. Hence, they could not take the right decisions and adopt preliminary restrictions and additional control measures rapidly to contain the spread of the disease, as they had undertaken in response to a previous recommendation of the Commission services.

The increasing delays in the killing and disposal of animals and of other products that may be contaminated, gradually undermined the effectiveness of other containment measures and was one of the main drivers of the further spread of the disease during the worst of the epizootic. 5.1.2Diagnosis of HPAI

The impossibility to apply targeted preventive killing in protection zones in some of the high-risk affected areas did not allow the competent authorities to reduce the density of susceptible poultry as quickly within those zones as the epidemiological situation required. Considering that that was the preferred choice of the competent authorities based on their experience and the analysis of the situation, that cannot be considered fully in line with provisions of Article 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2020/687. 5.1.3.3 Further restricted zones

Although the competent authorities established restricted zones rapidly once they confirmed the presence of HPAI in poultry establishments, other shortcomings, such as the limited availability of means to apply animal depopulation and carcass disposal and the shortage of personnel to visit quickly high-risk establishments within those zones, undermined the quick application of measures to contain the disease and the prevention of its spread.

The application of preventive killing to sufficiently reduce the poultry population in high-risk areas quickly and stop the spread of the disease was not possible due to resource constraints as all animal depopulation capacity was compromised by the numerous affected establishments the. The impact of that shortcoming was partially mitigated by the decisive action of the competent authorities and the cooperation of the industry to send for slaughter as many poultry as possible from establishments situated within restricted zones.

The shortcomings highlighted in the previous points are not in line with requirements of Articles 13(1)(a), 43(2)(c)(i) and (iii), and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on the responsibilities of the competent authorities to have access to adequate facilities and equipment and to have an effective organisation to be capable to take the necessary disease control measures, including disposal of animals that may be contaminated or contribute to the spread of the disease, in the event of an animal health crisis like the recent HPAI epizootic.

The competent authorities had not taken adequate administrative steps and made the necessary logistical arrangements to ensure sufficient capacity to collect and dispose safely of the carcases of dead and killed poultry in establishments where the presence of HPAI was confirmed or as a preventive measure in areas affected by the disease. This was even more evident in the region of Veneto and caused significant delays in the depopulation of establishments and accumulation of carcases, which significantly undermined the effectiveness of other measures to contain the spread of the disease. 5.1.5Cleaning and disinfection

However, certain shortcomings, such as a) the lack of adequate epidemiological expertise to analyse the dynamics of the disease quickly, anticipate its evolution, and advice appropriately on actions to curtail its spread, b) the delays during the initial stages of the epizootic to decide on establishing a further restricted zone, and c) the incapability to find quickly adequate solutions to the problems experienced with application of animal depopulation, indicate that the operation of the national and regional disease control centres was not fully operational, which is not in line with Article 43(2)(a) and (d) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Neither the national nor the regional disease control centres reacted quickly enough to make available sufficient additional staff to attend the demands of that SVL during the worst weeks of the epizootic. That was not in line with requirements laid down in Articles 13(1)(a) and 43(2)(c)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on responsibilities of the competent authorities to have qualified personnel and an effective organisation to apply disease control measures effectively, and on application of the contingency plan for HPAI. 5.2.5 Availability of equipment and materials

The shortcomings described above are not in line with requirements of Articles 13(1)(a), 43(2)(c)(i) and (iii), and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 on the responsibilities of the competent authorities to have access to adequate facilities and equipment and to have an effective organisation to be capable to take the necessary disease control measures, including the rapid killing of animals from affected establishments, in the event of an animal health crisis like the recent HPAI epizootic. They are not in line either with provisions on the application of the contingency plan for HPAI laid down in Article 43(2)(c)(iii), (v) and (vi) of the said Regulation to make available all appropriate materials and resources necessary for the rapid and efficient eradication of the disease. 5.2.6Diagnostic capacity in case of an emergency

The competent authorities counted on well-developed and up-to-date contingency plans and operational manuals to respond to outbreaks of HPAI. However, some authorities responsible for some of the high-risk areas more affected by the 2021-2022 epizootic, had not taken adequate action to make sure that they could avail timely of adequate human, 30 technical and material resources to contain the disease rapidly and effectively. Those shortcomings were instrumental in facilitating the spread and long duration of the epizootic in those areas, and thus contributed to its high economic impact.

The disease control centres established at national, regional, and local level during the epizootic coordinated application of the main control measures in the affected areas effectively. However, they all failed to take certain important decisions at critical times, and thus, they did not prevent the spread of the disease effectively.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls on biosecurity on pig establishments are carried out with appropriate frequency, in particular to ensure that requirements for derogations of movements of porcine animals kept in restricted zones I, II and III as laid down in Article 16 (1), point b) are complied with, taking into account biosecurity requirements as laid down in Annex III of Regulation (EU) 2023/594. citations.text: A recent Ministerial decree in 2022 has consolidated biosecurity rules for pig establishments, taking into account requirements of the EU ASF Regulation and strengthening protection of establishments against the infection. A new dedicated IT tool is available for categorisation of establishments and selection for official controls. The system is however still under development, and the frequency of regular official controls to verify operators' compliance is not clear yet, even for restricted and infected zones. Hence results from the above efforts to increase biosecurity are yet to yield.

The laboratory network provides reliable and consistent support for the implementation of the ASF control programme. The competent authorities need to ensure that all regional laboratories which carry out confirmatory tests are accredited for the test method used as required by Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Audits of the Regional authorities on the implementation of control measures take place but focus more on procedures rather than on operational activities, thus not fully ensuring that official controls ensure compliance with animal health regulations.

Data submitted on the inspections carried out show that the competent authorities followed so far in general the 1 % approach which is the same as 11 Repopulation will for official controls on registration and identification. One Region only be allowed (Piedmonte) visited had increased it to 3% in the free zone, other Regions when biosecurity reportedly apply still higher frequencies. In the restricted zones, the competent requirements are authorities had carried out inspections on biosecurity in all establishments, as adhered to. requested by the decrees of the Ministry of Health, without delay. It remained unclear however, at the time of the audit what the system of regular official controls, in particular in restricted zone I and in the free area, would be in the future.

The results of the biosecurity inspections varied in the Regions visited, some local health units (ASLs) reported a high number of non-compliances in 2022, following the new rules, but also in 2023. The audit team visited one newly registered establishment, and one existing, located in restricted zone II, which had upgraded their biosecurity measures to the standard as requested following official controls. In both cases, the authorities had approved the biosecurity plans before the establishments could start or continue their activities; the audit team assessed that both plans were generally in compliance with Annex III of Regulation (EU) 2023/594.

The official controls are carried out supported by, in general, adequate documented procedures. Certain shortcomings were noted concerning the implementation of the procedures for registration/approval and the interpretation of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.

In respect of registration of establishments and activities subject to registration, the audit team noted that the guidance document on Regulations (EC) Nos 852/2004 and 853/2004, issued by the national competent authority both to assist operators requesting registration/approval of their facilities and to assist officials in the performance of their official tasks, is not aligned with the EU rules, as follows: a. Contrary to point 4(b) of Section VIII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Italy considers the removal of skin of the fish (Selachii species) as an operation (associated operation) included in the primary production sector. This type of activity should only be allowed on approved vessels/establishments. b. Contrary to point 4(b) of Section VIII of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, Italy considers that the associated operations allowed on board fishing vessels can also be carried out in an establishment of an aquaculture farm as a primary production activity and covered solely by the registration of the aquaculture farm. An establishment of an aquaculture farm can perform this type of activities only if that establishment has been approved as required by Article 4(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. citations.text: This annual plan determines the total number of tests that each region must carry out on fishery products. The total number of tests is divided as follows: 45% of tests performed from samples taken from the production sector and 45% from the distribution sector. The remaining 10% are, by default, to be taken from the distribution sector, but each region decides the best allocation of these 10%.

The competent authority of the region visited provided the audit team with the regional sampling plan stemming from the national plan. The samples assigned to the region are then distributed by the different ASLs. The audit team noted that, in cases that could not be justified by the small number of samples, or the specificity of the parameter (e.g. environmental contaminants), the national instruction to distribute 45% of the samples at production and 45% at distribution, has not been followed. As examples, testing for histamine is only carried out on samples from the distribution sector, and the same for testing for Listeria monocytogenes in ready-to-eat food. Conclusions on official controls of fishery products

However, the non-adherence by the regional authorities to the distribution of samples defined by the national authority casts doubt on the complete adequacy of the regional control plan to achieve the objectives of the official controls set in the EU food law (verification of compliance with the applicable rules).

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should ensure that the laboratories designated to test official control samples use analytical methods that comply with the EU rules concerning the performance criteria of the methods, defined in table 5 of point C.3.3.1. of part C of the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 333/2007, in order to guarantee the reliability of the test results.

citations.text: With regard to the analytical methods for testing official control samples for the quantification of the level of heavy metals, the audit team noted that for one IZS the limit of detection of the method for cadmium does not respect the EU rules, in particular table 5 of point C.3.3.1 of Part C of the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 333/2007. The same finding was noted for another IZS in the case of the limit of detection for the method for lead.

However, and specifically for the testing of fishery products for cadmium in one IZS and for lead in one IZS, that reliability can be compromised by EU rules not being respected in relation to the EU rules on the limits of detection of the analytical methods used for that testing.
