audits.title: evaluate the implementation of official controls on animal by-products (ABP) and derived products (DP)

recommendations.text: To ensure that the lists of approved petfood plants are kept up- to-date and contain all required information.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 47(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, Article 20a(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011

citations.text: The audit team noted that the national list of approved and registered petfood plants published on the Ministry of Health website did not contain information on the product types placed on the market, contrary to the Commission technical specifications (4) and the requirements of Article 20a(a) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

The list of Italian petfood plants on the Commission's Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES NT) was not up to date; 125 plants were listed vs. 184 on the website of the Ministry of Health. Thus, the requirements of Article 20a(b) of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 are not met.

Based on the review of documents submitted by the Ministry of Health, the audit team noted that, in several regions, petfood plants that had stopped their activities for a long while were still present on the published list of petfood plants, despite several reminders sent by the Ministry of Health to RVS to ensure the timely removal of inactive operators from the national lists. Therefore, it cannot be considered that the list of petfood plant is kept up-to-date as required by Article 47(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. Conclusions on registration, approval, and listing

There are arrangements in place for the registration, approval, and listing which should provide assurances that the operators active along the chain of petfood production are known and thus facilitate the implementation of official controls throughout this supply chain. However, the fact that the registration/approval data are not kept up to date (as evidenced by the disparity between the data in the national list and TRACES-NT), weakens an otherwise satisfactory system for approval and registration. 5.2.2 Planning of official controls

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls in ABP processing plants and petfood manufacturing plants are effective in verifying operator compliance with applicable requirements regarding the suitability of raw material used (including the presence and completeness of commercial docu- ments for such raw material), operators' own checks and hygienic conditions of production.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 in conjunc- tion with Article 4(3), Articles 21(2), Article 25(1)(a), Article 31(1)(a) and 35(aa)(iii) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and Point 6 of Chap- ter II of Annex XIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011

citations.text: In both of the raw petfood plants, the operators had received (and accepted) incomplete commercial documents for incoming Category 3 materials. These documents did not contain information demonstrating that, as required by Article 35(aa)(iii) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, the ABP consisted of exclusively Category 3 material of the sub- categories defined in Article 10(a),(b)(i) and/or (ii) of the said Regulation, which are the only sub-categories allowed for the production of raw petfood in the EU.
The internal procedures of both operators did not mention any restrictions on the sub- categories of Category 3 material that could be used for production of raw petfood.

In one of the raw petfood plants, some raw materials of animal origin were not accom- panied by any ABP commercial documentation, contrary to the requirements of Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The operator stated that such raw materials were considered food and, in its opinion, ABP documentation was not necessary. How- ever, by definition, in accordance with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, these raw materials are ABP and must be accompanied by ABP commercial documents.

The incompleteness and absence of commercial documentation for ABP dispatched from food establishments (such as slaughterhouses and cutting plants) is also an indica- tion that official controls at food business operators where these ABP originate have not effectively verified compliance with ABP requirements. 5.2.3.2 Official controls in ABP plants

Firstly, storage conditions for PAP destined for use in petfood were unhygienic. Before bagging or dispatch in bulk, PAP were stored on an unclean and damaged concrete floor contrary to the requirements of Article 25(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and point C of Section I of Chapter II of Annex X to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

Secondly, Category 3 material used for the production of PAP were stored on the floor before processing, mixed with dirt from cleaning operations. Pits in which these materi- als were subsequently placed prior to their processing, were unclean and with remains of ABP from previous days. The raw materials used in production during the visit were highly contaminated with foreign bodies and therefore they should have been catego- rised as Category 2 material (Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009) and not used for production of PAP (Article 31(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009). Company staff were removing foreign bodies from the raw materials before their shredding but, in spite of these measures, foreign bodies were still present in the shredded material sent to 8 cookers for their processing into PAP. Foreign bodies were also present in the final product (PAP). Representatives of the Ministry of Health informed the audit team that instructions regarding the need to monitor (and ensure absence of) foreign bodies in ABP from the food sector had been circulated to the RVS and ASL, and also to the in- dustry, on several occasions.

Thirdly, materials recovered from cleaning the processing equipment were recycled into processing. Such materials included sludge and remains of spoiled ABP that stayed in the unclean processing equipment for several days. Such materials should have been categorised as Category 2 material (Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009) and not used for production of PAP (Article 31(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009).

In the raw petfood plants visited, the reports of the inspections reviewed by the audit team made no reference to the following serious non-compliances. In one of the plants, the operator did not carry out own testing for Enterobacteriaceae (hygiene criteria). On- ly a subset of this family of microorganisms was tested for. Testing by operator of raw petfood for Enterobacteriaceae is a requirement under EU rules (Point 6 of Chapter II of Annex XIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011) as it provides an assessment of the overall hygienic conditions at the plant. The same operator carried out analyses for Salmonella in raw petfood but only on one sample, instead of five, contrary to the aforementioned requirements of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

In the other plant, the audit team reviewed the operator's own-check Enterobacteriaceae results from 2023 to date. Several results were non-compliant (there were three or more samples with a bacterial count between 500 and 5000 colony forming units in 1 gramme of raw petfood). However, the operator did not consider the results to be non-compliant and therefore did not take any corrective actions to improve the hygienic conditions of the process, contrary to the requirement of Point 6 of Chapter II of Annex XIII to Regu- lation (EU) No 142/2011. This was not detected during official inspections carried out in that plant.

Notwithstanding these positive aspects, the official controls are not effective in verify- ing operator compliance with some of the applicable requirements as evidenced by the serious non-compliances identified by the audit team in establishments and plants visit- ed. These concerned the unsuitability of raw material used for the production of petfood (including lack of or incomplete commercial documents for any such raw material used), serious breaches of hygiene rules and absence of required own-testing of final product or absence of corrective actions by the operators following non-compliant own- testing results.

recommendations.text: To ensure that raw fish and other fish derived ABP is not being used in the manufacturing of raw petfood.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 4(3) and Article 35(a)(iii) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009

citations.text: The audit team noted that ABP consisting of raw fish were used for production of raw petfood in the two petfood plants visited. In January 2024, the Ministry of Health made use of a derogation laid down in Article 16(g) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 to au- thorise the use of raw fish and other fish derived ABP, under specific conditions and on- ly for direct sale to the final consumer within the territory of Italy. ABP from raw fish to 9 be used in the manufacture of raw petfood must not show signs of alterations (from an organoleptic point of view) and be subjected to freezing at -20°C for at least 24 hours.

For petfood placed on the market, Article 35(a)(iii) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 states that raw petfood must derive only from material referred to in Article 10(a) and (b)(i) and (ii) of that Regulation. As fish-derived ABP fall under Article 10(i) and (j), they cannot be used for the production of raw petfood in an approved petfood plant. 5.2.3.3 Actions taken in the event of non-compliance and follow-up
The competent authority has allowed the use of raw fish and ABP derived from fish for the manufacture of raw petfood at approved petfood plants, contrary to the EU require- ments.

audits.title: evaluate the system of official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union and verification of compliance of border control posts with European Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that documentary checks, identity checks and physical checks on con- signments of goods of animal origin are carried out in accordance with legisla- tion applicable to the performance of those checks, and that the Common Health Entry Document is duly completed by the competent authorities to record the outcome of official controls performed and any decisions taken on that basis. Legal requirements: Articles 2(3), 3(2) and 4(4) and point 4(b) of Annex II to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130, Article 40(2)(b)(ii) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715 and Article 3(2)(b) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2074

citations.text: The audit team evaluated selected CHEDs validated for consignments in transit to ap- proved warehouses and CHEDs issued consequently for consignments split after storage in transit to BCPs of exit. The audit team noted that in some of those CHEDs, the goods have been described with the customs nomenclature (CN) code 9930 for goods delivered to vessels and aircraft rather than the relevant CN code for each of the commodities men- tioned in the accompanying official certificate according to the model referred to in Part I of the Annex to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2128.

The audit team further noted that, based on data in TRACES-NT for 2023 and 2024, the majority of CHEDs issued for non-conforming goods intended either for storage in ap- proved warehouses, ship supply vessels leaving the EU, or exit at BCPs for ship supply vessels located in a third country port relied on the use of the CN code 9930, which is not 10 in line with Article 40(1) and Part I of Annex II to Commission Implementing Regula- tion (EU) 2019/1715 and does not allow traceability of goods in transit.

Whilst the Ministry of Health stated that identity checks are full checks or limited to a checks on the seals on containers or means of transport, the audit team noted that, at the BCP with the highest throughput of consignments of goods of animal origin, identity checks are being carried out digitally based on information provided by the terminal op- erator on such consignments, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. The Ministry of Health was not able to explain to the audit team how this digital control system operated. The Ministry of Health took action during the audit to discontinue this method and resume visual seal checks by staff at the BCP, albeit with stated reservations on its ability to fully implement those identity checks with current staff resources given the volume of containers arriving at this port.

During the visit to the one port BCP, the audit team noted that the minimum number of items or packages in a consignment selected for identity checks and physical checks of goods of animal origin intended for human consumption were not in line with Articles 3(2) and 4(4) and point 4(b) of Annex II to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130 and documented procedures.

The audit team evaluated five CHEDs for consignment of goods of animal origin re- entering the EU, of which three consignments were authorised to re-enter in compliance with Articles 2 and 3 of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2074. The re- maining two consignments were not accompanied by the official declaration referred to in Article 3(2)(b) of the same Regulation. In addition, both consignments underwent identity checks by means of a seal check in the absence of an official seal, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. 5.2.4.3 Checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin and food contact materials

The audit team identified that for several consignments of goods of animal origin evalu- ated, the CHEDs were not completed correctly in Part II by the competent authority, which is not in line with Article 40(2)(b)(ii) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1715. In six cases, the type of identity check was not indicated, in a further two cases the documentary check was considered satisfactory whilst the documentation ac- companying the consignment was not, in another case the physical check was considered satisfactory whilst the laboratory test results of a suspect sample were unfavourable, and the laboratory test results were only partly entered for another suspect sample. Conclusions on the implementation of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU

The official controls on consignments of categories of animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Italy are generally carried out in line with relevant EU legislation, documented procedures and planned arrangements. However, shortcomings were identi- fied in the performance of official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin, of which the digital seal checks at one BCP was the most significant, and in decisions taken on consignments of goods of animal origin. In addition, for certain products of non- animal origin, the required frequency rate of identity and physical checks was not im- plemented at a small number of BCPs. These shortcomings collectively undermine the overall effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compli- ant consignments of animals and goods enter the EU.

recommendations.text: To ensure that identity and physical checks on consignments of goods of non- animal origin are carried out at the set frequency for goods subject to measures requiring a temporary increase of official controls or emergency measures re- spectively. Legal requirements: Articles 6 and 8 of, and Annexes I and II to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793

citations.text: However, the audit team further noted, based on the same data, that the identity and physical checks on consignments of certain goods of non-animal origin subject to tempo- rary or emergency measures set out in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 had, in some cases, not been carried out in line with the minimum frequency rates required by Articles 6 and 8 and Annexes I and II to that Regulation. The majority of the shortfalls in implementation of the required frequency rates concerned a small number of BCPs only. 5.2.5 Decisions on consignments and follow-up

The official controls on consignments of categories of animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Italy are generally carried out in line with relevant EU legislation, documented procedures and planned arrangements. However, shortcomings were identi- fied in the performance of official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin, of which the digital seal checks at one BCP was the most significant, and in decisions taken on consignments of goods of animal origin. In addition, for certain products of non- animal origin, the required frequency rate of identity and physical checks was not im- plemented at a small number of BCPs. These shortcomings collectively undermine the overall effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls to ensure that only compli- ant consignments of animals and goods enter the EU.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the border control posts and control points comply with the mini- mum requirements for the categories of goods for which the post has been desig- nated and are only listed if compliant with those requirements. Legal requirements: Articles 53(1)(a), 62(1), 63(1) and 64(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3, 4, 6 and 8 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the port BCPs Livorno, La Spezia, Genova and Vado Ligure Savona, including seven inspection centres thereof visited, were not compliant with cer- tain minimum requirements for BCPs laid down in Article 64(3) of the OCR and Articles 3, 4, 6 and 8 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014, for the categories of goods for which they had been designated.

The audit team noted the following non-compliances at the four port BCPs Livorno, La Spezia, Genova and Vado Ligure Savona, including seven inspection centres thereof vis- ited, designated for categories of goods of animal and non-animal origin: · the unloading facilities at the BCP La Spezia port, the inspection centres Calata San- ità (Terminal Sech) and Calata Massaua (Terminal Rebora) at the BCP Genova port and the inspection centre Terminal Lorenzini at the BCP Livorno port were con- structed in such a way that containers with consignments of goods cannot be appro- priately placed with handling equipment and consequently unloaded under a roof, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. · the unloading and storage rooms of the inspection centre Terminal Lorenzini at the BCP Livorno port were poorly maintained and consequently, not easy to clean or disinfect, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In addition, the inspection rooms at that centre were not appropriately equipped to examine and sample consignments, which is not in line with Article 4(2) of that Regulation. · the inspection centre PNAO at the BCP Livorno port did not have adequate drainage in the unloading, inspection and storage areas or rooms, which is not in line with Ar- ticle 3(2) and (3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. · at the inspection centre Terminal San Giorgio at the BCP Genova port, the inspec- tion room did not have a supply of hot and cold running water, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(b) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. The BCP staff confirmed that inspection of goods takes place in part of the unloading area adjacent to the inspection room which does have these facilities. The Ministry of Health took action during the audit and modified the layout to include the area adjacent to the in- spection room as part of the inspection facilities. · in the case of the BCP Vado Ligure Savona port, shortcomings were identified by the Ministry of Health at the facilities for controls on consignments of goods of ani- 16 mal and non-animal origin. Its control report concluded that the facilities were non- compliant for serious health reasons, but the Ministry of Health had not taken any corrective actions such as the withdrawal or suspension of designation of the BCP in line with Articles 62(1) and 63(1) of the OCR respectively. The audit team con- firmed that the facilities were not compliant with the requirements laid down in Ar- ticles 3, 4, 6 and 8 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. The audit team vis- ited the new facilities at this BCP intended for goods of animal origin, which were not yet equipped, and which were found not to meet the minimum requirements for BCPs mainly due to the fitting of some walls, floors and ceilings which were not easy to clean and disinfect, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of that Regulation.

The audit team visited two control points designated by the competent authority for the performance of identity and physical checks on consignments of non-animal origin and noted that neither control points were compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs, which is not in line with Articles 53(1)(a) of the OCR. In particular: · at one control point, part of the storage area adjacent to the inspection room is also used for the inspection of goods and did not have a supply of hot and cold running water and facilities for washing and drying hands which is not in line with Article 3(1)(b) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. · at the second control point, the audit team noted that part of the unloading area was rusty with flaking paint and there were cracks in the floors, and storage rooms were not maintained. The floors, walls, ceilings and fittings of the unloading area and storage rooms were dirty. The unloading area had pooled water in one part and was used to store cleaning and other equipment which was visibly soiled. The audit team noted that these facilities were therefore not easy to clean or disinfect, which is not in line with Article 3(2) and (3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In addition, two uncovered waste containers were present at one open unloading bay with decomposing fruit which had attracted fruit flies and other insects which were consequently also present in the internal facilities. Evidence of rodents was also not- ed in one storage room. The audit team therefore noted that the arrangements in place do not ensure compliance with relevant biosecurity standards required by Arti- cle 64(3)(i) of the OCR. The Ministry of Health took action during the audit and suspended the designation of this control point.

The BCPs, including inspection centres thereof, and two control points visited were found to be not compliant with certain minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of goods for which they had been designated.

audits.title: Evaluate the system of official controls relating to microbial safety of food of non-animal origin

recommendations.text: Ensure that, in all regions, the registration system of farms (primary producers of food of non-animal origin) allows identification of farms with productions of high microbiological risk products (as per EFSA opinions) in order to comply with the requirements of risk-based official controls as per Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: However, these registers do not include relevant information on the crops being grown. Different strategies have been followed by the regional CAs to overcome the lack of detailed information in the register: · In some cases, regional CAs have got access to the data bases of the Chambers of Commerce. These databases only provide for general activity groups, which in the case of primary production comprises permanent crops and other general activities such as "cereals", or "horticulture". · In Sicily, there are 53 000 farms dedicated to primary production of FNAO, including permanent and non-permanent crops. The regional CAs of Sicily indicated that 8 000 farms were dedicated to horticulture. In Campania, CAs indicated that there were 39 000 farms of non-permanent crops. These systems do not provide enough information to CAs to identify growers producing crops with a higher microbiological risk. Therefore, recommendations No 4 and 5 of the DG(SANTE) 2021-7175 audit report have not been addressed. · In other cases, as for example in Veneto and Emilia Romagna, CAs have an agreement with the Department of Agriculture which provides accurate information on the type of crops grown in the farms. The information provided is updated around every 18 months. CAs of Veneto indicated that this frequency of exchanges will be increased to every six months. The information of the register of the Department of Agriculture indicates the type of crop except for seeds for sprouting, which are not identified as such. 7

There are procedures in place to ensure that FBOs of FNAO are registered and are known to CAs which have the possibility to access to different sources of registers. However, the lack of direct access to relevant information and proper coordination between CAs prevents regional and therefore, local CAs to avail updated information of farms growing crops potentially posing higher microbial risk, thus limiting the adequate prioritisation of official controls in accordance with Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the registration system of primary producers of food of non-animal origin allows for the identification of farms producing seeds for sprouting, in order to comply with the requirements of risk-based official controls as per Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Regarding seeds for sprouting, the current available registers do not provide information on the farms producing this type of product. To overcome this lack of information, one local SIAN has requested to a FBO placing seeds for sprouting in the market the list of farms supplying seeds for sprouting located in the territory under the remit of the SIAN. However, this was an initiative of the local SIAN that it has not been systematically taken by the rest of local, regional or central CAs to identify the farms producing seeds for sprouting. Processors

The lack of information on farms growing seeds for sprouting, together with the fact that CAs do not enforce the registration of such FBOs, hinders the capacity of CAs to prioritise official controls to these FBOs in accordance with Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 to verify compliance with applicable hygiene rules during primary production pre-during and post-harvest. 8

There is not a reliable official system to identify growers producing seeds for sprouting, and therefore they are not subject to official controls to verify compliance with hygiene requirements to address microbiological risks. In some cases, this lack of official control is mitigated by controls carried out by the downstream FBO (the one who place the seeds on the 14 market) on its suppliers of seeds for sprouting.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the existing registration system for food business operators placing seeds for sprouting on the market includes all food business operators involved in this activity in order to comply with the requirements of risk-based official controls as per Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Regarding operators placing seeds for sprouting on the market, MoH has incorporated this type of FBOs in the SINTESIS database (Integrated System for Trade, Imports and Structures - Sistema Integrato per gli Scambi, le Importazioni e le Strutture). SINTESIS is the register of Italian establishments for the production of food of animal origin which in 2013 was extended to other categories of establishments to cover, among others, sprout-producing establishments, and FBOs producing seeds for sprouting. At the time of the audit, there were nine FBOs registered as producers of seeds for sprouting. However, the audit gathered evidence demonstrating that there are other FBOs placing seeds for sprouting on the market that are not included in the SINTESIS register (see paragraphs 53 and 57). Approval of sprout-producing establishments

During visits to the sprout-producing establishments, inspectors overlooked some aspects: · The health certificate associated to a batch of seeds of mungo beans (Vigna radiata) was not authentic, as the stamp and signature was not from CAs but from the exporter. · CAs have requested the FBO to conduct a preliminary test of a new batch of seed before resuming production. Instead, at the time of the visit the production was at full capacity and inspectors accepted a sample from the production as valid for the preliminary test. · The testing reports of sprouts provided by the FBO shows that only one subsample has been taken for STEC. This is not in line with point 1.29 of chapter 1 on food safety criteria of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No. 2073/2005. · Final product and seeds stored in the same room · Some of the suppliers of seeds for sprouting were not included in the official list issued by MoH in the SINTESIS data base. This did not trigger any reaction of the inspectors. · To verify that the chlorine used to wash sprouts was suitable for food. · The official testing of final product was cancelled because the label indicates that sprouts were not ready to eat (RTE) and should be cooked before consumption. However, analysis for STEC in sprouts (point 1.29 of Chapter 1 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) 2073/2005) is not linked to whether the sprouts are considered RTE products or not. · Inspectors did not immediately request the FBO to remove a product affected by dripping condensation. 12 · Inspectors did not further investigate if preliminary testing was done by the FBO in line with point 3.3 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) 2073/2005, as the bags of a large batch of seeds apparently were not opened to take samples.

The audit team visited one FBO placing seeds for sprouting in the market. This FBO has an internal system in place for controlling growers producing seeds. Farms producing seeds for sprouting are bounded by contracts to the FBO placing seeds for sprouting on the market. All his growers, both producing seeds for sowing and for sprouting, are required to comply with hygiene requirements of Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. The company also purchases seeds from another Italian FBO that places seeds for sprouting on the market, which is not included in the SINTESIS list. The authorities were made aware of this "non-listed" company in previous official inspections.

CAs have not taken actions when they were aware of FBOs supplying seeds for sprouting which were not included in the official register. This, in combination with the lack of cooperation with CCA and regional CAs have prevented effective official controls in the production chain of seeds for sprouting.

recommendations.text: Ensure that in all regions, at primary production of food of non-animal origin, including seeds for sprouting, competent authorities perform official controls on microbiological risks also at the stage of pre-harvest and during harvest, on a risk basis as required by Article 1(2)(a) in conjunction with Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

However, the lack of direct access to relevant information and proper coordination between CAs prevents regional and therefore, local CAs to avail updated information of farms growing crops potentially posing higher microbial risk, thus limiting the adequate prioritisation of official controls in accordance with Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Sicily has communicated to the local ASLs the plan for official controls on primary production of FNAO for 2025. A total of 38 official controls are planned for one ASL (at the time of the audit, 2 had been carried out), and 45 (of which 41 should be greenhouses) for a second ASL. According to the regional CAs, these controls are to be carried out to crops posing a higher microbial risk, as for EFSA opinions.

In Campania, there are 39 000 classified as non-permanent crops (therefore including cereals, fruits and vegetables). There is not in place a plan for official controls related to microbial risk on FNAO primary production. The new checklist including microbial risks was introduced in October 2024 to be used for the planned controls on chemical risks (around 40 controls per year, equivalent to 0,1% of the number of farms). However, a low number of inspections have taken place using this new checklist, and mainly related to farms involved in RASFF notifications.

For primary production, there is no uniformity in the planning and implementation of official controls. In some regions CAs addressed adequately the recommendations of the 2021 DG Health and Food Safety audit report allowing them to conduct appropriate risk-based controls following clear guidelines and checklists. The delay in implementing the necessary measures in other regions, compromises the risk-based official controls system and hinders the effectiveness of such controls.

recommendations.text: Ensure that, in all regions, inspectors involved in official controls acquired adequate knowledge by providing them with the relevant tools (i.e. training and technical support, including sufficiently detailed checklists) in order to ensure effective and appropriate official controls as required by Article 5(1)(e)(f) and 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Regions are responsible for planning and organising training of staff, both for regions and their ASLs. Regarding specific training on primary production of FNAO, the audit team observed significant differences in the visited regions. In Veneto, since the previous audit, specific courses on official controls of primary production have been organised every year. The courses included an on-site component to conduct inspections on production farms, and attendees were subject to a written test at the end of the course to assess the acquired capacities of staff.

Opposite to this situation, in Sicily or Campania, no training has taken place regarding official controls in primary production of FNAO. In Sicily, the first training in the matter is planned for September 2025. As seen in paragraphs 42, 44 and 46, both regions had started to conduct inspections at primary production including microbiological risks in October 2024 (Campania) and from May 2025 in Sicily. This absence of training for staff is not in line with the Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and calls into question the effectiveness of the implementation of the action plan submitted to address recommendation No 6 of the DG (SANTE) 2021-7175 audit report.

During official inspections witnessed by the audit team, inspectors and their supervisors overlooked some critical deficiencies (e.g., risk of cross-contamination, lack of hygiene and staff misconduct). Official staff acknowledged that these deficiencies represent a risk for food safety (see paragraphs 47, 53, 59 and 62). Audit / Supervision

The level of training provided to staff performing official controls on FNAO varies significantly between regions. While some regions offer thorough and specialised training to cover new areas of official controls for Cas, other provides little to no training. This disparity in training levels compromise the effectiveness of official controls in several regions.

During the inspections witnessed by the audit team, inspectors used the new checklist and followed the guideline for primary production of FNAO. They assessed various factors, including water used for irrigation and irrigation methods, enquired about the sources of manure, and evaluated the availability of toilets, hand washing facilities for staff and hygiene protocols. However, regarding some aspects that may present a microbiological risk, the inspectors: · did not address to the presence of crates used for harvesting kept outside the greenhouses, even though harvest was not occurring at that time; · did not respond to the presence of crates for harvested products placed directly on the soil; · did not raise concerns about the FBO parking vehicles inside a warehouse where empty crates ready for packing harvested product were stored; · did not challenge the FBO to demonstrate the quantities of "certified" manure used, nor were they aware of the appropriate quantities for the size of the farm; · explained that samples had been taken for microbiological testing from living plants, rather than from products already harvested. 11

During visits to the sprout-producing establishments, inspectors overlooked some aspects: · The health certificate associated to a batch of seeds of mungo beans (Vigna radiata) was not authentic, as the stamp and signature was not from CAs but from the exporter. · CAs have requested the FBO to conduct a preliminary test of a new batch of seed before resuming production. Instead, at the time of the visit the production was at full capacity and inspectors accepted a sample from the production as valid for the preliminary test. · The testing reports of sprouts provided by the FBO shows that only one subsample has been taken for STEC. This is not in line with point 1.29 of chapter 1 on food safety criteria of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No. 2073/2005. · Final product and seeds stored in the same room · Some of the suppliers of seeds for sprouting were not included in the official list issued by MoH in the SINTESIS data base. This did not trigger any reaction of the inspectors. · To verify that the chlorine used to wash sprouts was suitable for food. · The official testing of final product was cancelled because the label indicates that sprouts were not ready to eat (RTE) and should be cooked before consumption. However, analysis for STEC in sprouts (point 1.29 of Chapter 1 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) 2073/2005) is not linked to whether the sprouts are considered RTE products or not. · Inspectors did not immediately request the FBO to remove a product affected by dripping condensation. 12 · Inspectors did not further investigate if preliminary testing was done by the FBO in line with point 3.3 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) 2073/2005, as the bags of a large batch of seeds apparently were not opened to take samples.

During the visit to the pre-cut establishment, inspectors overlooked some aspects, which were not identified in previous inspections: · Although there were designated high risk areas, there were no adequate access areas with adequate hygienic procedures to prevent contamination from dirty areas. · Staff touched a pipe on the floor and did not wash their hands before returning to handle lettuce. · Despite there were three cooling devices over the production lines, CAs have only required isolation to prevent condensation dripping from one of the devices above one line, but not the for the other two cooling units. Condensation dripping was evident over the production lines without triggering any reaction from the inspectors. · The company was cleaning the automatic weighting equipment prior to packing with high pressure water.

For primary production, there is no uniformity in the planning and implementation of official controls. In some regions CAs addressed adequately the recommendations of the 2021 DG Health and Food Safety audit report allowing them to conduct appropriate risk-based controls following clear guidelines and checklists. The delay in implementing the necessary measures in other regions, compromises the risk-based official controls system and hinders the effectiveness of such controls.

The low number of sprout-producing establishments, along with the territorial organisation of the official controls hinders the capacity of the staff conducting official controls to gain sufficient know-how and experience with the relevant requirements to this type of FBOs. This compromises the effectiveness of the official controls.

recommendations.text: Ensure that competent authorities effectively implement adequate procedures in order to verify the effectiveness of official controls over food of non-animal origin and to ensure that corrective measures are taken when shortcomings are identified, as required by Article 12(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Examples of planned audit reports were provided to the audit team: Friuli Venezia Giulia in November 2021, Sicily in 2022, Lombardy in June 2023 and Sardinia in May 2024. recommendations.text: Ensure coordination and cooperation within competent authorities, as required by Article 4(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in particular, as regards the exchange of information to properly identify the food business operators and their activities.

citations.text: Nonetheless, the audit team observed shortcomings in the cooperation between ASL, region and MoH (see paragraphs 18, 20, 30, 32, 42 and 57). Official staff and Training

Despite several RASFF notifications on seeds for sprouting (4) mentioning both FBOs placing seeds for sprouting on the market and farms producing seeds for sprouting, none of them were included by the Italian CAs in the national list of FBOs producing seeds for sprouting. MoH informed the audit team that this was due to poor cooperation between local and central CAs. This is not in line with Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

However, these registers do not include relevant information on the crops being grown. Different strategies have been followed by the regional CAs to overcome the lack of detailed information in the register: · In some cases, regional CAs have got access to the data bases of the Chambers of Commerce. These databases only provide for general activity groups, which in the case of primary production comprises permanent crops and other general activities such as "cereals", or "horticulture". · In Sicily, there are 53 000 farms dedicated to primary production of FNAO, including permanent and non-permanent crops. The regional CAs of Sicily indicated that 8 000 farms were dedicated to horticulture. In Campania, CAs indicated that there were 39 000 farms of non-permanent crops. These systems do not provide enough information to CAs to identify growers producing crops with a higher microbiological risk. Therefore, recommendations No 4 and 5 of the DG(SANTE) 2021-7175 audit report have not been addressed. · In other cases, as for example in Veneto and Emilia Romagna, CAs have an agreement with the Department of Agriculture which provides accurate information on the type of crops grown in the farms. The information provided is updated around every 18 months. CAs of Veneto indicated that this frequency of exchanges will be increased to every six months. The information of the register of the Department of Agriculture indicates the type of crop except for seeds for sprouting, which are not identified as such. 7

Regarding operators placing seeds for sprouting on the market, MoH has incorporated this type of FBOs in the SINTESIS database (Integrated System for Trade, Imports and Structures - Sistema Integrato per gli Scambi, le Importazioni e le Strutture). SINTESIS is the register of Italian establishments for the production of food of animal origin which in 2013 was extended to other categories of establishments to cover, among others, sprout-producing establishments, and FBOs producing seeds for sprouting. At the time of the audit, there were nine FBOs registered as producers of seeds for sprouting. However, the audit gathered evidence demonstrating that there are other FBOs placing seeds for sprouting on the market that are not included in the SINTESIS register (see paragraphs 53 and 57). Approval of sprout-producing establishments

In the absence of a register detailing the crops, the staff indicates that different strategies have been adopted to select high risk farms, for example by searching in internet websites of FBOs. However, due to the high number of farms in the region (around 8 000 registered as horticulture production, without distinction between products that are consumed raw and others consumed after cooking such as potatoes, aubergines, etc.), and the limited staff resources, this approach does not constitute an effective method to characterise the universe of farms that should be subject to controls.

CAs have not taken actions when they were aware of FBOs supplying seeds for sprouting which were not included in the official register. This, in combination with the lack of cooperation with CCA and regional CAs have prevented effective official controls in the production chain of seeds for sprouting.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the equipment used for planning, recording and monitoring progress of sur- veys allows the annual and multi-annual surveys to be performed efficiently and effec- tively as required by Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In the context of surveys, the CAs do not have appropriate and properly maintained facilities and equipment to perform surveys efficiently and effectively as required by Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The National Plant Health Service uses the Monitoring of Harmful Pests (MORGANA) IT system to plan and record surveys, to send samples to laboratories, and to manage the resultant data. Sixteen of the 21 RPSs input survey data directly into MORGANA, while the remaining five use their own systems and transfer relevant data into MORGANA periodically throughout the year. The MAFF explained that deficiencies in MORGANA make it very difficult to extract data from the system. As a practical example, the MAFF are unable to monitor the implementation of surveys on an ongoing basis to check progress towards annual targets or to check that 5 surveys are being done at the appropriate times of the year as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 due to these deficiencies.

At an operational level, there is clear, legally binding guidance for the planning and implementation of surveys, but deficiencies in the IT system used means that the central competent authority is unable to monitor the implementation of surveys by the regions.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the annual risk-based survey programmes for priority pests comprise a suffi- ciently high number of visual examinations, sampling and testing, as appropriate for each pest, to ensure, as far as it is possible given the respective biology of each pest and the ecoclimatic conditions, with a high degree of confidence, the timely detection of those pests as required by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

citations.text: The three RPSs met by the audit team stated that they propose survey numbers for risk- based surveys for all Union quarantine pests (including priority pests) and pests provisionally qualifying as Union quarantine pests based on available resources, rather than phytosanitary risks. The MAFF acknowledged that the majority of RPSs follow this same approach. The MAFF and CREA-DC stated that they do not have the human resources to critically analyse the survey proposals of the RPSs (in terms of numbers of planned surveys, locations for surveys and survey methodology) as foreseen under the structures described in findings 4 and 5, with the result that the proposals of the RPSs are aggregated to form the multi-annual and annual survey programmes, without any analysis to determine if the resultant national programmes comply with Article 22(2) (for Union quarantine pests) and Article 24(1) (for priority pests) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

The system for planning the multi-annual and annual survey programmes, as currently in operation, does not ensure that the resultant plans comprise a sufficient number of risk- based surveys, to be carried out in all appropriate locations, and based on sound scientific and technical principles, to ensure the timely detection of any outbreaks of these pests.

The multi-annual risk-based survey programme is drawn up by the CREA-DC based on proposals from the RPSs. CREA-DC explained that annual survey plans are also drawn up using this approach. Due to the weaknesses described in finding 9, the resultant risk- based (as distinct from statistically-based) survey programmes for Union quarantine pests and pests provisionally qualifying as Union quarantine pests are not risk-based, not carried out in all appropriate locations, nor based on sound scientific and technical principles as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. In addition, in the case of priority pests, surveys do not include a sufficiently high number of visual examinations, sampling and testing, to ensure, as far as it is possible given the respective biology of each priority pest and the ecoclimatic conditions, with a high degree of confidence, the timely detection of those pests as required by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, and are not conducted in line with pest-specific legislation.

The number of planned and completed visual examinations and traps under the S. frugiperda risk-based survey programme in Italy (as recorded in MORGANA) are summarised in Table 1. CREA-DC and the three RPSs met by the audit team stated that visual examinations refer exclusively to examining plants, rather than examining the contents of traps. The planned numbers and types (visual examinations or traps) of surveys are based on the proposals of the RPSs. The three RPSs met by the audit team acknowledged that their proposed survey numbers for S. frugiperda are based on the available resources as described in finding 9. Table 1. Surveys are not planned (and subsequently implemented) based on risk as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and by Article 3(2)(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134. Article 3(2)(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 requires MS to conduct risk-based surveys in line with the the EFSA pest survey card, in particular at areas where host plants enter the EU, where they are handled and repacked, and where their waste is disposed of, at airports and seaports, and at nurseries, garden centres and retail shops, as appropriate. The EFSA pest survey card suggests placing traps in fields of host plants and at storage and handling facilities dealing with host plants. The EFSA pest survey card indicates that S. frugiperda can establish in four regions of Italy ­ Calabria, Campania, Sardinia and Sicily, with transient populations possible in other regions. In total, 217 traps were planned in Italy in 2024, but just 35 of these, were in the four regions of Italy where the pest can establish. Sardinia planned 30 traps, Campania planned five, and both Calabria and Sicily planned zero traps. On the other hand, some regions such as Emilia-Romagna (30), Lombardy (42), Piedmont (20), Tuscany (10) and 12 Veneto (10) have relatively higher numbers of traps given that the EFSA pest survey card indicates that the pest cannot establish in these regions. The MAFF explained that these disparities are due to the limited human resources to conduct surveys in some regions, and the lack of resources in MAFF/CREA-DC to analyse the data and seek changes to the RPSs proposals to ensure a consistent distribution of surveys based on phytosanitary risk.

Sicily has 4 000 ha of tomatoes and 1 400 ha of peppers and aubergines. Solanum lycopersicum L. (tomatoes) are listed as host plants in Annex I, while Capsicum L. (peppers) are listed as specified plants in Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134. It has approximately 5 000 nurseries. It also has five international airports (four civilian and one military) and four commercial seaports. The RPS in Sicily has not determined the number of traps needed, but in July 2025, it established two traps and had conducted three visual examinations at the time of the audit in September. Calabria has 1 500 ha of tomatoes and almost 400 nurseries. It has three international airports and four commercial seaports. In the 2021-2025 multi-annual survey programme, Calabria planned no surveys of any type for S. frugiperda, despite being one of the four regions of Italy where the pest can establish. In 2025, the RPS in Calabria noted this omission and had installed five traps and completed 10 visual examinations by the time of the audit but had not yet determined the number of traps needed based on risk. Lazio grows about 9 500 ha of Zea maize L. (maize) (a specified plant) and about 24 000 ha of vegetables, which include Solanum melongena L. (aubergines) (a specified plant) and peppers. Lazio has about 450 nurseries, two international airports and one seaport. In both 2024 and 2025, the RPS installed three traps for S. frugiperda. In all three cases, the RPSs acknowledged that this level of trapping is not sufficient to address the phytosanitary risk as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and by Article 3(2)(a) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134.

Surveys for S. frugiperda are not planned based on the scientific and technical information referred to in the EFSA pest survey card as required by Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1134. The EFSA pest survey card for S. frugiperda clearly states that "detection surveys to substantiate pest freedom should be based on a trapping strategy" while Article 3(3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134 states that surveys shall consists of traps, and where appropriate, visual examinations. In both 2024 and 2025, approximately 1 000 - 1 100 visual examinations and 220 traps were planned throughout Italy for S. frugiperda. The three RPSs met by the audit team explained that they prioritise visual examinations during which inspectors can observe multiple pests during a single visit, instead of traps which are pest specific and require monitoring on an ongoing basis. This overall approach of focusing on visual examinations rather than traps is in conflict with the EFSA Pest Survey Card (which MS are obliged to follow under Article 3(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134) and Article 3(3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1134. 13 Planning annual risk-based survey programmes for A. ludens, B. dorsalis, B. zonata and R. pomonella

Surveys for B. dorsalis and B. zonata are not planned based on "the scientific and technical information" in the EFSA pest survey cards as required by Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2025/311. Both pest survey cards clearly state that "trapping is the recommended method for surveillance and detection". In addition, Article 3(2)(c) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/311 states that surveys for B. dorsalis and B. zonata shall be conducted by trapping and makes no reference to visual examinations in the case of routine surveys. Finally, the OTSS guidance documents for B. dorsalis and B. zonata state that surveys should be predominantly based on monitoring with traps.

In the 2021-2024 period, the ratio of traps to visual examinations for B. dorsalis (detailed in Table 2) ranged from 1:6 to 1:10 at national level. The ratio of traps to visual examinations is broadly similar for B. zonata and for other years. The three RPSs met by the audit team explained that they prioritise visual inspections due to a lack of staff. They explained that inspectors can observe up to 30 pests in fruit orchards in a single visit. On 14 the other hand, traps are pest specific, and they plan to check them every 7-10 days, which is much more demanding on staff resources. However, they acknowledged that it is not possible to identify the four relevant species of fruit flies by visual examination in the field but explained that these visual examinations are useful to assess the general health status of the plants.

Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2025/311 requires surveys for B. dorsalis and B. zonata to be based on EFSA's General guidelines for statistically sound and risk-based surveys and the scientific and technical information referred to in relevant EFSA pest survey cards. The EFSA pest survey card for B. dorsalis identifies citrus and prunus species (particularly peach and nectarine) as the primary host species for detection surveys (these are also listed as host plants in Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2025/311). Sicily has about 70 000 ha of these host plants (62 000 ha citrus and 7 000 ha of peaches and nectarine). Calabria has about 35 000 ha (32 000 ha citrus and 3 200 ha of peaches and nectarines). Finally, Lazio has about 1 500 ha (800 ha citrus, 600 ha peaches and 50 ha nectarines). The EFSA pest survey card for B. dorsalis refers to the International Standard for Phytosanitary measures - ISPM 26 on Establishment of pest free areas for fruit flies in terms of trapping density. ISPM 26 recommends 0.25-1trap/100 ha in production areas, with higher trap densities in higher risk areas. The OTSS for B. dorsalis also uses the values in ISPM 26 for recommended trap densities. The mid-point value in this range of 1 trap/200ha is used in Table 3. The data shows that both Sicily and Calabria establish approximately 10% of the recommended number of traps, whereas Lazio region establishes a sufficient number of traps based on the EFSA pest survey card.
