The huge variation between regions in the intensity of surveys for specific pests is a result of the weakness in risk-based planning under Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 16 This results in an inconsistent approach to surveys in different regions which can be seen by comparing Lazio to Sicily and Calabria in Tables 3, 4 and 5.

While Italy's multi-annual survey programme includes all (approximately 400) relevant pests, significant weaknesses in the planning (and subsequent implementation) of the annual risk-based survey programme, including for priority pests, means that the resultant surveys do not provide a reasonable level of assurance that these pests have not established in Italy.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the surveys on Union quarantine pests and pests provisionally qualifying as Union quarantine pests are carried out in compliance with Article 22 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, and in particular that they are; - risk-based as required by Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 - based on sound scientific and technical principles and take account of scientific and technical evidence as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031

citations.text: The multi-annual risk-based survey programme is drawn up by the CREA-DC based on proposals from the RPSs. CREA-DC explained that annual survey plans are also drawn up using this approach. Due to the weaknesses described in finding 9, the resultant risk- based (as distinct from statistically-based) survey programmes for Union quarantine pests and pests provisionally qualifying as Union quarantine pests are not risk-based, not carried out in all appropriate locations, nor based on sound scientific and technical principles as required by Article 22(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. In addition, in the case of priority pests, surveys do not include a sufficiently high number of visual examinations, sampling and testing, to ensure, as far as it is possible given the respective biology of each priority pest and the ecoclimatic conditions, with a high degree of confidence, the timely detection of those pests as required by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, and are not conducted in line with pest-specific legislation.

While Italy's multi-annual survey programme includes all (approximately 400) relevant pests, significant weaknesses in the planning (and subsequent implementation) of the annual risk-based survey programme, including for priority pests, means that the resultant surveys do not provide a reasonable level of assurance that these pests have not established in Italy.

recommendations.text: Ensure that contingency plans: - are drawn up for all priority pests which are capable of entering into and becoming established in Italy as required by Article 25(1) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 - are communicated to the Commission and other Member States as required by Article 25(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (by uploading them to the internet Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (iRASFF) plant health portal as agreed by the Commission and Member States and as requested by the Commission in a let- ter to Italy in March 2024)

citations.text: At the time of the audit in September 2025, Italy had finished the process of drawing up contingency plans for just four of the 20 priority pests which are capable of entering into and becoming established in its territory on the basis of Article 25(1) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 (X. fastidiosa), Article 4 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/1584 (P. japonica) and Article 4 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/311 (B. dorsalis and B. zonata). The finalised contingency plans relate to X. fastidiosa, P. japonica and a combined contingency plan for B. dorsalis and B. zonata. (In all cases, Italy has outbreaks of the pests).

In the case of the contingency plans for the remaining 16 pests, CREA-DC had drawn up 15 of these plans, which had subsequently been approved by the NPC. The MAFF stated that the final step of the process, a series of Decrees of the MAFF to formally adopt these plans were under preparation. The NPC was working on the contingency plan for S. frugiperda, with a view to finalising it by the end of 2025.

At the time of the audit in September 2025, the four completed contingency plans were published at https://www.protezionedellepiante.it/. However, these plans had not been communicated to the Commission and to other MS, as requested by the Commission in a letter to Italy in March 2024, by uploading them to the internet Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (iRASFF) plant health portal, as required by Article 25(5) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

The failure to finalise three quarters of the required contingency plans almost two years after the legal deadline means that Italy has yet to establish a solid starting point to deal with outbreaks for the majority of priority pests.

recommendations.text: Ensure that simulation exercises take place with regard to all priority pests (except those where Italy has a notified outbreak) within a reasonable period of time and with the in- volvement of the relevant stakeholders as required by Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031.

citations.text: MS are not required to carry out simulation exercises in cases where they have recently taken measures to eradicate the pest(s) concerned, given what they have learned from the practical experiences gained ­ this applies to six of the 20 priority pests in the case of Italy. Therefore, Italy is obliged to carry out simulation exercises for 14 priority pests. The MAFF stated that Italy has not completed any simulation exercises to date and has no documented plans to conduct such exercises, which is not in line with Article 26(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 23 Conclusions on contingency plans

In the absence of contingency plans, the CAs have not conducted simulation exercises for relevant pests and therefore cannot demonstrate that they will be able to eradicate or, where appropriate, contain outbreaks of these priority pests, if and when they are detected.

audits.title: evaluate official controls on Genetically Modified Organisms

recommendations.text: Ensure that procedures and/or arrangements are in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls in the feed and seed areas as required by Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: There are insufficient procedures and arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls in the areas of feed and seed contrary to Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The MH has developed detailed checklists for conducting official controls on feed operators. The NCPAN provides sampling guidelines and sampling report templates based on the requirements laid down in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. All controls on feed operators are recorded in a harmonised manner in the Veterinary Information system for food safety (SINVSA), a national Information Technology (IT) system used by all regions. However, the checklists used for controls on feed mills do not include any specific references to controls relating to labelling and traceability of feeds containing GMOs, or the requirement for operators to have a system to avoid the adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds. Consequently, the MH could provide no documentary evidence that these requirements are systematically controlled during inspections at feed business 4 operators. The guidance/instructions for taking seed samples for GMO analysis is deficient in a number of areas as described in findings 38 and 40. Conclusions on the organisation of official controls on GMOs

The procedures and arrangements on which controls on trials and food are based provide a sound basis for ensuring the consistent implementation of legislation on GMOs in these areas. Deficiencies in the checklists used by inspectors in the feed area mean that there is no documentary evidence that controls relating to labelling, traceability and the requirement for operators to have a system to avoid the adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds are performed.

Sampling of seed lots, which forms the basis of the control system for seeds, is not performed consistently due to significant deficiencies in the procedures provided to inspectors, which compromises the reliability of the control system on seeds.

The audit team observed official sampling of a lot of maize seed by ICQRF inspectors at a seed distribution premises; · There was no single guidance document to guide the inspectors. They used an International Seed Testing Association (ISTA) guidance document to determine the number of incremental samples to take from the seed lot, and four different ICQRF documents (a Ministerial Decree of 22 December 1992 on seed sampling, the Ministerial Decree of 27 November 2003 on controlling GMOs, a Circular Letter and an ICQRF handbook) to determine how to take the sample, · The inspectors acknowledged that they used the ISTA guidance based on their own initiative, and that this guidance was not specifically referred to in any of the other guidance documents, · The seed lot comprised 1.1 tonnes (65 bags x 17kg), and the inspectors decided to take 30 incremental samples based on the ISTA guidance, · The aggregate sample was not homogenised in a methodical manner as this is not covered in any guidance provided to the inspectors. (Homogenisation of the 10 aggregate sample is a critically important step in the process as any GM seeds present are likely to be heterogeneously distributed at low levels), · The inspectors took five final samples from the aggregate sample and weighed all five samples to ensure that they were at least 1.2kg, which equates to 3 000 seeds, in line with ICQRF guidance, · The samples were sealed and the sampling recorded in a national IT system, with one of the final samples and a copy of the sample report form provided to the operator, · Of the five final samples, two go to CREA-DC, one to the operator, one is kept for expert analysis if required by a judicial authority and one is kept for analysis by CREA Bergamo, in case of a dispute on the result of the first sample.

The audit team did not observe inspectors from CREA-DC sample a seed lot, but in the course of meetings during the audit, CREA-DC stated that it follows the same procedures and takes seed samples in the same way as the ICQRF.

The audit team was unable to observe official sampling of a seed lot at the point of import as there had been no consignment imported in the few days prior to the audit. It met with the Regional Phytosanitary Services of Tuscany, which shares responsibility for taking samples of soya seed imports at Livorno port with Customs. The Regional Phytosanitary Services explained that in practice, it controls every second import of soya seeds, with Customs controlling the other 50%. The Regional Phytosanitary Services explained how it had taken a sample from a recent import of soya seeds, and based on these discussions, the audit team noted that; · The Regional Phytosanitary Services determined the number of incremental samples solely based on a Ministerial Decree of 22 December 1992, whereas ICQRF determined this based on ISTA guidance, · It had taken 24 incremental samples from a 12-tonne consignment of soya seeds packaged in 10 bulk bags. The Ministerial Decree of 22 December 1992 requires one incremental sample per 500kg, and no fewer than ten incremental samples regardless of the lot size. (This approach results in a sampling intensity which is significantly lower than when using the ISTA guidance), · The inspectors took five final samples from the aggregate sample. Of these five samples, two go to a private laboratory for analysis and three are kept in a Customs warehouse to be used if the initial sample tests positive, · In all cases where the initial sample tests positive, rather than in cases where the operator challenges the result, the Regional Phytosanitary Services of Tuscany sends two of the remaining three final samples to CREA Bergamo for confirmatory analysis. 11

There are insufficient procedures and arrangements in place to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls in the seed area as required by Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 as demonstrated by deficiencies and inconsistencies in the sampling methodologies implemented by the ICQRF and the Regional Phytosanitary Services of Tuscany as described above.

The deficiencies in checklists described in finding 11 means that there is no documentary evidence that controls determine if feed business operators comply with traceability and labelling requirements in line with Articles 24 and 25 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003 and Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003 and the obligation to have a system in place to avoid adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds in line with Article 24(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003.

While considerable operational resources are invested in controlling seeds, there are significant weaknesses relating to sampling and analysis, with the result that the control system does not provide reasonable assurances that seeds sown in Italy are free from GMOs. The importance of establishing an effective control system is demonstrated by the fact that in 2024, notwithstanding the weaknesses in controls, 3% of samples of imported soya seeds and almost 4% of soya seed samples tested under own-controls contained GMOs.

The system of official controls in feed is weakened by the failure to satisfactorily address risks linked to imported feed materials, the failure to test all samples for all relevant GM events, and the absence of documentary evidence demonstrating controls on labelling and traceability requirements, and the requirement for operators to have a system to avoid the adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds. Consequently, official controls do not provide a satisfactory level of assurance that feed marketed in Italy complies with EU requirements regarding GMOs.

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls in the feed area; Are planned taking account of identified risks, including those associated with imported feed materials and their country of origin, in line with Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires official controls to be performed on a risk basis, Are completed as planned, specifically in relation to sampling and analysis of imported feed materials, so as to fully implement the planned risk-based control programme as required by Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 2017/625.

citations.text: The NCPAN requires that at least 3% of imported feed consignments are sampled and analysed, but there are no specific targets for sampling and analysis related to GMOs, with one exception. The BCPs are instructed to sample all consignments of linseed from Canada and wheat from the United States of America (USA) due to previous detections of unauthorised GM events in these commodities from these countries. The NCPAN notes the low numbers of controls on imported feed materials in previous years and the risks associated with these products, given that GM crops are grown in many of the countries of origin. However, it does not establish targets for sampling and analysis for these materials, either at the point of entry, or during controls on the internal market. Given that Italy imports six to seven million tonnes of maize and maize derived products and about 2.5 million tonnes of soya and soya derived products each year, the failure to prioritise the sampling and analysis of imported feed materials for GMOs linked to the country of origin is not in line with Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, which requires official controls to be carried out on a risk basis.

The planned official controls for GMOs in feed fail to address risks related to imported feed materials and organic feed, thereby weakening the assurance that animal feed marketed in Italy complies with legislation on GMOs.

In 2023, ASLs took 546 samples (99% of the planned number) of animal feed (comprising 155 feed materials and 391 compound feeds) which were analysed for GMOs. In the first nine months of 2024, 246 samples (86% of the planned number up to that point of the year) of animal feeds (comprising 79 feed materials and 197 compound feeds) were sampled and analysed for GMOs. While the NCPAN clearly states that at least 50% of samples should be feed materials, in both years, less than 30% of feed samples were feed materials, thereby failing to fully implement the planned risk-based programme as required by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) No 2017/625.

The BCPs sampled just four consignments of imported feed materials for GMO analysis in 2023, which is broadly in line with other years. While the risk arising from imported feed materials is identified in the NCPAN, samples of specific matrixes from specific countries are not prioritised for sampling and analysis for GMOs, as explained in finding 19.

The system of official controls in feed is weakened by the failure to satisfactorily address risks linked to imported feed materials, the failure to test all samples for all relevant GM events, and the absence of documentary evidence demonstrating controls on labelling and traceability requirements, and the requirement for operators to have a system to avoid the adventitious presence of GMOs in non-GM feeds. Consequently, official controls do not provide a satisfactory level of assurance that feed marketed in Italy complies with EU requirements regarding GMOs.

recommendations.text: Ensure that: All laboratories used for official controls on food, feed and seeds are designated, and that laboratories are only designated if they have the expertise, equipment and infrastructure required to carry out the required analyses on samples as required by Article 37(4)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 2017/625. All designated laboratories used for official controls on food and feed can deliver analysis results in a timely manner a s required by Article 37(4)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. All designated laboratories used for official controls on seeds are accredited in accordance with the EN ISO/IEC 17025 standard for the required analysis as required by Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. All designated laboratories used for official controls on seeds use analytical methods complying with internationally recognised rules or protocols or methods developed and recommended by the EU Reference Laboratory (EURL), where these methods exist, a s required by Article 34(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The designation of laboratories used for official controls on food, feed and seed complies with Article 37(3) of Regulation (EC) No 2017/625.

citations.text: Sixteen Environmental Protection Agency (Aziende provinciale per la Protezione Ambientale and Aziende Regionali per la Protezione Ambientale) (APPA and ARPA), IZS and ASL laboratories (including the NRL) are designated to do all official analysis on GMOs in food and comprise the Italian Network of Official GMO Laboratories. Ten of the sixteen laboratories are designated to do all official analysis on GMOs in feed. These laboratories are designated by the regions and autonomous provinces, rather than the MH. The audit team examined the designation provided by the two regions visited in the course of the audit. In neither case did it include a detailed description of the tasks to be carried out and the conditions under which these should be carried out as required by Article 37(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Whereas the NRL is accredited for the analysis of 178 GM events, seven of the 16 designated official laboratories are accredited for less than 20 GM events, with a further four accredited for less than 40 GM events. The designation of these laboratories is not in line with Article 37(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which states that CAs may only designate official laboratories which have the expertise, equipment and infrastructure 16 required to carry out the required analyses. This weakness has been highlighted by the MH over several years, particularly at the regional coordination committee on GMOs.

The NRL explained that while many of the designated laboratories are accredited for a limited range of analysis, the network of laboratories can analyse for all relevant events. The NRL explained that the rationale in adopting this approach was that laboratories would focus on screening, and in case of a positive screening result, they either undertake quantitative analysis in-house or forward the sample to the NRL for further analysis. The NRL stated that approach, while ensuring all GM events are analysed, results in delays in completing analysis. In 2023, a quarter of feed samples and 10% of food samples were forwarded to the NRL following initial screening analysis by another laboratory in the network.

The NRL did not have detailed data on turnaround times for all laboratories in the network, but provided data for the NRL. This data showed an average turnaround time from sampling to the final analytical result of 39 days for GMO analysis in food and feed samples in 2023. This increased to an average of almost 80 days for positive samples. Turnaround times of this magnitude are not in line with Article 37(4)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which requires official laboratories to deliver analysis results in a timely manner.

Seed samples are analysed for the presence of GMOs in five laboratories. While these laboratories have been designated, the designations do not systematically include a detailed description of the tasks to be carried out and the conditions under which these should be carried out as required by Article 37(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. · All samples taken on the internal market, either by CREA-DC or the ICQRF, are analysed in the CREA-DC laboratory in Tavazzano. This accounts for about 50% of all seed samples tested under official controls each year. The laboratory is ISTA accredited for 13 GM events. It is not accredited for analysis of GMOs in accordance with the EN ISO/IEC 17025 standard as required by Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The laboratory plans to seek this accreditation in 2025. The laboratory screens samples for the 35S promoter and the Tnos terminator, techniques which are capable of detecting 80% of GM events in maize and 33% of GM events in soya, · All samples taken by the regional Plant Health Services of Tuscany (i.e. samples of 50% of lots of imported soya seeds) are analysed in a private laboratory. (In December 2024, the CA changed to use a different private laboratory). In both cases, the laboratory was chosen by the seed industry and subsequently designated by the CA following a check to determine if it was accredited in accordance with the EN ISO/IEC 17025 to analyse for the presence of the 35S promoter. The operator pays for the analysis even though it is conducted as part of an official control. Both laboratories test samples by screening for the 35S promoter, which 17 can be used to detect 66% of GM events in maize and less one third of GM events in soya. · All samples taken by Customs (i.e. samples of imported soya and maize seeds) are analysed by the Customs laboratory in Genoa. This laboratory is accredited for analysis of GMOs (20 methods) in accordance with the EN ISO/IEC 17025 standard as required by Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. · All samples taken by the regional Plant Health Services of Friuli-Venezia Giulia (i.e. samples of imported maize seeds) are analysed by the Phytopathology and biotechnology laboratory of the region. This laboratory is accredited in accordance with the EN ISO/IEC 17025 for screening analysis for the 35S promoter, which can be used to detect 66% of GM events in maize and less one third of GM events in soya, · Finally, in cases where the initial laboratory result indicates the presence of GM material at, or greater than, a level of 0.1%, if the operator challenges the initial laboratory result, the sample is analysed by CREA Bergamo to get the definitive result. By exception, the regional Plant Health Services of Tuscany forwards all positive samples to CREA Bergamo for confirmatory analysis.

The CREA Bergamo laboratory is explicitly named as the laboratory for confirmatory analysis of GMOs in seeds under Ministerial Decree 27 November 2003. It is only capable of analysing samples for the presence of the 35S promoter. The laboratory is not accredited for analysis of GMOs in accordance with the EN ISO/IEC 17025 standard as required by Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and does not participate in proficiency tests as required by Article 38(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

CREA-DC uses both analytical methods validated by the EU Reference Laboratory (EURL) and internally validated methods. The CREA Bergamo laboratory uses commercial test kits for its analysis. This approach is not in line with Article 34(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 which states that official laboratories should only use methods complying with internationally recognised rules or protocols or methods developed or recommended by the EURL, where these methods exist.

The deficiencies relating to designation, accreditation and the limited analytical scope of laboratories used for official controls of GMOs in seeds means that controls do not satisfy Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC, i.e. that seeds sown in Italy are free of GMOs. 18 Conclusions on the implementation of official controls

While considerable operational resources are invested in controlling seeds, there are significant weaknesses relating to sampling and analysis, with the result that the control system does not provide reasonable assurances that seeds sown in Italy are free from GMOs. The importance of establishing an effective control system is demonstrated by the fact that in 2024, notwithstanding the weaknesses in controls, 3% of samples of imported soya seeds and almost 4% of soya seed samples tested under own-controls contained GMOs.

The continued designation of official laboratories which are not capable of conducting the required analysis has resulted in significant delays in processing food and feed samples, with the result that non-compliances are not detected in a timely manner.

recommendations.text: Ensure that all feed samples are analysed for all GM events, so as to effectively verify compliance with Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003, i.e. to verify that all feed materials used in feeds not labelled as containing GM, contain either no GMOs, or contain GMOs at levels less than or equal to 0.9%.

citations.text: Under the NCPAN for the period 2021-2023, 549 feed samples were planned for GMO analysis each year. Under the NCPAN for the period 2024-2026, this has been reduced to 380 samples per year. The MH explained that under the 2021-2023 plan, 389 samples were tested for authorised GMOs only, with the remaining 160 samples tested for unauthorised GMOs only. Under the 2024-2026 plan, all samples of conventional feed are being tested for both authorised and unauthorised events, with organic samples (which typically comprise about 10-12% of samples) being tested for unauthorised 5 GMOs only. This approach of analysing organic feed samples for unauthorised events only is sufficient to meet the requirements of Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC, but it is not sufficient to meet the requirements of Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003, as authorised GM events may be present at levels greater than 0.9%, (which requires the feed to be labelled as GM, and its marketing as conventional feed), but this non-compliance would not be detected if the analysis is only for unauthorised events.

The planned official controls for GMOs in feed fail to address risks related to imported feed materials and organic feed, thereby weakening the assurance that animal feed marketed in Italy complies with legislation on GMOs.

recommendations.text: At a national strategic level; Ensure that the sampling and analysis programme for GMOs in seeds is reviewed and updated to reflect all identified risks as required by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, so that it meets the requirements of Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC. Ensure that the legal criteria to determine compliance/non-compliance of seed samples is reviewed and updated so as to provide a clear legal basis in the case of non-compliances under Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC.
recommendations.legal_basis: in the case of non-compliances under Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC.

citations.text: While maize and soya are the two most widely grown crops in Italy which have been subject to genetic modification, the MAFF acknowledged that the sampling and analysis programme for GMOs in seeds has not been reviewed, and revised as necessary, since its inception in 2003 to reflect all identified risks as required by Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Therefore, the programme does not meet the requirements of Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC, as other seeds which may be subject to GM modification, e.g. tomato, are not included in the scope of the control programme. 7 Conclusions on the planning of official controls
Official controls on seeds are based on an outdated plan that does not reflect all known risks, thereby failing to provide sufficient assurance that seeds sown in Italy are free from GMOs.

The MAFF stated that a Ministerial Decree of 27 November 2003 specifies the legal criteria for a seed sample to be deemed to contain GMOs, i.e. the sample is considered positive if the 35S promoter is detected at, or greater than, a level of 0.1%. The MAFF acknowledged that this criterion is outdated and does not meet the requirements of Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC as screening for 35S will not detect all GM events. It clarified that in practice, if any GM material is found in a seed lot at, or greater than, a level of 0.1%, it is deemed to be non-compliant. There is no tolerance for GM material in seeds in EU legislation, and therefore the presence of GM material at or above the limited of detection is a non-compliance. The operational criteria of 0.1% for all GM material adopted by MAFF is not in line with Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC, as CREA-DC, in which 50% of seed samples are tested, confirmed that its LOD is considerably lower than 0.1%.

The overall control system on seeds has not evolved to reflect new risks over the last 20 years and to define appropriate criteria to determine compliance. Finally, all available information is not used to target official controls on a risk basis.

recommendations.text: At an operational level; Ensure that in all cases of non-compliances related to seeds, that the CAs undertake actions to determine the origin and extent of the non-compliance as required by Article 138(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Ensure that the CAs consider the outcome of these investigations as a risk factor when selecting seed lots for official controls in line with Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In cases where GMOs are detected in imported seeds, the seed lot is either sent abroad or destroyed at the expense of the importer. When GMOs are detected in seeds produced in Italy, the seed lot is destroyed at the expense of the operator by incineration or exported outside the EU. The ICQRF are satisfied that the destruction of seed lots is effectively a financial penalty, and on that basis, no further sanctions applied to the operator. Neither the ICQRF nor CREA-DC undertake any action to determine the origin and extent of the non-compliance as required by Article 138(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and do not prioritise sampling and analysis of associated seeds lots or further seeds lots from the same operator in line with Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.
The failure to investigate the origin and extent of these breaches is a missed opportunity to gain information which could subsequently be used to improve the effectiveness of the control system.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the Central Competent Authorities (in the context of the overall planning of controls on seeds) and Regional/Local Competent Authorities (in the context of determining which operators and seed lots to target for sampling under their official controls) seek, and take account of, results of own controls that have been performed by the operators, or by a third party at their request, as required by Article 9(1)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 2017/625.

citations.text: It confirmed that in the case of this private sampling and analysis it uses the same sampling methodology and analytical scope as for samples under official controls. The results showed that in 2023 and 2024 just 0.3% of all maize seed lots tested positive for GMOs, but almost 4% of soya seed lots tested positive, i.e. greater than 0.1% GM material. CREA-DC reports the results of these private samples to the relevant operator. It does not report these results to ICQRF or to the MAFF, and the operator is not obliged to inform the CAs of these results under national legislation. Neither MAFF in the context of the overall planning of controls, nor CREA-DC and ICQRF in the context of determining which operators and seed lots to target for sampling under their official controls seek, and take account of this data, which is not in line with Article 9(1)(d) of Regulation (EU) No 2017/625. 5.3.3 Controls on GMOs in food and feed Legal requirements Articles 4(2), 12, 13, 16(2), 24 and 25 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003 Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003 Article 4 and Annex I to Commission Regulation (EU) No 619/2011 Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009 Article 4(5) of Directive 2001/18/EC Articles 9 and 13 of Regulation (EU) No 2017/625 12 Findings

The overall control system on seeds has not evolved to reflect new risks over the last 20 years and to define appropriate criteria to determine compliance. Finally, all available information is not used to target official controls on a risk basis.

audits.title: evaluate the implementation of official controls on medicated feed

recommendations.text: To verify that veterinary prescriptions contain all information set out in the relevant legal requirements and that manufacturing of medicated feed containing antimicrobials takes place within the period the prescription is valid.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 16(6) in conjunction with Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4, and Article 16(8).

citations.text: While all analysed inspection reports and corresponding checklists assessed prescriptions as compliant, the audit team noted that prescriptions regularly missed some mandatory information set out in Annex V to Regulation 2019/4 in accordance with Article 16(6) to the said Regulation. Missing information concerned: a) the category and age of animals, or where appropriate, weight of the animals (identification), b) the name of the active substance (designation), c) inclusion rate of the active substance (or substances), and d) the mention: `This prescription shall not be re-used'. In addition, the REV system does not allow for the possibility of inserting the prescription expiry date in case it would be shorter than that referred in Article 16(8) to the said Regulation. 7

The prescriptions also missed the information that can be added to a prescription only after a medicated feed is produced, namely the information set out in Annex V to Regulation 2019/4, in particular its: a) Point 15: With respect to supplier of the medicated feed, its name or business name and address, date of delivery, and the batch number of medicated feed delivered under the veterinary prescription, and b) Point 16: Signature of the supplier to the animal keeper or of on-farm mixer. However, the audit team noted that the medicated feed producers regularly inserted this information directly in the REV system, and once inserted, this information could not be altered.

The competent authorities' representatives explained that REV system may hold some of the missing information and in case it does not, a veterinarian issuing the prescription could insert the required information using a dedicated field or a box for entering a `free text'. The audit team confirmed that, for some missing information, such possibilities indeed exist but veterinarians issuing prescriptions did not use them or they very seldom used them. In response to the audit findings on prescriptions, yet during the audit, DGAH launched an update aiming at adding all missing information into prescription.

The vast majority of FeBOs manufacturing medicated feed complied with the requirement laid down in Article 16(8) Regulation 2019/4 on validity of prescription issued for manufacturing medicated feed containing VMP with antimicrobial(s). However, there were situations where FeBOs split the production in different days and manufactured the prescribed amount of medicated feed with few days' intervals, eventually exceeding the five-day limit of the prescription validity. Except in one feed mill visited, official controls did not consider such practice as a non-compliance.

DGAH explained that such a practice happens occasionally and mainly concerns situations where an animal keeper cannot store the full prescribed amount at once due to inadequate storage capacity. As a result, the FeBO produces the first batch of feed within the five-day validity period, with the remaining produced a few days later. To support this explanation, DGAH provided data (6) showing that in 2025, out of 23 174 prescriptions for medicated feed containing antimicrobials, 529 involved multiple shipments. Among these, only 75 prescriptions involved shipments produced and delivered beyond the five-day validity period, even though the first shipment was made within those 5 days. The audit team noted that the situation affected about 0.32% of all prescriptions for medicated feed in 2025. Despite the incidental nature of this split manufacturing practice, DGAH has committed to issue a national instruction on this aspect to ensure that the production of medicated feed takes place within the period the prescription is valid, even in case of multiple shipments. Moreover, DGAH would improve control checklists to harmonise official controls on this aspect.

Official controls verifying requirements applicable to prescriptions, overlooked that prescriptions missed some of the obligatory information and that the manufacturing of some medicated feed containing antimicrobials had taken place outside the 5 days of the prescription validity. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling
